entries.title: The Peopling of the Americas
entries.subtitle: How and when the first people arrived, a question science is still answering
entries.summary: People have lived in the Americas for well over twenty thousand years. For much of the twentieth century, scientists believed the first arrivals came roughly 13,000 years ago, walking from Asia across a land bridge exposed by low Ice Age seas. Newer evidence, above all human footprints preserved at White Sands, New Mexico, and dated to about 23,000–21,000 years ago, has pushed that date much earlier. How and when people first came remains one of the liveliest questions in archaeology.

cards.q: Why does the Peopling of the Americas matter?
cards.a: The story of American history begins not in 1492 or 1607 but more than twenty thousand years ago, with the people whose descendants built the societies Europeans later encountered.

cards.q: What led to the Peopling of the Americas?
cards.a: People moved for the same reasons as later migrants: to find food and survive. Over generations, small groups of hunters and gatherers spread into a continent of enormous ecological variety, adapting to tundra, forests, plains, deserts, and coasts.

For decades, the leading model held that people entered the interior around 13,000 years ago, once an ice-free corridor opened between the great glaciers, and that a distinctive stone-tool tradition called Clovis represented the first Americans.

entries.title: Chaco Canyon
entries.subtitle: Ceremonial center of the ancestral Pueblo world
entries.summary: In a high, dry canyon in northwestern New Mexico, ancestral Pueblo people built a center unlike anything else in North America. Beginning in the mid-800s they raised planned, multistory stone “great houses” with hundreds of rooms, aligned buildings to the sun, moon, and cardinal directions, and built long, strikingly straight roads. By about 1050 Chaco was the ceremonial, administrative, and economic center of the San Juan Basin, linked to more than 150 great houses across the region. Historians still disagree about how many people lived there and why the center declined. Pueblo and Navajo peoples regard it as a sacred place today.

quotes.text: The monumental scale of its architecture, the complexity of its community life, the high level of its community social organization, and its far-reaching commerce created a cultural vision unlike any other seen before or since.
quotes.speaker: National Park Service

quotes.text: In a society that had neither pack animals nor wheeled vehicles it is unclear what, if any, practical need could have required roads thirty feet wide.
quotes.speaker: National Park Service
quotes.context: on the debate over the Chacoan roads

cards.a: Chaco Canyon

Chaco is evidence of large-scale planning, astronomy, engineering, and regional organization in North America centuries before Europeans arrived. It also shows how historians and archaeologists can read the same ruins differently, and it remains a living sacred place for the Pueblo and Navajo peoples connected to it.

Chaco Canyon’s long winters, short growing seasons, and scant rainfall make it, in the Park Service’s words, “an unlikely place for a major center of ancestral Puebloan culture to take root and flourish.” Yet its builders used masonry techniques unique for their time.

The great houses. In the middle and late 800s the people of Chaco built Pueblo Bonito, Una Vida, and Peñasco Blanco, then Hungo Pavi, Chetro Ketl, Pueblo Alto, and others. Pueblo Bonito, built in stages between about 850 and 1150, was “the center of the Chacoan world,” a world that eventually reached across parts of present-day New Mexico, Colorado, Utah, and Arizona. The American Yawp notes that it covered more than two acres and rose five stories. Chetro Ketl, the second largest great house, covers more than three acres and includes a great kiva and an elevated plaza twelve feet above the canyon floor. The buildings were often oriented to solar, lunar, and cardinal directions, with lines of sight between them and astronomical markers, water-control features, and earthen mounds around them. Their builders imported an astonishing amount of material, including some 200,000 wooden beams, often whole ponderosa pine trunks, carried from the Chuska Mountains and Mount Taylor.

entries.title: Cahokia
entries.subtitle: The largest city in North America north of Mexico before 1492
entries.summary: Around a thousand years ago, Cahokia, near the Mississippi River in present-day Illinois, was the greatest city north of Mexico. Estimates of its population at its height range from about 10,000 to 30,000, comparable to many cities of the time in Europe and the ancient Near East, and its builders raised more than a hundred earthen mounds around great plazas. Cahokia was the leading center of the Mississippian culture, which spread across the Mississippi Valley and the Southeast.

Cahokia shows that Native North Americans built urban societies with monumental architecture, long-distance trade, and complex political organization centuries before European contact, a powerful corrective to the myth of an untouched wilderness.

Cahokia Mounds State Historic Site lies a few miles east of the Mississippi River and St. Louis. It preserves the remains of a planned city: neighborhoods of houses, large plazas, public buildings, and more than one hundred earthen mounds, the largest of which is known as Monks Mound.

Cahokia was the pre-eminent cultural, religious, and economic center of the Mississippian culture, which flourished across the Mississippi Valley and the southeastern United States between roughly 1000 and 1350.

entries.title: Mesa Verde
entries.subtitle: Cliff dwellings of the Ancestral Pueblo people
entries.summary: Mesa Verde, in southwestern Colorado, has some of the largest and best-preserved cliff dwellings in North America. People lived in the area for about 12,000 years, and Ancestral Pueblo farmers built villages on the mesa tops for centuries. Then, between about 1180 and 1300, they built stone villages tucked into the cliff alcoves, most likely to be near the springs as droughts made water scarce. Within a few decades of the late 1200s they had moved south to join communities in present-day New Mexico and Arizona, where their Pueblo and Hopi descendants live today. In 1906 Mesa Verde became the first national park created to protect cultural heritage.

Mesa Verde shows how Ancestral Pueblo communities adapted to a demanding environment, and its creation as the first national park devoted to cultural heritage began federal efforts to protect the archaeological record of Native America. It remains a sacred place for the 27 Pueblos, Tribes, and Nations connected to it.
The cliff dwellings sit in alcoves that water and frost carved out of the Cliff House Sandstone.

Before the cliff dwellings. Human history at Mesa Verde goes back about 12,000 years, to hunters who used spear points to kill mammoths, ground sloths, and giant bison. Between about 500 and 1300 CE, tens of thousands of Ancestral Pueblo people lived across the Four Corners region.

entries.title: The Haudenosaunee Confederacy
entries.subtitle: The League of the Iroquois, a union of nations governed by the Great Law of Peace
entries.summary: The Haudenosaunee, “People of the Longhouse,” are a confederacy of Native nations whose homelands lie mostly in present-day New York. According to their tradition, a prophet called the Peacemaker, helped by Aionwatha (Hiawatha), persuaded five warring nations, the Mohawk, Oneida, Onondaga, Cayuga, and Seneca, to join a Great League of Peace; the Tuscarora joined later. Each nation runs its own affairs, while a Grand Council of fifty chiefs, chosen and held to account by Clan Mothers, decides matters that concern them all. Long a major power between the French and British empires, the Confederacy was split by the American Revolution but still exists today.

cards.q: Why does the Haudenosaunee Confederacy matter?
cards.a: The Haudenosaunee Confederacy is a living system of Native self-government that long predates the United States.

The Confederacy’s own account says it “has been in place since time immemorial,” and its exact founding date is unknown. In that account, the Peacemaker was sent by the Creator to spread the good mind.

cards.q: What can it do, and what limits it?
cards.a: Each nation keeps its own council and handles its internal affairs, while the Grand Council deals with issues that affect the whole Confederacy. Within the metaphorical longhouse, the Mohawk, Seneca, and Onondaga sit as Elder Brothers and the Oneida and Cayuga as Younger Brothers. The Onondaga, the Fire Keepers, open the council.

entries.title: The Voyages of Columbus
entries.subtitle: Spanish-sponsored voyages that began sustained contact between Europe and the Americas
entries.summary: On October 12, 1492, Christopher Columbus, a Genoese sailor sailing for Spain in search of a western route to Asia, came ashore on an island in the Bahamas that its Lucayan people called Guanahani. He never reached Asia. His four voyages between 1492 and 1504 began lasting contact between Europe and the Americas, and set off the Columbian Exchange and the Spanish conquest. They also brought catastrophe to the Taíno and other peoples of the Caribbean: enslavement, forced labor, and epidemics destroyed much of the population within a few decades. Columbus is still honored by some Americans and condemned by others, and the old language of “discovery” describes only one side of the encounter.

cards.q: Why does the Voyages of Columbus matter?
cards.a: Whatever one thinks of Columbus, 1492 began lasting contact between the Eastern and Western Hemispheres. It transformed the peoples, plants, animals, and diseases of both and began a long collision of cultures.

cards.q: What led to the Voyages of Columbus?
cards.a: After being refused in several European courts, Columbus won the backing of Isabella and Ferdinand. The Spanish monarchs hoped to reach the riches of Asia without the Italian and Portuguese middlemen. The World History Encyclopedia adds that they told him to claim any land not already under a sovereign for Spain and the Catholic Church, and gave him a contract making him governor of the lands he took. Columbus himself, according to the American Yawp, was “confoundingly wrong about the size of the earth and spectacularly lucky that two large continents lurked in his path.”
First voyage (1492–1493). Columbus sailed from Spain on August 3, 1492, with three small ships, the Niña, Pinta, and Santa María, and some ninety men.

entries.title: St. Augustine
entries.subtitle: The oldest continuously occupied European-founded city in the United States
entries.summary: Spanish forces under Pedro Menéndez de Avilés founded St. Augustine on September 8, 1565, beside a Timucua village called Seloy. They came to guard the route of Spain’s treasure fleets and to destroy a nearby French Protestant colony, Fort Caroline, which they did within weeks, killing hundreds of French prisoners at an inlet afterward named Matanzas, “slaughters.” The town survived English raids and sieges behind its stone fort, the Castillo de San Marcos, and passed from Spain to Britain, back to Spain, and in 1821 to the United States.

St. Augustine is a reminder that the European colonization of what became the United States began with Spain, in the South, and that the colonial story was shaped by Spanish, French, British, African, and Indigenous peoples as much as by the English.
St. Augustine stands on the Atlantic coast of northeast Florida, south of the St. Johns River.
The Timucua. People had lived in Florida for about 12,000 years before Europeans came.

entries.title: The Roanoke Colony
entries.subtitle: England’s “Lost Colony,” 1587
entries.summary: Sponsored by Sir Walter Raleigh, England’s first attempts at a colony in North America centered on Roanoke Island in present-day North Carolina between 1584 and 1590. The last group, 118 men, women, and children led by John White, arrived in 1587. When White returned with supplies three years later, the settlers were gone, leaving the word “CROATOAN” carved into a post. What became of them has never been solved.

videos.title: What Happened to the Lost Colony at Roanoke? | National Geographic

1584–1590 · Roanoke Island, North Carolina

cards.q: Why does the Roanoke Colony matter?
cards.a: Roanoke was England’s first serious attempt at settlement in America, and its failure showed how fragile, and how dependent on Native peoples, early colonies were.

cards.q: What led to the Roanoke Colony?
cards.a: The 1587 expedition was meant to be different: a settlement of families, intending to establish itself on the Chesapeake Bay. Instead the colonists were left at Roanoke.
The 118 colonists began their journey in April 1587 under John White, intending to settle on the Chesapeake Bay but left instead at Roanoke.

entries.title: The Founding of Jamestown
entries.subtitle: The first permanent English settlement in North America, 1607
entries.summary: In May 1607, 104 English men and boys sent by the Virginia Company, a private company of investors, chose a marshy riverside site on the James River for a settlement they named for King James I. Jamestown nearly failed from disease, hunger, and conflict with the Powhatan peoples whose lands it occupied, and in the winter of 1609 to 1610 most of the settlers died. The colony was saved by gifts of food from Chief Powhatan, by new settlers and supplies, and, from 1612, by John Rolfe’s tobacco. In 1619 it held the first representative assembly in English North America, and within weeks the first documented Africans arrived. Its growth onto Powhatan land led to two major Powhatan attacks, in 1622 and 1644.

cards.q: Why does the Founding of Jamestown matter?
cards.a: Jamestown was where English America began, and where the contradictions of American history first took shape together: self-government alongside slavery and the dispossession of Native peoples.

cards.q: What led to the Founding of Jamestown?
cards.a: The settlers left London in December 1606 on three ships, the Susan Constant, the Godspeed, and the Discovery. The National Park Service dates the departure to December 6, and Historic Jamestowne’s biography of John Smith says the fleet sailed December 20. They reached the Chesapeake in April 1607.

The fort. Within days of landing the colonists were attacked by Powhatan warriors, and Historic Jamestowne’s timeline records an attack by about two hundred, in which at least one settler was killed and eleven were wounded. By June 15 they had built a triangular fort with a bulwark at each corner for artillery. Captain Newport sailed for England on June 22, and soon the settlers began to die of disease, hunger, and war. Archaeology has recovered the site of the original fort, which many had thought lost to the river.

entries.title: The First Africans in Virginia
entries.subtitle: 1619: Enslaved Angolans arrive at Point Comfort
entries.summary: In late August 1619, the English privateer White Lion arrived at Point Comfort, Virginia, and traded about twenty Africans for food; the ship Treasurer soon brought a few more. They had been captured in west central Africa, most likely from the kingdom of Ndongo in present-day Angola, and taken from a Portuguese slave ship bound for Mexico. They were the first documented Africans in English Virginia, and their arrival is often taken as the beginning of the history of slavery in what became the United States.

cards.q: Why does the First Africans in Virginia matter?
cards.a: The arrival of the first Africans at Point Comfort marks the beginning of the African American experience in English North America and of the system of racial slavery that shaped the country’s economy, politics, and conflicts for nearly 250 years.

cards.q: What led to the First Africans in Virginia?
cards.a: In 1619 a Portuguese slave ship sailed from west central Africa for New Spain (Mexico) carrying captives from Ndongo. Two English privateers, the White Lion and the Treasurer, attacked it and took some of the captives.
The White Lion reached Point Comfort in late August 1619, and about twenty Africans were sold in exchange for food. A few days later the Treasurer arrived and sold two or three more.

entries.title: Plymouth Colony and the Wampanoag
entries.subtitle: The Pilgrims’ settlement and the alliance that kept it alive, 1620–1621
entries.summary: In December 1620, English colonists from the Mayflower, many of them religious Separatists later called Pilgrims, settled at Plymouth, in the homeland of the Wampanoag people. Half of them died that first winter. In March 1621, the Wampanoag leader Massasoit, whose people had been devastated by diseases brought by earlier English visitors and who faced pressure from the rival Narragansett, made an alliance with the newcomers. That treaty kept the colony alive, and Massasoit honored it for the rest of his life.

cards.q: Why does Plymouth Colony and the Wampanoag matter?
cards.a: Plymouth is a founding myth of the United States, but its real history is one of mutual dependence: the colony survived because of an alliance with a Native nation already reeling from European diseases.

cards.q: What led to Plymouth Colony and the Wampanoag?
cards.a: The colonists, who had signed the Mayflower Compact before landing, arrived too late in the year to plant. Living in temporary shelters and aboard ship, they died in large numbers: by the spring of 1621, 50 of the 102 people who had come on the Mayflower were dead.

After a series of encounters, Massasoit and a party of his men approached the English on March 22, 1621. With help from Squanto, a Patuxet man who had been taken as a slave by an Englishman and had lived in England, the two sides negotiated.

entries.title: The Mayflower Compact
entries.subtitle: Passengers bound for Virginia agree to govern themselves at Plymouth
entries.summary: Before going ashore in November 1620, the male passengers of the Mayflower signed a short agreement to “covenant and combine ourselves together into a civil Body Politick” and to obey the laws that body would make. They had landed far north of the Virginia territory their patent covered, so they had no legal charter for where they were. The Mayflower Compact became the basis of government at Plymouth Colony and an early example of self-government by mutual consent.

videos.title: Chapter 1 | The Pilgrims | American Experience | PBS

cards.q: Why does the Mayflower Compact matter?
cards.a: Later generations, especially in the nineteenth century, celebrated the Compact as a seed of American constitutional government. That interpretation can be overstated, but the document is a real early instance of colonists creating civil authority by agreement among themselves.

The Mayflower carried a mix of religious Separatists, who had broken from the Church of England, and other passengers recruited by the colony’s investors. Their voyage was meant “to plant the first Colony in the northern Parts of Virginia,” but they made landfall at Cape Cod, outside the territory their patent covered.

The Compact is brief. The signers, describing themselves as loyal subjects of King James, declare that they undertook the voyage “for the Glory of God, and Advancement of the Christian Faith, and the Honour of our King and Country.”

entries.title: The Pueblo Revolt
entries.subtitle: Pueblo nations unite to drive Spanish colonizers out of New Mexico, 1680
entries.summary: In August 1680, the Pueblo peoples of New Mexico, who lived in dozens of independent towns and spoke several languages, rose together against eight decades of Spanish rule. Planned by a religious leader from San Juan Pueblo known as Popé or Po’pay, the revolt killed hundreds of settlers and missionaries, burned the missions, and forced the Spanish out of Santa Fe. They stayed away for twelve years, and the Penn Museum calls it arguably the most successful Indigenous uprising against a European colonial power in the New World. When the Spanish returned in 1692, they did not restore everything they had lost: the forced labor and aggressive suppression of Pueblo religion did not come back.

cards.q: Why does the Pueblo Revolt matter?
cards.a: The Pueblo Revolt shows that Native peoples did not simply endure colonization. They organized across linguistic and political lines to resist it, and for twelve years they won.

cards.q: What led to the Pueblo Revolt?
cards.a: Franciscans, according to EBSCO, “recognized no belief system except their own” and saved their harshest punishments for those who kept the old religion.
Planning. In hiding at Taos Pueblo, Popé built a coalition across languages.

entries.title: The Salem Witch Trials
entries.subtitle: The 1692 witch hunt in Puritan Massachusetts that sent twenty people to their deaths
entries.summary: In 1692 a panic over witchcraft swept Salem Village and neighboring towns in Puritan Massachusetts. It began when two girls in the household of the village minister fell into fits and three women were arrested for bewitching them; within months hundreds of people had been accused. A special court, relying on “spectral evidence” (testimony that an accused person’s spirit had tormented the victims), sentenced people to death. Nineteen people were hanged and one man was pressed to death with stones before the governor shut the court down. The trials became America’s most famous warning against mass hysteria and false accusation.

cards.q: Why does the Salem Witch Trials matter?
cards.a: Salem showed how fear, local feuds, and unsound legal procedure could combine to destroy innocent lives. It has become the American byword for a “witch hunt” and a lasting argument for due process.

cards.q: What led to the Salem Witch Trials?
cards.a: Historians point to many causes: local rivalries and family feuds, political turmoil, the enduring trauma of war, and a faulty legal process in which confessing, and accusing others, became the surest way for the accused to save their own lives. Some scholars have even suggested low-level environmental contamination.
In early 1692 Parris’s daughter Betty and her twelve-year-old cousin Abigail Williams began to suffer strange fits, which were diagnosed as witchcraft.

entries.title: The First Great Awakening
entries.subtitle: A wave of evangelical revivals across the colonies, 1730s–1770s
entries.summary: The First Great Awakening was a surge of evangelical Protestant revival that swept the American colonies from the 1730s to the 1770s, part of a movement also stirring Britain and Germany. Fiery preachers such as Jonathan Edwards and the traveling English evangelist George Whitefield urged listeners to experience a heartfelt conversion. The revivals split churches, challenged the authority of established clergy, and gave many colonists, including women and African Americans, new religious voices.

cards.q: Why does the First Great Awakening matter?
cards.a: The Great Awakening was the first movement to touch nearly every colony, and it left American Protestantism more diverse, more democratic in style, and deeply divided over religious authority.

Revivalists sought to awaken what they saw as spiritually complacent congregations. They taught that sinners were totally dependent on God’s grace for salvation and that true religion was felt in the heart, not merely reasoned in the head, a reaction against the rationalism of the Enlightenment.

cards.q: How did it pursue its goals?
cards.a: Preachers delivered emotionally charged, often extemporaneous sermons. The Tennents founded a seminary, the “Log College,” to train ministers in this style; its successor institution became Princeton University.

entries.title: The French and Indian War
entries.subtitle: The North American front of the Seven Years’ War, 1754–1763
entries.summary: The French and Indian War was the North American part of a world war, known elsewhere as the Seven Years’ War, between Britain and France. It began in 1754 when a young George Washington led Virginia militia into the Ohio Valley, a region both empires claimed. France and its Native allies won the early battles, but British victories at Louisbourg, Quebec, and Montreal ended French rule in Canada by 1760. The Treaty of Paris of 1763 gave Britain most of eastern North America. Victory left Britain deep in debt, faced with Pontiac’s War, and determined to tighten control of its colonies, which set off the conflicts that led to the American Revolution.

cards.q: Why does the French and Indian War matter?
cards.a: The French and Indian War made Britain the dominant power in eastern North America, but the costs of victory and the problems of governing a vast new empire pushed Britain and its colonies into the conflict that became the American Revolution.

Of the eighty-seven years between 1688 and 1775, the Yawp counts thirty-seven in which Britain was at war with France and its Native allies, with raids and captive-taking along the border of New England and New France. By the 1750s the two empires were feuding over their boundaries, especially the upper Ohio Valley, which Britain and Virginia land speculators claimed. In late 1753 Virginia’s lieutenant governor, Robert Dinwiddie, sent the young Major Washington with six frontiersmen to demand that the French leave.

Sea power. British naval victories allowed reinforcements to reach North America and isolated French Canada. Louisbourg (1758) and Quebec (1759). The fall of France’s great Atlantic fortress and of Quebec broke French power in Canada. Colonial unity. At the Albany Congress of 1754 Benjamin Franklin proposed a plan of union to coordinate colonial defenses, and tens of thousands of colonists fought in the war, which the Yawp says “pushed the thirteen American colonies closer together politically and culturally than ever before.”

entries.title: The Stamp Act Crisis
entries.subtitle: The first great colonial protest against taxation by Parliament
entries.summary: In March 1765 Parliament passed the Stamp Act, which required newspapers, legal documents, diplomas, and even playing cards in the colonies to be printed on stamped paper showing a tax had been paid. It was the first direct tax Parliament had ever laid on the colonists. Colonists answered with resolutions, a congress of nine colonies, boycotts of British goods, and crowd violence, until no one would serve as a stamp distributor. Parliament repealed the act early in 1766 but declared its power to bind the colonies “in all cases whatsoever.” The crisis gave colonists the argument, “no taxation without representation,” and the methods of resistance that would carry them toward independence.

cards.q: Why does the Stamp Act Crisis matter?
cards.a: The Stamp Act crisis was the moment colonists first acted together against Parliament and spelled out the principle, no taxation without representation, that would lead them to independence. Parliament’s answer, that it could bind them “in all cases whatsoever,” defined the conflict that followed.

cards.q: What led to the Stamp Act Crisis?
cards.a: Until 1765 the colonies had paid only “external” taxes, such as customs duties that regulated trade. The Stamp Act was different: it created a new, direct, “internal” tax to raise revenue.
The Yawp describes three kinds of resistance, roughly divided by class.

entries.title: The Boston Massacre
entries.subtitle: British soldiers fire into a Boston crowd, killing five, in March 1770
entries.summary: On the evening of March 5, 1770, a crowd confronted a small group of British soldiers outside the Custom House on King Street in Boston. Taunted and pelted with snowballs, ice, and sticks, the soldiers fired, killing five men, among them Crispus Attucks, a sailor of African and Indigenous ancestry, and wounding six. Patriots called it a massacre of civilians; loyalists called it self-defense against a mob. John Adams defended the soldiers in court and won acquittals for most of them, but the killings became one of the most powerful stories of the coming Revolution.

cards.q: Why does the Boston Massacre matter?
cards.a: The Boston Massacre was the first time British soldiers shed colonists’ blood in the quarrel that became the American Revolution. Patriots turned it into propaganda and an annual day of remembrance, while the trials that followed showed that even hated soldiers could get a fair hearing in a Massachusetts court, a principle later written into the Sixth Amendment.

cards.q: What led to the Boston Massacre?
cards.a: By the winter of 1769–1770 the confrontations had become personal and violent.

On the evening of March 5, 1770, just eleven days after Seider’s death, Private Hugh White of the 29th Regiment of Foot stood sentry outside the Custom House. When a young wigmaker’s apprentice, Edward Garrick, shouted that a British officer had not paid his bill, White reprimanded him, the two argued, and White struck the young man on the side of the head with his musket.

entries.title: The Boston Tea Party
entries.subtitle: Colonists destroy East India Company tea in Boston Harbor
entries.summary: On the night of December 16, 1773, a few dozen men disguised as Indians boarded three ships at Griffin’s Wharf in Boston and dumped 342 chests of East India Company tea into the harbor. They were protesting the Tea Act, which made the company’s tea cheaper but kept a tax that colonists refused to pay to a Parliament in which they had no representatives. Britain answered with the Coercive Acts, which closed Boston’s port and put Massachusetts under tighter royal control. Instead of isolating Boston, the punishment drew the colonies together and led to the First Continental Congress.

cards.q: Why does the Boston Tea Party matter?
cards.a: By destroying the tea and provoking Britain’s crackdown, Boston’s protesters turned a dispute over a tax into a confrontation over Parliament’s power to govern the colonies at all, and forced the other colonies to decide whether they stood with Massachusetts. Most did.

cards.q: What led to the Boston Tea Party?
cards.a: In 1773 the East India Company was deep in debt and, the Yawp writes, “drowning in tea,” with almost fifteen million pounds stored in warehouses. Parliament passed the Tea Act on May 10, 1773, letting the company sell tea directly in the colonies without paying the usual export tax in London; the tax would be collected when the tea landed in colonial ports. The tea would be cheaper, but merchants resented the company’s monopoly, and many colonists saw a trap: by buying it they would pay the duty and accept Parliament’s right to tax them. A Pennsylvania newspaper called Prime Minister Lord North a “great schemer” trying “to out wit us.” Agents were appointed to receive the tea in Boston, New York, Philadelphia, and Charleston.
The Dartmouth, carrying 114 chests of tea, arrived in Boston Harbor on November 28, 1773.

entries.title: The Continental Congress
entries.subtitle: The colonies’ revolutionary assembly, and the first national government
entries.summary: The Continental Congress began as a meeting of colonial delegates coordinating protest against British policy and became, almost by accident, the government of a new nation. The First Continental Congress, which met in Philadelphia on September 5, 1774, issued a declaration of colonial rights and organized a boycott of British trade through the Continental Association. The Second Continental Congress, which met in May 1775 after fighting had begun, created the Continental Army under George Washington, voted for independence on July 2, 1776, adopted the Declaration of Independence, won French support, and wrote the Articles of Confederation.

cards.q: Why does the Continental Congress matter?
cards.a: The Continental Congress turned thirteen separate colonies into a single political community that could declare independence, raise an army, make foreign alliances, and win a war. Its weaknesses, especially its dependence on the states for money, also taught the lessons that shaped the Constitution.
After the Boston Tea Party, Parliament’s Coercive Acts of 1774 closed Boston’s port and put Massachusetts under royal control.

cards.q: What can it do, and what limits it?
cards.a: Its first great act was the Continental Association of October 20, 1774, a continental agreement not to import, consume, or export British goods and to “wholly discontinue the slave trade.” It recommended that every county, city, and town choose a committee to watch for violators and publish their names so they would be “universally condemned as the enemies of American liberty.”

entries.title: Abolitionism
entries.subtitle: The movement to end slavery in the United States
entries.summary: Abolitionism was the movement to end slavery in the United States. Early antislavery reformers, many of them Quakers, worked for gradual emancipation and an end to the slave trade. In the 1830s a new generation, led by Black activists and white evangelicals such as William Lloyd Garrison, demanded immediate, uncompensated emancipation and equal rights for Black Americans. A small and often hated minority, abolitionists used newspapers, lectures, petitions, and the Underground Railroad to make slavery the central moral question of American politics. Their cause triumphed only through the Civil War and the Thirteenth Amendment.

Abolitionists turned slavery from an accepted institution into the great moral issue of American politics. Their agitation helped bring about the political crisis of the 1850s, and the Civil War that followed ended slavery.

cards.q: How did it pursue its goals?
cards.a: Petitions and early societies. Quakers questioned slavery as early as the late seventeenth century and worked with British reformers against the slave trade. In February 1790, Benjamin Franklin, as president of the Pennsylvania Society for Promoting the Abolition of Slavery, signed a petition asking the First Congress to “devise means for removing the Inconsistency from the Character of the American People.”

entries.title: Battle of Bunker Hill
entries.subtitle: The bloody 1775 fight outside Boston, actually waged on Breed’s Hill
entries.summary: On June 17, 1775, two months after Lexington and Concord, British troops attacked a fort that New England militiamen had built overnight on Breed’s Hill in Charlestown, across the harbor from Boston. The Americans threw back two assaults and gave way on the third only when they ran out of powder. The British took the hill, but the American Battlefield Trust counts 282 British dead and another 800 wounded, more than twice the American losses. The battle showed that the rebellion would not be easily put down and, in the Trust’s words, that reconciliation was “no longer possible.”

cards.a: The British won the ground but suffered more than a thousand casualties. The battle ended hopes of a quick end to the rebellion and showed the colonists they could fight a professional army.

cards.q: What led to Battle of Bunker Hill?
cards.a: A leaked plan. Word of the British plan got out, and about 1,000 Massachusetts and Connecticut men, among them several enslaved and free African Americans, moved to defend high ground in Charlestown. A provocation. On the nights of June 15 and 16 they fortified Breed’s Hill, a position that, the Battlefield Trust writes, “all but invites a British response.”
On the hot afternoon of June 17 British regulars crossed the harbor and landed in Charlestown.

entries.title: Lexington and Concord
entries.subtitle: April 19, 1775: the first fighting of the American Revolution and “the shot heard ’round the world”
entries.summary: Before dawn on April 19, 1775, about 700 British soldiers marched from Boston to seize military supplies that Massachusetts patriots had stockpiled at Concord. Warned by Paul Revere, William Dawes, Samuel Prescott, and church bells across the countryside, militia turned out. On Lexington Green a shot was fired, no one knows by whom, and British volleys killed eight militiamen. At Concord’s North Bridge the militia fired back, and on the long road back to Boston thousands of them harried the retreating regulars. The day’s fighting, by the Park Service’s count involving some 1,700 British regulars and over 4,000 colonial militia, began the Revolutionary War.

entries.title: The American Revolution
entries.subtitle: The war for independence from Britain, 1775–1783, and the revolution in ideas that made a new nation
entries.summary: In little more than a decade after 1763, colonists who had been proud to be British came to see Parliament’s taxes and controls as a threat to their liberty, and in 1776 they declared independence. The war that followed, from the first shots at Lexington and Concord in April 1775 to the Treaty of Paris in September 1783, pitted the new United States, with France as its ally from 1778, against the world’s largest military. The Revolution created a republic founded on the idea that government rests on the consent of the governed, but it left slavery in place and opened Native lands to settlement, contradictions that shaped the nation for generations.

cards.q: Why does the American Revolution matter?
cards.a: The American Revolution created the United States and launched what historians call the age of democratic revolutions, followed by revolutions in France, Haiti, and South America. Its ideals, above all the Declaration’s claim that “all men are created equal,” became the shared language that later movements, from abolitionists to suffragists and civil rights activists, used to demand that the nation live up to its founding.

Seen from 1763, nothing would have seemed less likely than an American revolution. Colonists had just helped Britain win the Seven Years’ War, and most had never been prouder to be British. Over the previous century they had grown used to running their own affairs.
Saratoga (1777) was the decisive turning point. The surrender of an entire British army convinced the French government that the American cause could succeed.

entries.title: Common Sense
entries.subtitle: Thomas Paine’s 1776 pamphlet that made the case for independence
entries.summary: Common Sense was a pamphlet of about fifty pages, published in Philadelphia on January 10, 1776, by Thomas Paine, an Englishman who had arrived in America little more than a year before. At a time when most colonial leaders still hoped to reconcile with Britain, Paine attacked not just British policy but monarchy itself and called for an independent American republic. Written in plain language full of biblical references, it became, according to the American Battlefield Trust, one of the best-selling works in America after the Bible. Six months later Congress declared independence.

47 pages (American Battlefield Trust) or 46 (American Yawp)
Monarchy is illegitimate; America should declare independence and form a republic
“There is something very absurd, in supposing a continent to be perpetually governed by an island”
The American Crisis essays, 1776–1783

Common Sense turned independence from a whispered possibility into a public cause. Its plain style reached ordinary readers in taverns and town meetings, and its attack on monarchy gave the Revolution a democratic, republican goal.

Thomas Paine was born in Norfolk, England, in 1737. He worked as a staymaker’s apprentice, customs officer, privateer, and schoolteacher before becoming an advocate for his fellow excise officers. In London he met Benjamin Franklin, who in 1774 encouraged him to go to Pennsylvania.

Government is a necessary evil. “Society in every state is a blessing, but government even in its best state is but a necessary evil; in its worst state an intolerable one.” Monarchy and hereditary rule are absurd. Paine attacked the idea of kingship itself, not just King George III’s policies, and called for a republic, a government that is a “public affair.” Geography argues for independence. “There is something very absurd, in supposing a continent to be perpetually governed by an island.” The time has come. “The blood of the slain, the weeping voice of nature cries, ’Tis time to part.” America’s cause is universal. “The cause of America is in a great measure the cause of all mankind,” he wrote, and he urged Americans to “prepare in time an asylum for mankind.”

entries.title: Independence Day
entries.subtitle: The nation’s birthday, celebrated since 1776 and a federal holiday since 1870
entries.summary: Independence Day marks July 4, 1776, when the Continental Congress adopted the Declaration of Independence, two days after voting for independence. John Adams expected July 2 to become “the great anniversary Festival,” celebrated “with Pomp and Parade… Bonfires and Illuminations from one End of this Continent to the other.” Americans adopted his program but chose the Fourth. The day became the stage for national celebration and for protest, from William Lloyd Garrison and Frederick Douglass to later reformers, and in 1870 it became one of the first federal holidays.

The Fourth of July is the nation’s chief civic holiday, a celebration not of a battle or a ruler but of a document and its ideas. Because the Declaration promised that all men are created equal, the day has also given every generation of reformers a stage on which to ask whether the nation is living up to its creed.
The holiday grew directly from the vote.
On July 2, 1776, Congress adopted the Lee Resolution, twelve colonies in favor and New York not voting, and immediately began revising Jefferson’s draft.

entries.title: The Declaration of Independence
entries.subtitle: The Continental Congress explains why thirteen colonies are breaking with Britain
entries.summary: The Declaration of Independence, adopted by the Second Continental Congress on July 4, 1776, announced that the thirteen American colonies were “Free and Independent States” and explained to the world why they were breaking with Great Britain. Drafted mainly by Thomas Jefferson, it is best remembered for its preamble: “We hold these truths to be self-evident, that all men are created equal,” with rights to “Life, Liberty and the pursuit of Happiness.” The men who adopted it did not mean it to end slavery or give everyone political rights. Yet, as the American Yawp observes, most of the conflicts of American history since then have been struggles over what it means to believe that “all men are created equal.”

cards.q: Why does the Declaration of Independence matter?
cards.a: The Declaration made the United States an independent nation in the eyes of the world and opened the way to the French alliance of 1778. Its preamble became the founding statement of American ideals and the standard by which Americans have judged their country ever since.

By 1776 the colonies and Britain had been at odds for more than a decade over taxes, trade, and the powers of Parliament, and fighting had begun at Lexington and Concord in April 1775. The Second Continental Congress, which met in May 1775, gradually took on the work of a national government.
The National Archives divides the Declaration into five parts: an introduction, a preamble, a two-part body, and a conclusion.

entries.title: Battles of Saratoga
entries.subtitle: The 1777 American victory that brought France into the war
entries.summary: In the autumn of 1777 a British army under General John Burgoyne, marching south from Canada to take the Hudson River Valley, was stopped and forced to surrender near Saratoga, New York. American forces under Horatio Gates fought Burgoyne at Freeman’s Farm on September 19 and at Bemis Heights on October 7, then surrounded his army, which surrendered on October 17. The American Yawp calls the victory “a major turning point in the war”: it convinced France that the American cause could succeed, and France signed treaties with the United States in February 1778.

cards.q: Why does Battles of Saratoga matter?
cards.a: Saratoga ended Burgoyne’s attempt to control the Hudson River Valley. It proved the Americans could defeat a professional army in the field and persuaded France to enter the war, which made eventual independence far more likely.

cards.q: What led to Battles of Saratoga?
cards.a: The Hudson strategy. Burgoyne’s campaign depended on the river route and on help from other British forces, above all Gen. Henry Clinton coming up from New York City. Losses on the march. A detachment of Burgoyne’s troops was defeated at the Battle of Bennington, and his reduced army marched toward Saratoga in early September. A strong American position. Gates had his men fortify Bemis Heights, bluffs overlooking both the Hudson and the only road south.

Freeman’s Farm, September 19. Burgoyne split his army into three columns to probe the American defenses. Daniel Morgan’s riflemen and light infantry met the center column near Freeman’s Farm, and the field changed hands several times.

entries.title: The Articles of Confederation
entries.subtitle: The first constitution of the United States, 1781–1789
entries.summary: The Articles of Confederation were the first constitution of the United States. Drafted mainly by John Dickinson and adopted by the Continental Congress on November 15, 1777, they created “a firm league of friendship” among thirteen states that each kept their “sovereignty, freedom and independence.” They took effect only on March 1, 1781, when Maryland ratified. Congress had one house, and each state one vote. It could make war and treaties but could not tax, regulate commerce, or establish federal courts, weaknesses that, after the war, led James Madison, George Washington, and others to fear the union would collapse and to replace the Articles with the Constitution in 1787.

cards.q: Why does the Articles of Confederation matter?
cards.a: The Articles carried the United States through the end of the Revolution and produced the Northwest Ordinance, but their weaknesses convinced many leaders that the union needed a stronger government.
After Richard Henry Lee proposed independence in June 1776, the Second Continental Congress appointed three committees on June 11.

A league of states. “The said States hereby severally enter into a firm league of friendship with each other, for their common defense, the security of their liberties, and their mutual and general welfare.” State sovereignty. Each state kept “its sovereignty, freedom and independence, and every Power, Jurisdiction and right, which is not by this confederation expressly delegated to the United States.” One state, one vote. “In determining questions in the United States in Congress assembled, each State shall have one vote.” Supermajorities. War, treaties, coining or borrowing money, and other major acts required the assent of nine states. No power to tax. Congress could request money from the states but had no power to levy or collect taxes, regulate foreign or interstate commerce, or create a federal judiciary. Hard to change. No alteration could be made unless agreed to by Congress “and be afterwards confirmed by the legislatures of every State.” Cooperation among states. States had to give “full faith and credit” to each other’s court records and hand over fugitives from justice.

entries.title: Valley Forge
entries.subtitle: The Continental Army’s winter encampment of 1777–78
entries.summary: From December 19, 1777, to June 19, 1778, George Washington’s Continental Army camped at Valley Forge, Pennsylvania, about twenty miles from British-occupied Philadelphia. More than 12,000 soldiers, together with about 400 women and children, built a city of log huts there. Shortages of food and clothing and outbreaks of disease killed about 2,000 people, though no battle was fought. Over the same months the Prussian officer Baron von Steuben drilled the troops into a disciplined army. The National Park Service treats Valley Forge as both a real event and a national myth, and the two are worth telling apart.

No battle was fought at Valley Forge, yet it is one of the most famous places of the Revolution. Washington held the army together through a hard winter, and the army that left in June was better trained, better organized and allied with France.

The loss of Philadelphia. Washington wanted to stay close to the British in the city. A defensible site. The plateau offered water and firewood and could be fortified. The need to rebuild. The army, still largely a collection of state militias, needed rest, supplies and training.
The army marched in on December 19 and set to work.

entries.title: The Siege of Yorktown
entries.subtitle: The 1781 American and French victory that effectively won the Revolutionary War
entries.summary: In the fall of 1781, an American army under George Washington and a French army under the Comte de Rochambeau trapped the British general Charles Cornwallis at Yorktown, Virginia, while a French fleet under the Comte de Grasse kept the Royal Navy from rescuing him. After a three-week siege, including a night assault on two British redoubts led in part by Alexander Hamilton, Cornwallis surrendered on October 19, 1781. It was the last major land battle of the Revolution. Britain’s will to fight collapsed, and the war formally ended with the Treaty of Paris in 1783.

cards.q: Why does the Siege of Yorktown matter?
cards.a: The siege of Yorktown was the decisive engagement of the American Revolution. It ended Britain’s attempt to defeat the rebellion by force and led directly to the peace that recognized the United States as an independent nation.

cards.q: What led to the Siege of Yorktown?
cards.a: In 1780 and early 1781 Cornwallis led his army through the Carolinas, suffering defeats at Kings Mountain and Cowpens and a costly victory at Guilford Courthouse in March 1781. Convinced that the southern colonies could not be held “until Virginia was reduced,” he marched into Virginia, a decision his commander, Sir Henry Clinton in New York, never approved. The young Marquis de Lafayette, with a much smaller American force, shadowed him all summer, avoiding a pitched battle. Under orders from Clinton to take a defensive post at Williamsburg or Yorktown and send part of his army to New York, Cornwallis fortified Yorktown, on the York River, to refit and wait for supplies and reinforcements by sea.

The Battle of the Capes. On September 5, while the allied armies were still marching, the French fleet met a British fleet at the mouth of the Chesapeake Bay and drove it off, leaving Cornwallis cut off by sea. The siege lines. The allies arrived near Yorktown on September 28.

entries.title: Treaty of Paris (1783)
entries.subtitle: The peace that ended the Revolutionary War and recognized American independence
entries.summary: The Treaty of Paris, signed on September 3, 1783, ended the American Revolution. In it Great Britain recognized the thirteen states as “free sovereign and Independent States” and accepted boundaries that ran west to the Mississippi River. The American negotiators, John Adams, Benjamin Franklin and John Jay, had already agreed preliminary articles with Britain in November 1782. The treaty also dealt with fishing rights, debts, prisoners and the property of Loyalists, and some of its promises were broken almost at once.

cards.q: Why does Treaty of Paris (1783) matter?
cards.a: The treaty made the United States an independent nation in international law and gave it a territory reaching to the Mississippi, which opened the way west. Its unkept promises, on Loyalist property and on enslaved people, shaped the politics of the next decades.

The National Archives calls the War for Independence “actually a world conflict,” involving France, Spain and the Netherlands as well as Britain and the United States. In 1782 Britain offered the states some autonomy inside the empire.
Independence (Article 1). The king “acknowledges the said United States … to be free sovereign and Independent States” and gives up all claims to govern them.

entries.title: Shays’ Rebellion
entries.subtitle: An armed uprising of indebted farmers that shook the new nation
entries.summary: In 1786 and 1787 thousands of farmers in western Massachusetts, many of them Revolutionary War veterans, rose against heavy state taxes and debt collection that threatened to cost them their farms. Led in part by Daniel Shays, a former Continental Army captain, they closed courts and in January 1787 tried to seize the federal arsenal at Springfield, where militia drove them off. The national government under the Articles of Confederation could do nothing to help. The uprising alarmed leaders across the country and helped bring about the Constitutional Convention.

quotes.context: letter to Henry Knox, quoted by the National Constitution Center

quotes.text: Liberty may be endangered by the abuses of liberty as well as the abuses of power.
quotes.speaker: James Madison

A local revolt over debt became a national turning point. It exposed the weakness of the Articles of Confederation and convinced key leaders that the union needed a government strong enough to keep order, while raising a question that never went away: when is protest the spirit of 1776, and when is it rebellion?

The farmers asked the state government to protect them from their creditors, but it refused to consider debt relief. Many of them saw their protest as a continuation of the “Spirit of 1776,” and they turned to tactics the patriots had used against Britain: blocking courthouses so judges could not issue foreclosure orders.

In August 1786 armed protesters, the “Shaysites,” began seizing county courts to stop debt cases. Governor James Bowdoin called them rebels who wanted to rule by mob violence, and he raised thousands of militiamen under the former Revolutionary general Benjamin Lincoln, who said Massachusetts must prevent “a state of anarchy, confusion and slavery.” The militia was paid for by private Boston businessmen, because the national government had no money to act. In late January 1787 Shays led about 1,500 men toward the federal arsenal at Springfield.

entries.title: Anti-Federalists
entries.subtitle: The opponents of the Constitution whose objections produced the Bill of Rights
entries.summary: The Anti-Federalists were the Americans who opposed ratifying the Constitution in 1787 and 1788. They feared that the new national government would swallow the states and threaten liberty, and they rallied above all around its lack of a bill of rights. Leaders included George Mason and Patrick Henry of Virginia, and essayists such as “Brutus” in New York. They lost the fight over ratification, but their pressure led several states to ratify only with proposed amendments, and those proposals became the Bill of Rights in 1791.

The Anti-Federalists lost the ratification fight but shaped the result. Their insistence on written protections for liberty gave the Constitution its Bill of Rights, and their warnings about centralized power began a debate over federalism that has never ended.

Anti-Federalists did not agree on everything, but most shared a few aims. They wanted power kept close to the people in the states, and they distrusted a strong central government far away. Most of all, they wanted a written guarantee of individual rights.

cards.q: How did it pursue its goals?
cards.a: Opponents argued their case in pamphlets and newspapers, in the same public debate that produced the Federalist Papers. Mason, one of three delegates present on the convention’s last day who refused to sign the Constitution, wrote a pamphlet that the National Archives says persuaded many Americans to oppose it. In New York a writer calling himself “Brutus” published essays beginning on October 18, 1787. In the state ratifying conventions Anti-Federalists either voted no or demanded amendments as the price of approval.

entries.title: The Constitution of the United States
entries.subtitle: The framework of the federal government, written in 1787 and amended twenty-seven times
entries.summary: The Constitution, drafted in secret at a convention in Philadelphia in the summer of 1787 and signed on September 17, replaced the weak Articles of Confederation with a strong national government of three branches, each able to check the others. It was a document of compromises: between large and small states, between North and South, and between those who wanted a powerful central government and those who feared one. Ratified in 1788 after a fierce public debate, and soon amended by the Bill of Rights, it has governed the United States ever since.

cards.q: Why does the Constitution of the United States matter?
cards.a: The Constitution created a national government strong enough to tax, regulate commerce, and act directly on citizens, while dividing power to guard against tyranny. Its compromises over slavery helped hold the convention together, but the National Archives calls the slave-trade bargain “a crippling blow to those working to abolish slavery,” and later antislavery leaders blamed the three-fifths clause for giving slaveholders outsized power in Washington.
Under the Articles of Confederation, in force since 1781, the United States was a “league of friendship” among thirteen sovereign states.

A national government. On May 29 Edmund Randolph presented the Virginia Plan, drafted largely by Madison: a government of three branches, legislative, executive, and judicial, “each branch structured to check the other,” with power to veto state laws. By mid-June it was clear that the convention would write an entirely new frame of government rather than amend the Articles. Small states rallied behind William Paterson’s New Jersey Plan, which would only have strengthened the existing Congress, but the convention rejected it. Hamilton’s proposal, modeled on the British government, with an executive and senate serving for life, found no following.

entries.title: The Constitutional Convention
entries.subtitle: Fifty-five delegates meet in secret to redesign the American government
entries.summary: In the summer of 1787, delegates from twelve of the thirteen states met in secret in Philadelphia, officially to revise the Articles of Confederation. Instead, they wrote a new Constitution. They argued bitterly over how to represent large and small states, how much power to give the central government, and how to count enslaved people, and they settled each dispute by compromise. Only 55 of the 74 delegates appointed ever attended. Three of those who stayed to the end refused to sign. The document the others signed on September 17 became the framework of the United States government.

cards.q: Why does the Constitutional Convention matter?
cards.a: In four months the convention replaced a failing confederation with a national government designed to be strong enough to govern but divided enough to restrain itself.

cards.q: What led to the Constitutional Convention?
cards.a: James Madison had spent years studying the history of confederacies and republics and was convinced that the Articles had to be replaced. The research gave him a bold idea.

Opening and secrecy. The convention formally got under way on May 25, 1787, when a quorum of seven states was finally present. Dirt was spread on the street outside the State House to muffle the noise of carriages, and guards kept the curious away.

entries.title: The Federalist Papers
entries.subtitle: Eighty-five essays defending the proposed Constitution
entries.summary: The Federalist, commonly called the Federalist Papers, is a series of 85 essays written between October 1787 and May 1788 by Alexander Hamilton, James Madison, and John Jay under the shared pen name “Publius.” Published mainly in New York newspapers, they urged New Yorkers to ratify the proposed Constitution and explained its provisions in detail. Hamilton wrote more than half and Madison twenty-nine. The essays on faction, checks and balances, and the courts became the classic explanation of American constitutional design, and judges still cite them to understand what the framers intended.

cards.q: Why does the Federalist Papers matter?
cards.a: New York, the state the essays were written to persuade, ratified by just three votes. Whatever their effect on that vote, the Federalist Papers became the classic exposition of the American constitutional system.

After the Constitutional Convention finished its work in September 1787, the Constitution had to be approved by special ratifying conventions in the states. Critics, the Anti-Federalists, organized against it.

A test for the world. In No. 1 Hamilton wrote that Americans would decide “whether societies of men are really capable or not of establishing good government from reflection and choice, or whether they are forever destined to depend for their political constitutions on accident and force.” A large republic controls faction. In No. 10 Madison defined a faction as citizens “united and actuated by some common impulse of passion, or of interest, adversed to the rights of other citizens.”

entries.title: The Northwest Ordinance
entries.subtitle: The plan for governing the Old Northwest and admitting new states
entries.summary: Passed by the Confederation Congress on July 13, 1787, the Northwest Ordinance set out how the lands north of the Ohio River would be governed and how they would become new states “on an equal footing with the original States in all respects whatever.” It laid out a three-stage path from territory to statehood, guaranteed a bill of rights, encouraged education, promised “utmost good faith” toward Indian nations, and banned slavery in the territory. The National Archives notes that its plan “was subsequently used as the country expanded to the Pacific.” Its promises to Native peoples were broken almost at once, and they fought a long war to keep their lands.

The Northwest Ordinance Explained | A Primary Source Close Read w/ BRI

cards.q: Why does the Northwest Ordinance matter?
cards.a: The Northwest Ordinance decided that the United States would grow as a union of equal states, not as an empire with permanent colonies. Its ban on slavery kept slavery out of the territory by law, and its pledge of good faith toward Native nations stands in sharp contrast to the wars and land cessions that followed.

After independence, the United States claimed the territory northwest of the Ohio River, a region that was home to many Native nations. The Confederation Congress, which had no power to tax, needed a plan to govern it, and American surveyors and settlers were already crossing the Ohio. In 1784 Thomas Jefferson had drafted an ordinance on governing the West.

Equal states. The territory would be divided into “not less than three nor more than five States,” each to be admitted “on an equal footing with the original States in all respects whatever.” A three-stage path to statehood. First Congress would appoint a governor, a secretary, and three judges.

entries.title: Congress
entries.subtitle: The legislative branch: the Senate and the House of Representatives
entries.summary: Article I of the Constitution vests “All legislative Powers” in a Congress made up of a Senate and a House of Representatives. The House, elected every two years, gives each state seats according to its population; the Senate gives every state two members, whatever its size. This design, the Great Compromise of 1787, saved the Constitutional Convention from collapse. Congress makes the laws, controls taxing and spending, declares war, confirms the president’s nominees, and can impeach and remove officials. As the branch closest to the people, it has been the stage for many of the great debates of American history.

Congress is the first branch of government in the Constitution and the institution through which Americans’ elected representatives make law, control spending and hold presidents to account. Its structure still reflects the bargains of 1787 between large states and small, and between free states and slave states.
The Revolution was partly a quarrel about representation.

cards.q: What can it do, and what limits it?
cards.a: Article I, Section 8 gives Congress power “To lay and collect Taxes,” to borrow money, to regulate commerce, “To declare War,” to raise armies and a navy, and “To make all Laws which shall be necessary and proper” for carrying out its powers. Every bill must pass both houses and go to the president, and Congress can override a veto by two-thirds of each house.

entries.title: Thanksgiving Day
entries.subtitle: How a New England harvest custom became a fixed national holiday, from Washington to Roosevelt
entries.summary: Thanksgiving was built step by step. In 1621 the Plymouth colonists and about ninety Wampanoag men shared a three-day harvest celebration, which nineteenth-century writers came to call the “First Thanksgiving.” In 1789 the first Federal Congress asked George Washington to proclaim a national day of thanks, and he chose Thursday, November 26. After decades of varying dates, the editor Sarah Josepha Hale persuaded Abraham Lincoln to proclaim the last Thursday of November in 1863. When Franklin D. Roosevelt moved it a week earlier in 1939, the country briefly kept two Thanksgivings, until Congress fixed the fourth Thursday of November by law in 1941.

Who is the mother of Thanksgiving? Meet Boston's Sarah Josepha Hale.

Thanksgiving is one of the most widely shared American holidays. Its history shows how a regional custom became a symbol of national union, promoted by a magazine editor in the middle of a civil war and fixed in the calendar during the Depression.

Sarah Josepha Hale’s campaign. Born in New Hampshire in 1788, Hale became editor of Godey’s Lady’s Book, one of the most widely read magazines in the country, and used it to promote New England’s Thanksgiving customs, from roast turkey to pumpkin pie. She petitioned governors and presidents to adopt a single national day, and in one editorial she reported that the last Thursday of November had been kept in twenty-four of the twenty-nine states that held a Thanksgiving at all. Union in wartime. Hale argued that a fixed national festival would bind the states together, and she pressed the point during the Civil War.
Lincoln acted within days.

entries.title: The Presidency
entries.subtitle: The executive branch, from Washington’s precedents to the modern office
entries.summary: Article II of the Constitution vests “the executive Power” in a president elected for four years, who commands the armed forces and must “take Care that the Laws be faithfully executed.” The framers argued for months over how to choose such an officer and how much power to give him. George Washington shaped the office by his example: he created the cabinet and stepped down after two terms. Crises later expanded it, above all under Abraham Lincoln and Franklin D. Roosevelt, until it became the most powerful position in American government, still checked by Congress, the courts and the voters.

The presidency has become the center of American government and politics, embodying the nation at home and abroad. Its history is a long tension between Hamilton’s “energy in the executive” and the founders’ fear of a king.
Under the Articles of Confederation there was no national executive at all. At the Constitutional Convention of 1787 the delegates struggled to design one.

cards.q: What can it do, and what limits it?
cards.a: Article II makes the president “Commander in Chief of the Army and Navy” and gives the power, “by and with the Advice and Consent of the Senate,” to make treaties, “provided two thirds of the Senators present concur,” and to appoint ambassadors, judges and other officers. The president may veto bills, which Congress can override by a two-thirds vote of each house, and can be removed through impeachment by the House and conviction by the Senate. The president is supported by the vice president and the cabinet, whose members require Senate approval.

entries.title: The Supreme Court
entries.subtitle: The nation’s highest court and interpreter of the Constitution
entries.summary: The Supreme Court is “the highest tribunal in the Nation for all cases and controversies arising under the Constitution or the laws of the United States.” The Constitution created it but said little about how it should work, so Congress and the justices themselves built the federal judiciary over time. It began as a weak body whose first justices complained of its “limited stature.” Beginning with Chief Justice John Marshall, it became a co-equal branch that can strike down laws as unconstitutional, and its rulings have shaped every era of American history, for better and for worse.

cards.q: Why does the Supreme Court matter?
cards.a: The Supreme Court is where Americans have brought their deepest disputes about rights and power, from slavery and segregation to the limits of government, and its interpretations of the Constitution have shaped every era of American history.

Article III of the Constitution vests “the judicial Power of the United States” in “one supreme Court” and in such lower courts as Congress creates, and provides that judges hold office during good behavior. Beyond that, the Supreme Court’s own history notes, the Constitution “elaborated neither the exact powers and prerogatives of the Supreme Court nor the organization of the Judicial Branch as a whole.”

cards.q: What can it do, and what limits it?
cards.a: The Court hears a few cases directly, such as disputes between states, and many more on appeal on questions of federal law. Its most important power, judicial review, the authority to declare laws unconstitutional, is not written in the Constitution.

entries.title: The Bill of Rights
entries.subtitle: The first ten amendments to the Constitution
entries.summary: The Bill of Rights is the first ten amendments to the Constitution, ratified on December 15, 1791. It protects freedom of religion, speech, the press, and assembly, the right to bear arms, security against unreasonable searches, and the rights of people accused of crimes, and it reserves undelegated powers to the states or the people. It was added to answer Anti-Federalist critics who feared that the new national government would trample individual liberties. James Madison, once its opponent, guided it through the First Congress. At first it limited only the federal government. The author of the Fourteenth Amendment (1868) meant that amendment to make the Bill of Rights binding on the states as well, a question the Supreme Court long resisted.

cards.q: Why does the Bill of Rights matter?
cards.a: The Bill of Rights helped win acceptance of the Constitution, and its guarantees became central to how Americans understand their freedoms.
The Constitution signed in Philadelphia in 1787 contained no list of individual rights.
On June 8, 1789, Madison introduced his amendments in the House, meeting in Federal Hall in New York.

entries.title: Political Parties
entries.subtitle: How Americans organized to win elections, from Federalists and Republicans to today’s two-party system
entries.summary: Political parties appear nowhere in the Constitution, and many founders hoped to avoid them. George Washington warned against “the baneful effects of the spirit of party.” Yet parties formed within a few years and have organized American politics ever since. Hamilton’s Federalists and Jefferson’s Democratic-Republicans gave way to Andrew Jackson’s Democrats and their Whig opponents. In the 1850s the antislavery Republican Party was born, and since then Democrats and Republicans have dominated a two-party system, even as their coalitions and ideas have changed dramatically.

Parties are the machinery of American democracy: they turn public opinion into governing coalitions. Their realignments mark the great turning points in American political history, from 1800 to the Civil War, the New Deal and beyond.
The founders distrusted parties.

cards.q: What can it do, and what limits it?
cards.a: Parties have no formal powers under the Constitution, but they do much of the work of democracy: they nominate candidates, organize voters, run campaigns and organize Congress. They also adapted the constitutional machinery.

entries.title: The White House
entries.subtitle: The president’s home and office since 1800
entries.summary: The White House has been the home and workplace of every American president since John and Abigail Adams moved in, in November 1800. Designed by the Irish-born architect James Hoban, it was built between 1792 and 1800 by free workers and by enslaved people hired out by their owners. British troops burned it in 1814, and it was rebuilt by 1817. Long called the “President’s House” or “Executive Mansion,” it got its official name from Theodore Roosevelt in 1901. Today it is a residence, an office, a stage for ceremonies and a museum that welcomes over 500,000 visitors a year.

cards.q: Why does the White House matter?
cards.a: The White House is one of the best-known symbols of the American presidency and of the nation itself.

The White House stands on Pennsylvania Avenue in Washington, D.C., on a site chosen by George Washington’s commissioners and the city’s planner, Pierre (Peter) Charles L’Enfant. Its sandstone came from a quarry on Aquia Creek in Stafford County, Virginia, which the federal government bought in 1791. The main house is flanked by the West Wing, with the president’s offices, and the East Wing.

Building the President’s House. After the Residence Act of 1790 placed the capital on the Potomac, Washington appointed three commissioners to manage construction. In March 1792 they announced a national design competition, and in July they chose Hoban’s design. The cornerstone was laid on October 13, 1792.

entries.title: The Election of 1800
entries.subtitle: The first transfer of power between rival parties
entries.summary: In 1800 the Democratic-Republicans under Thomas Jefferson defeated President John Adams and the Federalists in a campaign so bitter that each side predicted disaster, even war, if the other won. A flaw in the Constitution then produced a tie between Jefferson and his own running mate, Aaron Burr, and the Federalist-controlled House of Representatives had to decide. After thirty-five deadlocked ballots it chose Jefferson. Adams accepted defeat and left office peacefully, the first transfer of power from one party to another in the United States.

cards.q: Why does the Election of 1800 matter?
cards.a: The election of 1800 established that an American government could be voted out and would leave. That precedent of peacefully handing power to the opposition became the foundation of American democracy.

cards.q: What led to the Election of 1800?
cards.a: A divided Federalist Party. Many Federalists turned against Adams because he made peace with France instead of fighting a war. A private letter in which Hamilton described Adams’s “great and intrinsic defects in his character” was obtained by Burr and leaked to the press. New York. Jefferson knew he had to carry New York, so Burr, a New Yorker, joined the ticket.

Neither candidate campaigned in person; the battle was fought in party newspapers. One Federalist paper warned that under Jefferson “murder, robbery, rape, adultery, and incest will be openly taught and practiced,” and others attacked him as an infidel.

entries.title: Marbury v. Madison
entries.subtitle: The case in which the Supreme Court first struck down an act of Congress
entries.summary: In Marbury v. Madison, Chief Justice John Marshall turned a small dispute over an undelivered commission into the foundation of American judicial power. The Court ruled that William Marbury had a right to his appointment as a justice of the peace, but that it could not order the commission delivered, because the part of the Judiciary Act of 1789 that gave it that power conflicted with the Constitution. It was the first time the Supreme Court declared an act of Congress unconstitutional. In doing so it asserted the power of judicial review, the authority to decide whether laws conform to the Constitution, which the Constitution itself nowhere spells out.

entries.title: The Louisiana Purchase
entries.subtitle: The United States doubles in size, 1803
entries.summary: In 1803 the United States bought the Louisiana Territory from France for $15 million. The land stretched from the Mississippi River to the Rocky Mountains, covered 828,000 square miles, and doubled the size of the country. President Thomas Jefferson had only wanted to buy New Orleans and the Floridas, but Napoleon, who had just lost an army to yellow fever and revolt in Haiti and expected war with Britain, offered the whole territory. The purchase secured the Mississippi for American farmers and opened the way west. It also raised questions that would trouble the country for decades: whether the Constitution allowed it, whether slavery would spread into the new land, and what would become of the many Native nations who lived there.

cards.q: Why does the Louisiana Purchase matter?
cards.a: The Louisiana Purchase made the United States a continental power and secured the Mississippi, but it also planted the conflicts over slavery and Native land that would define the next half-century.

cards.q: What led to the Louisiana Purchase?
cards.a: Westerners were alarmed to see the stronger power of France at New Orleans. Jefferson wrote that “there is on the globe one single spot, the possessor of which is our natural and habitual enemy.
The French offered a surprised Monroe and Livingston not only New Orleans but the entire territory for $15 million.

entries.title: The Lewis and Clark Expedition
entries.subtitle: The Corps of Discovery crosses the continent, 1804–1806
entries.summary: At Thomas Jefferson’s direction, Meriwether Lewis and William Clark led the Corps of Discovery, a small party made up mostly of U.S. Army enlisted men, up the Missouri River from near St. Louis in May 1804. They crossed the Rocky Mountains, reached the Pacific coast in November 1805 and returned to St. Louis on September 23, 1806, after a journey the National Archives puts at 8,000 miles. They mapped the West, recorded its plants and animals, and met more than fifty Native nations. Their survival depended on Native hosts and guides, among them Sacagawea, a Lemhi Shoshone woman, and on the labor of York, a man enslaved by Clark.
