cards.q: Why does the Harlem Renaissance matter?
cards.a: The Harlem Renaissance made Black writers, artists, and musicians central to American culture and gave later civil rights generations a powerful tradition of self-expression.

Black Americans entered the 1920s weighed down by Jim Crow segregation, lynching, and the racial violence of 1919’s “Red Summer.” Harlem Renaissance writers and artists sought to define Black life on their own terms.

cards.q: How did it pursue its goals?
cards.a: The movement worked through culture: novels, poetry, short stories, theater, painting, and music. Locke’s anthology The New Negro (1925) gathered writing by men and women, young and old, Black and white, a book, as The American Yawp puts it, of African Americans rather than only about them.

entries.title: Immigration Act of 1924
entries.subtitle: The Johnson-Reed Act and the national origins quota system
entries.summary: The Immigration Act of 1924, also called the Johnson-Reed Act, sharply limited immigration through a national origins quota. Each nationality was allotted visas equal to 2 percent of the number of people of that nationality in the United States in the 1890 census, a formula designed to favor immigrants from northern and western Europe and to cut immigration from southern and eastern Europe. The law also barred virtually all immigration from Asia. The quota system it created remained the main way the United States selected immigrants until 1965.

cards.q: Why does Immigration Act of 1924 matter?
cards.a: The 1924 act wrote ideas about racial and national hierarchy into federal law and sharply curtailed immigration from southern and eastern Europe and Asia.

In 1917, amid wartime anxiety about national security, Congress passed the first broadly restrictive immigration law. It required a literacy test for immigrants over 16 and barred people from an “Asiatic Barred Zone.”

The 1924 law lowered the quota from 3 to 2 percent and moved the base year back from 1910 to 1890: before the largest waves of immigration from Italy, Poland, Russia, and other parts of southern and eastern Europe.

entries.title: Route 66
entries.subtitle: The “Mother Road” from Chicago to Santa Monica
entries.summary: U.S. Highway 66 was created in 1926 as part of the first national system of numbered highways, to meet the growing demand for automobile travel. Its roughly 2,400 miles linked the main streets of small towns to cities from Chicago to Southern California. It carried families fleeing the Dust Bowl in the 1930s and military convoys in World War II, then fed the postwar boom in road-trip tourism. Decommissioned as a federal highway in 1985, “Route 66” lives on in literature, film, and song as a symbol of mobility, freedom, and the American Dream.

videos.title: Why Route 66 became America’s most famous road
Route 66: The Asphalt Soul of America

quotes.text: Perhaps more than any other highway, Route 66 has come to symbolize hope, progress, and the spirit of adventure.
quotes.speaker: National Park Service

Route 66 is the classic American road: a record of how the automobile and federal highway planning remade everyday life, of Depression-era migration and wartime mobilization, and a lasting symbol of hope, progress, and the open road.

Route 66 did not run straight across the country. The Federal Highway Administration describes it as “a crescent route” from Chicago to the Pacific, which crossed most of the transcontinental highways and was bound to be one of the busiest. Much of the old road survives.

From trails to numbers. In the early twentieth century, long-distance roads were known by names such as the Lincoln Highway or the Dixie Highway, promoted by private trail associations. In 1925 the Secretary of Agriculture appointed a Joint Board of federal and state highway officials to lay out a national system of numbered routes with uniform signs, so that, as the Federal Highway Administration puts it, “people may travel across the continent following the same number.” One of its members was Cyrus Avery of Oklahoma.

entries.title: Mount Rushmore
entries.subtitle: Four presidents carved into the Black Hills, on land sacred to the Lakota
entries.summary: Between 1927 and 1941, sculptor Gutzon Borglum and about 400 workers blasted and carved the faces of George Washington, Thomas Jefferson, Theodore Roosevelt, and Abraham Lincoln into a granite mountain in South Dakota’s Black Hills. Meant to represent the nation’s birth, growth, development, and preservation, it draws more than two million visitors a year. But the Black Hills were recognized by treaty as Lakota land and are sacred to many tribes, and the memorial remains a contested symbol.

cards.a: Four presidents carved into the Black Hills, on land sacred to the Lakota

Mount Rushmore is both a celebration of American democracy and a reminder of broken treaties, one of the clearest places to see how a single monument can carry opposite meanings.
The memorial sits on a granite face of the Black Hills, the easternmost extension of the Rocky Mountains, in Pennington County, South Dakota.

The name Black Hills comes from the Lakota Paha Sapa, “hills of black.” By the late 1700s the Lakota controlled the region after defeating the Cheyenne, and religious ceremonies were held there every year.

entries.title: Stock Market Crash of 1929
entries.subtitle: The collapse that ended the Roaring Twenties boom
entries.summary: In October 1929 the great stock market boom of the 1920s collapsed. After panic selling on “Black Thursday,” October 24, the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell nearly 13 percent on Black Monday, October 28, and nearly 12 percent more on Black Tuesday, October 29. The slide continued until 1932, when stocks had lost 89 percent of their peak value. The crash did not by itself cause the Great Depression, but it frightened investors and consumers and exposed deep weaknesses in the economy.

cards.q: Why does Stock Market Crash of 1929 matter?
cards.a: The Crash of 1929 became the symbolic beginning of the Great Depression and a lasting warning about speculation and borrowed money.

cards.q: What led to Stock Market Crash of 1929?
cards.a: Federal Reserve officials believed speculation was diverting credit from productive uses. The Board urged reserve banks to deny credit to member banks that lent to speculators, and in August 1929 it allowed the New York Fed to raise its discount rate to 6 percent.

Prices peaked on September 3, 1929. As they fell in October, leading bankers met at the offices of J. P. Morgan, pooled funds, and publicly bought blocks of shares at high prices to restore confidence.

entries.title: The Great Depression
entries.subtitle: The deepest economic collapse in American history, 1929–1941
entries.summary: The Great Depression was the longest and deepest economic downturn in the history of the United States and the modern industrial economy. Beginning in 1929, it brought a stock market crash, thousands of bank failures, collapsing farm prices, and unemployment that reached about a quarter of the workforce. The Federal Reserve’s own historians now say its mistakes made the slump far worse. Herbert Hoover’s reliance on voluntary action gave way to Franklin D. Roosevelt’s New Deal, which transformed the federal government, but full recovery came only with World War II.

cards.q: Why does the Great Depression matter?
cards.a: The Great Depression was the worst economic disaster in American history. It discredited the belief that the economy would right itself without government help and gave rise to the New Deal and the modern federal government.

cards.q: What led to the Great Depression?
cards.a: Historians and economists still debate the Depression’s causes, and most see several working together. The Miller Center lists structural weaknesses in agriculture and industry, a fragile international economy, and a speculative, unstable financial sector, all of which created a badly unequal distribution of wealth: “a consumer economy in which few consumed.”
The crash. On Thursday, October 24, 1929, stock prices suddenly plunged.

entries.title: The Dust Bowl
entries.subtitle: Drought, dust storms, and migration on the southern Plains in the 1930s
entries.summary: During the 1930s, years of drought combined with farming practices that had stripped the Great Plains of its protective grass, and high winds lifted the exposed soil into enormous dust storms. The worst-hit area (the western third of Kansas, southeastern Colorado, the Oklahoma Panhandle, most of the Texas Panhandle, and northeastern New Mexico) became known as the Dust Bowl. Farms failed, hundreds of thousands of people left the region, and the disaster pushed the federal government to promote soil conservation.

videos.title: The Dust Bowl: Darkness in the Great Depression

cards.a: Drought, dust storms, and migration on the southern Plains in the 1930s

cards.q: Why does the Dust Bowl matter?
cards.a: The Dust Bowl was one of the worst environmental disasters in American history, a human-made catastrophe as much as a natural one, and it changed how Americans farm and manage land.

cards.q: What led to the Dust Bowl?
cards.a: Drought covered almost the entire Plains for nearly a decade, in at least four distinct episodes that came too quickly for the land to recover. With the ground cover gone and few windbreaks, high winds churned the dry topsoil into storms that people called “black blizzards” or “dusters.”
Dust storms blotted out the sun, choked people and livestock,. Some carried dirt as far east as Washington, D.C., New England, and ships on the Atlantic.

entries.title: Bonnie and Clyde
entries.subtitle: Depression-era outlaws whose short, violent crime spree became an American legend
entries.summary: Bonnie Parker and Clyde Barrow were young Texans who, from 1932 to 1934, robbed grocery stores, filling stations, and small banks across the Southwest and Midwest and killed a number of people, several of them law officers. A posse led by former Texas Ranger Frank Hamer killed them in a roadside ambush in Louisiana on May 23, 1934. Small-time criminals in life, they became one of America’s most enduring legends, above all through the 1967 film Bonnie and Clyde.

cards.q: Why does Bonnie and Clyde matter?
cards.a: Bonnie and Clyde show how Americans turned real Depression-era violence into romantic legend, and how popular culture, especially film, can reshape the memory of history.

cards.q: What led to Bonnie and Clyde?

The gang robbed stores, filling stations, and small banks in Texas, Oklahoma, New Mexico, Missouri, and beyond, and killed lawmen and civilians along the way.

entries.title: The New Deal
entries.subtitle: Franklin D. Roosevelt’s programs of relief, recovery, and reform, 1933–1939
entries.summary: The New Deal was President Franklin D. Roosevelt’s response to the Great Depression: a burst of federal programs to stabilize the banks, put the unemployed to work, raise farm prices, protect workers’ right to organize, and create a safety net for the elderly and the jobless. It did not end the Depression, and it left racial and gender inequalities largely in place. But it transformed the role of the federal government and the presidency, and it built a Democratic coalition that dominated politics for a generation.

cards.q: Why does the New Deal matter?
cards.a: The New Deal did not end the Great Depression, but it made the federal government responsible for the economic security of ordinary Americans. It created institutions, from Social Security to the FDIC, that still shape American life.

cards.q: What led to the New Deal?
cards.a: The New Deal had no single blueprint.

The Hundred Days. “The only thing we have to fear is fear itself,” Roosevelt said in his inaugural address. Two days later he declared a national bank holiday, and Congress passed his Emergency Banking Act almost sight unseen.

entries.title: Social Security Act
entries.subtitle: The 1935 law that created old-age pensions and unemployment insurance
entries.summary: Signed by President Franklin D. Roosevelt on August 14, 1935, the Social Security Act created a national system of old-age benefits for workers, funded by taxes on wages and payrolls, along with unemployment insurance and aid to dependent children, people who are blind, and people with disabilities. It was the centerpiece of the Second New Deal and the foundation of the American safety net, though at first it excluded farm and domestic workers, a policy that disproportionately affected African Americans.

cards.q: Why does Social Security Act matter?
cards.a: The Social Security Act established that the federal government shares responsibility for Americans’ economic security in old age and hard times. Expanded many times since, it became the centerpiece of the American social welfare state.

Before the 1930s, caring for the elderly was left to families, localities, and states; except for veterans’ pensions, Washington played no role. The Great Depression wiped out savings and jobs and built support for national old-age insurance.

Unlike many European systems, American old-age insurance was funded by “contributions”, taxes on individual wages and employer payrolls, rather than general government revenue. Roosevelt insisted on this design to separate Social Security from the stigma of welfare; “No dole,” he said repeatedly.

entries.title: Attack on Pearl Harbor
entries.subtitle: Japan’s surprise attack that brought the United States into World War II
entries.summary: On the morning of December 7, 1941, Japanese planes attacked the U.S. Pacific Fleet at Pearl Harbor, Hawaii. In less than two hours the fleet was devastated and more than 3,500 Americans were killed or wounded, about 2,400 of them killed. The next day President Franklin D. Roosevelt called December 7 “a date which will live in infamy,” and Congress declared war on Japan. The attack ended American isolationism and brought the United States into World War II.

cards.q: Why does Attack on Pearl Harbor matter?
cards.a: The attack on Pearl Harbor turned two regional wars into a true world war and committed the United States to global leadership.

cards.q: What led to Attack on Pearl Harbor?
cards.a: Facing severe shortages, unwilling to leave China, and convinced that American officials opposed further talks, Japan’s leaders decided to strike first. Their planners hoped to destroy enough battleships and aircraft carriers to cripple American naval power while Japan seized resource-rich territories in Southeast Asia.
Japanese aircraft struck the fleet at anchor. The battleship USS Arizona was sunk with the loss of 1,177 crew members; more than 900 of them remain entombed in the ship.

entries.title: World War II
entries.subtitle: The United States in the global war, 1941–1945
entries.summary: World War II was the deadliest and most destructive war in human history: perhaps eighty million people died. The United States entered after Japan’s attack on Pearl Harbor on December 7, 1941, and fought alongside Britain, the Soviet Union, China, and other Allies against Germany, Italy, and Japan. The Soviet Union bore the heaviest burden of the war against Germany and broke Hitler’s army, while American factories armed the Allies and American forces fought in North Africa, Italy, and France and across the Pacific. The war ended with Germany’s surrender in May 1945 and Japan’s in August, after the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki. It left the United States the world’s leading economic and military power.

cards.q: Why does World War II matter?
cards.a: World War II was the most destructive conflict in history. It defeated fascism and Nazism through the combined efforts of the Allies; the Soviet Union, at a cost of some 24 to 25 million lives, broke the German army, while Britain and the United States fought in the west and the Pacific.

For Japan, the war began a decade before Pearl Harbor. In September 1931 an explosion on a Japanese-owned railway in Manchuria, most likely staged by the Japanese themselves, gave Japan’s army a pretext to seize the region.
Midway (June 1942). The carrier battle, with the earlier fight in the Coral Sea, crippled Japan’s naval operations in the Pacific.

entries.title: Executive Order 9066
entries.subtitle: The 1942 order that led to the incarceration of Japanese Americans
entries.summary: Executive Order 9066, signed by President Franklin D. Roosevelt on February 19, 1942, ten weeks after Pearl Harbor, allowed the Secretary of War and military commanders to declare “military areas” and exclude “any or all persons” from them. It named no ethnic group, but it was used against only one. Under its authority the Army removed people of Japanese ancestry from the West Coast, about 120,000 people, most of them American citizens, and held them in camps. None was charged with a crime. President Gerald Ford formally declared in 1976 that the order’s authority had ended long before, calling its issuance “a sad day in American history.” In 1988 Congress apologized and paid redress.

Executive Order 9066 showed how a president’s wartime power could be turned against a group of Americans defined by their ancestry.
Between 1861 and 1940 about 275,000 Japanese immigrated to Hawaii and the mainland United States.

The order rested on wartime necessity: “the successful prosecution of the war requires every possible protection against espionage and against sabotage.” Acting “as President of the United States, and Commander in Chief of the Army and Navy,” Roosevelt authorized the Secretary of War and designated military commanders to prescribe military areas “from which any or all persons may be excluded.”

entries.title: Japanese American Incarceration
entries.subtitle: The forced removal and imprisonment of Japanese Americans during World War II
entries.summary: After Japan attacked Pearl Harbor, the United States government forced about 120,000 people of Japanese ancestry from their homes on the West Coast and held them in camps for most of World War II. Nearly 70,000 of them were American citizens. None was charged with a crime, and none could appeal. The removal rested on Executive Order 9066, signed by President Franklin D. Roosevelt on February 19, 1942, and the Supreme Court upheld it in Korematsu v. United States (1944). In 1988 Congress acknowledged that the incarceration was a “grave injustice” caused by “racial prejudice, wartime hysteria, and a failure of political leadership.” It apologized and paid $20,000 to each survivor.

entries.title: D-Day
entries.subtitle: The Allied invasion of Normandy, June 6, 1944
entries.summary: On June 6, 1944, nearly 160,000 American, British, Canadian, and other Allied troops landed along fifty miles of the heavily fortified Normandy coast of France, supported by more than 5,000 ships and 13,000 aircraft. Called Operation Overlord and commanded by General Dwight D. Eisenhower, it was the largest amphibious assault in history. More than 9,000 Allied soldiers were killed or wounded that day, but the Allies gained a foothold in western Europe that led to the liberation of France and the defeat of Nazi Germany.

entries.title: Korematsu v. United States
entries.subtitle: The Supreme Court upholds the wartime exclusion of Japanese Americans
entries.summary: Fred Korematsu, a 23-year-old American citizen of Japanese ancestry, refused to leave his home in the San Francisco Bay Area when the Army ordered all Japanese Americans removed under Executive Order 9066. In Korematsu v. United States, the Supreme Court upheld his conviction 6–3, accepting the government’s claim of military necessity. Three justices dissented, one of them condemning the decision as racism. Decades later, evidence that the government had suppressed proof undermining its case led a federal court to overturn Korematsu’s conviction.

cards.q: Why does Korematsu v. United States matter?
cards.a: Korematsu shows how courts can fail to protect constitutional rights in wartime, and Fred Korematsu’s long fight to clear his name became a symbol of resistance to injustice.

cards.q: What question did the Court have to answer?
cards.a: Did the president and Congress exceed their war powers by excluding Americans of Japanese descent from the West Coast and restricting their rights?
The Court upheld the exclusion order and Korematsu’s conviction by a vote of 6–3.

Designed by the American Legion and passed unanimously, the “G.I. Bill of Rights” helped some eight million veterans continue their education and millions more buy homes. It fueled the postwar boom and the growth of the suburbs. But its benefits were not shared equally: discrimination and segregation kept many Black veterans and women from using them fully.

cards.q: Why does the G.I. Bill matter?
cards.a: The G.I. Bill helped turn millions of veterans into college graduates and homeowners. The Yawp writes that it “established the hallmarks of American middle class life.”
While the war was still being fought, the Department of Labor estimated that 15 million men and women in uniform could come home to unemployment. Many feared a return of the Great Depression.

The act declared the Veterans Administration “an essential war agency,” second only to the War and Navy Departments in priority for personnel and supplies. It authorized $500 million for new veterans’ hospitals. Its best-known titles gave veterans four kinds of help.

entries.title: Atomic Bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki
entries.subtitle: The first and only use of nuclear weapons in war, August 1945
entries.summary: On August 6, 1945, an American B-29 bomber dropped an atomic bomb on Hiroshima, Japan; three days later a second bomb struck Nagasaki. Some 70,000 people probably died immediately at Hiroshima, and more than 100,000 by the end of 1945; the best estimate at Nagasaki is 40,000 initial deaths. Japan announced its surrender on August 15. The bombings ended World War II and opened the nuclear age, and whether they were necessary remains one of the most debated questions in American history.

cards.q: Why does Atomic Bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki matter?
cards.a: Hiroshima and Nagasaki ended the deadliest war in history and made the prospect of nuclear annihilation a permanent feature of world politics.

cards.q: What led to Atomic Bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki?
cards.a: After the bloody battles of Iwo Jima and Okinawa, U.S. officials expected Japanese forces to fight fiercely for their home islands; some estimated that an invasion could cost half a million American casualties and perhaps millions of Japanese civilians. These estimates were later cited to justify the bombings.

Hiroshima. Hiroshima, a city of almost 300,000 civilians and an important military center, was the primary target. At about 8:15 a.m. on August 6, the B-29 Enola Gay, piloted by Colonel Paul Tibbets, released “Little Boy,” which exploded 1,900 feet above the city.

entries.title: United Nations
entries.subtitle: The international organization founded in 1945 to keep the peace
entries.summary: The United Nations was founded in 1945 by the victorious Allies of World War II to prevent future wars through collective security and international cooperation. Unlike the League of Nations after World War I, it had strong American backing: the Senate approved the UN Charter 89 to 2. The United States is one of five permanent members of the Security Council, each holding a veto. The UN has been a central, and often contested, arena of American foreign policy ever since.

The United Nations embodied the American commitment, after two world wars, to lead a rules-based international order rather than retreat from the world.
On January 1, 1942, 26 nations at war with the Axis signed the Declaration of the United Nations in Washington, endorsing the Atlantic Charter and pledging not to make a separate peace.

cards.q: What can it do, and what limits it?
cards.a: The Charter created a General Assembly of all member states; a Security Council with five permanent members, each holding a veto, and elected non-permanent members; an Economic and Social Council; an International Court of Justice; a Trusteeship Council to oversee certain colonial territories; and a Secretariat headed by a Secretary-General.

entries.title: The Cold War
entries.subtitle: The global rivalry between the United States and the Soviet Union, 1947–1991
entries.summary: The Cold War was a global political and ideological rivalry between the capitalist countries led by the United States and the communist countries led by the Soviet Union. It grew out of the failure of the World War II allies to agree on the postwar world and lasted from the late 1940s until the Soviet Union dissolved in December 1991. The two superpowers never fought each other directly. Instead they built rival alliances, raced to build nuclear weapons and to reach space, and backed opposing sides in wars from Korea to Vietnam. The closest they came to nuclear war was the Cuban Missile Crisis of October 1962.

cards.q: Why does the Cold War matter?
cards.a: For more than four decades the Cold War defined world politics. It divided Europe, spread conflict and competition to every continent, and produced the nuclear arms race and the space race.
The Soviet Union and the United States had been allies against Germany, but the alliance rested on necessity.

The Truman Doctrine and Marshall Plan (1947–1948): committed the United States to containing Soviet influence in Europe. 1949: the end of the Berlin blockade, the founding of NATO, the first Soviet atomic bomb, and the communist victory in China. The Korean War (1950–1953): turned containment into a global military commitment. Sputnik (1957): opened the space race and shocked Americans into investing in science and rockets. The Cuban Missile Crisis (1962): the moment the superpowers came closest to nuclear war, followed by the first arms control agreements. The fall of the Berlin Wall (1989) and the end of the Soviet Union (1991).

entries.title: The Marshall Plan
entries.subtitle: The European Recovery Program, 1948–1952
entries.summary: The Marshall Plan was a massive American program to rebuild the war-ravaged economies of Western Europe after World War II. Proposed by Secretary of State George C. Marshall in a June 1947 speech at Harvard, it provided more than $12 billion between 1948 and 1952. American leaders saw it as both a humanitarian effort and a way to stop the spread of communism by restoring prosperity. The Soviet Union refused to take part and kept its Eastern European satellites out, deepening the division of Europe.

cards.q: Why does the Marshall Plan matter?
cards.a: The Marshall Plan was one of the most ambitious and successful foreign policy initiatives in American history, binding Western Europe to the United States at the start of the Cold War.

cards.q: What led to the Marshall Plan?
cards.a: Coming just months after the Truman Doctrine, Marshall’s proposal argued that the United States should help restore “normal economic health to the world, without which there can be no political stability and no assured peace.”

American aid poured into Western Europe for reconstruction while trade barriers were loosened. Participation by the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe was initially possible, but Stalin, suspicious of American economic domination and unwilling to open Soviet society to Westerners, refused.

entries.title: Korean War
entries.subtitle: The first major armed conflict of the Cold War, 1950–1953
entries.summary: On June 25, 1950, communist North Korea invaded South Korea. Under a United Nations mandate, the United States led a multinational force to defend the South. After dramatic swings (a near-collapse, the landing at Inchon, a drive to the Chinese border, and a massive Chinese intervention), the war settled into a bloody stalemate near the 38th parallel. An armistice in July 1953 ended the fighting but left Korea divided. More than 30,000 Americans and millions of Koreans died.

Korea was the first “hot” war of the Cold War, a limited war fought to contain communism without triggering a wider conflict with the Soviet Union or China.

At the end of World War II, the United States and the Soviet Union divided Korea at the 38th parallel to accept the surrender of Japanese forces. The Soviets backed a communist government in the North; the United States backed Rhee in the South.

The Inchon landing (September 1950): reversed the North Korean invasion. Chinese entry (late 1950): turned a near-victory into a long, bloody stalemate. MacArthur’s dismissal (April 1951): affirmed civilian control of the military and the decision to keep the war limited.

entries.title: McCarthyism and the Second Red Scare

Congressional committees, the FBI, loyalty boards, and private employers investigated thousands of Americans; many lost their jobs or were blacklisted for past political associations. The era takes its name from Senator Joseph McCarthy of Wisconsin, who from 1950 made sensational, unsupported charges that communists had infiltrated the government, until televised hearings in 1954 exposed his tactics and the Senate condemned him.

entries.title: Brown v. Board of Education
entries.subtitle: The Supreme Court strikes down school segregation
entries.summary: In Brown v. Board of Education of Topeka, decided May 17, 1954, a unanimous Supreme Court held that racial segregation in public schools violates the Fourteenth Amendment’s guarantee of equal protection of the laws. “Separate educational facilities are inherently unequal,” Chief Justice Earl Warren wrote, overturning the “separate but equal” doctrine of Plessy v. Ferguson in public education. The victory crowned decades of NAACP litigation led by Thurgood Marshall. But the Court’s vague order to desegregate “with all deliberate speed” met fierce resistance, and most Southern schools were not integrated until the late 1960s and early 1970s.

entries.title: The Civil Rights Movement
entries.subtitle: The mass struggle against segregation and disfranchisement, 1950s–1960s
entries.summary: The civil rights movement was a mass campaign by Black Americans and their allies to end legal segregation and win the right to vote in the South. Building on decades of NAACP lawsuits, it won the Supreme Court’s Brown v. Board of Education decision in 1954 and then turned to nonviolent direct action: the Montgomery bus boycott, the sit-ins, the Freedom Rides, the Birmingham campaign, the March on Washington, Freedom Summer, and the Selma marches. Its victories, the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and the Voting Rights Act of 1965, dismantled Jim Crow in law and transformed American democracy.

cards.q: Why does the Civil Rights Movement matter?
cards.a: The civil rights movement ended legal segregation in the United States, brought about the greatest change in federal protection of voting since Reconstruction, and showed how ordinary people using nonviolent mass action could change the law of a nation.

The movement set out to destroy Jim Crow, the system of laws and customs that segregated Black Southerners in schools, buses, restaurants, parks, and jobs and kept most of them from voting. After World War II, the “Double V” campaign for victory over fascism abroad and racism at home, and the postwar boom, raised expectations that persistent segregation then disappointed. The demands of the 1963 March on Washington summed up the movement’s program: a comprehensive civil rights bill ending segregated public accommodations, “protection of the right to vote,” “desegregation of all public schools,” a federal jobs program, and a law “barring discrimination in all employment.” King described the ultimate end as “the creation of the beloved community,” “a society at peace with itself, a society that can live with its conscience”; by the end of his life he argued that full citizenship also required economic security.

cards.q: How did it pursue its goals?
cards.a: In the courts. Beginning in the early 1930s, NAACP lawyers including Charles Hamilton Houston and Thurgood Marshall chose cases on education, voting, and juries to wear away the legal foundations of segregation, first arguing that Southern states failed to provide even “equal” facilities and then, by the late 1940s, that separation itself was unconstitutional. Brown v. Board of Education combined five cases from South Carolina, Virginia, Delaware, Washington, D.C., and Kansas.

entries.title: Montgomery Bus Boycott
entries.subtitle: The thirteen-month protest that launched the modern civil rights movement
entries.summary: The Montgomery bus boycott began on December 5, 1955, four days after Rosa Parks was arrested for refusing to give up her bus seat to a white passenger. For 381 days Montgomery’s Black residents walked, shared rides, and organized carpools rather than ride segregated city buses. The protest was planned by the Women’s Political Council and E. D. Nixon and led by the Montgomery Improvement Association. Its president was a twenty-six-year-old minister, Martin Luther King Jr. It survived bombings, mass indictments, and court injunctions, and it ended in victory after the Supreme Court affirmed, in Browder v. Gayle, that bus segregation was unconstitutional. The boycott made King a national figure and showed that nonviolent mass protest could defeat Jim Crow.

cards.q: Why does Montgomery Bus Boycott matter?
cards.a: Montgomery proved that ordinary people acting together could defeat Jim Crow, and it introduced Martin Luther King Jr. to the nation.

Eisenhower sent troops of the Army’s 101st Airborne Division to escort and protect the students, a dramatic use of federal power to enforce Brown v. Board of Education.

entries.title: The Space Race
entries.subtitle: From Sputnik to the moon: the Cold War contest for supremacy in space, 1957–1969
entries.summary: On October 4, 1957, the Soviet Union launched Sputnik, the world’s first artificial satellite, a beach-ball-sized sphere that circled Earth every ninety-eight minutes. Americans were shocked: if the Soviets could put a satellite in orbit, they could surely send nuclear missiles across the ocean. The Cold War rivalry moved into space. The United States answered with its own satellite, created NASA, and, after the Soviets put the first human in orbit in 1961, President John F. Kennedy pledged to land an American on the moon by the end of the decade, a goal reached with Apollo 11 in July 1969.

cards.q: Why does the Space Race matter?
cards.a: The space race turned science and engineering into instruments of Cold War competition, created NASA, and poured billions of dollars into research. Its triumph, the moon landing, restored American confidence after years of Soviet firsts.

cards.q: What led to the Space Race?
cards.a: The contest grew out of the Cold War rivalry between the United States and the Soviet Union and their competing ideologies. Each side wanted to prove its technological and military strength to the world, and the Soviet Union, with powerful rockets developed under the engineer Sergei Korolev, struck first.
Sputnik caught the American public off guard. A month later Sputnik 2 carried a dog, Laika, into orbit; she died soon after launch.

entries.title: Red Power and the American Indian Movement
entries.subtitle: Native activism for sovereignty and self-determination, 1960s–1970s
entries.summary: Inspired by the civil rights movement, young Native Americans in the 1960s and 1970s launched an intertribal movement known as Red Power to protest discrimination and assert tribal sovereignty. Activists held “fish-ins” to defend treaty fishing rights, occupied Alcatraz Island for nineteen months in 1969–1971, and, led by the American Indian Movement (AIM), occupied the town of Wounded Knee, South Dakota, for months in 1973. The movement helped end the federal policy of terminating tribes and win a policy of Indian self-determination.

cards.q: Why does Red Power and the American Indian Movement matter?
cards.a: Red Power made Native Americans’ demands for sovereignty visible to the nation and reshaped federal Indian policy.
Activists demanded respect for treaty rights, tribal sovereignty and self-determination, return of land, and an end to discrimination and to federal efforts to dissolve tribes.

cards.q: How did it pursue its goals?
cards.a: In 1961 Native university students founded the National Indian Youth Council, whose militant rhetoric and direct action began the Red Power movement. In 1964 it held “fish-ins” in the Pacific Northwest, casting nets in defiance of state laws to defend tribal fishing rights.

entries.title: Second-Wave Feminism
entries.subtitle: The women’s liberation movement of the 1960s and 1970s
entries.summary: In the 1960s and 1970s a new wave of feminism challenged discrimination against women at work, in law, in education, and in family life. Many of its activists had worked in the civil rights and labor movements and found that male leaders there were not interested in gender inequality. Galvanized by Betty Friedan’s The Feminine Mystique (1963), they founded the National Organization for Women, formed consciousness-raising groups, and fought for equal pay, reproductive rights, and an Equal Rights Amendment. They won major legal changes, including the use of Title VII against job discrimination and Roe v. Wade in 1973. But a conservative countermovement led by Phyllis Schlafly stopped the ERA three states short of ratification.

Second-wave feminism transformed women’s legal status and opportunities and changed American expectations about work, family, and equality, while also provoking a lasting conservative reaction.

Feminists sought equal treatment in jobs and pay, an end to sex discrimination in law, access to contraception and abortion, child care, and equality in marriage. NOW’s founding statement, written by Friedan, pledged “to bring women into full participation in the mainstream of American society now, exercising all the privileges and responsibilities thereof in truly equal partnership with men.” The movement’s central constitutional goal was the Equal Rights Amendment, first proposed in Congress in 1923, which declared: “Equality of rights under the law shall not be denied or abridged by the United States or any state on account of sex.”

cards.q: How did it pursue its goals?
cards.a: Working through government. In the early 1960s an older generation of women worked through official institutions. President John F. Kennedy’s Commission on the Status of Women, chaired by former first lady Eleanor Roosevelt, issued its report in 1963 as an “invitation to action.”

entries.title: The Cuban Missile Crisis
entries.subtitle: The October 1962 showdown in which the superpowers came closest to nuclear war
entries.summary: In October 1962 an American U-2 spy plane photographed Soviet nuclear missile sites under construction in Cuba. In the days that followed, President John F. Kennedy and Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev faced each other in the most dangerous confrontation of the Cold War, the moment when the two superpowers came closest to nuclear conflict. Kennedy imposed a naval “quarantine” of the island; Khrushchev finally agreed to remove the missiles in exchange for an American pledge not to invade Cuba, and a secret promise to pull U.S. missiles out of Turkey.

cards.q: Why does the Cuban Missile Crisis matter?
cards.a: The crisis brought the world to the edge of nuclear war and then pushed both superpowers to step back: they set up a direct line of communication and took the first steps toward controlling the nuclear arms race.

cards.q: What led to the Cuban Missile Crisis?
cards.a: The crisis grew out of the arms race and the Cold War rivalry over Cuba. The Soviets wanted to protect Castro’s government, to compete with China for the loyalty of revolutionaries worldwide, and to neutralize the large American advantage in nuclear weapons.

On October 14 a U-2 took pictures clearly showing sites for medium- and intermediate-range nuclear missiles; the next day the photographs reached the White House. Kennedy gathered his closest advisers in secret meetings.

entries.title: The Environmental Movement
entries.subtitle: From Silent Spring to Earth Day and the EPA
entries.summary: In the 1960s, growing alarm about pollution, pesticides, and the destruction of open space produced a mass environmental movement. Rachel Carson’s Silent Spring (1962) warned of the dangers of pesticides to wildlife and people. The first Earth Day, April 22, 1970, was, in the words of the American Yawp, the largest demonstration in history. A burst of lawmaking followed: the National Environmental Policy Act, the creation of the Environmental Protection Agency in 1970, and new laws to protect air, water, and endangered species.

cards.q: Why does the Environmental Movement matter?
cards.a: The environmental movement made protecting nature and public health a permanent responsibility of the federal government.

Environmentalists sought clean air and water, controls on pesticides and toxic chemicals, protection of wilderness and wildlife, and government accountability for the environmental effects of its projects.

cards.q: How did it pursue its goals?
cards.a: The movement grew from Americans’ postwar enjoyment of the outdoors and from science-based warnings like Carson’s. Dramatic events, such as the Cuyahoga River near Cleveland bursting into flames, drew attention.

Their Delano grape strike, begun in 1965, and a nationwide consumer boycott of table grapes led by Cesar Chavez, Dolores Huerta, and Larry Itliong won the first major union contracts in California agriculture by 1970. The United Farm Workers became both a union and a civil rights movement.

cards.q: Why does the Farm Workers Movement matter?
cards.a: The farm workers’ struggle joined labor organizing to the civil rights movement and made Chicano and Filipino workers visible in national politics.

Farm workers sought union recognition, higher wages (grape pickers averaged about 90 cents an hour in 1965), an end to child labor and dangerous conditions, protection from pesticides, and fair treatment. Chavez envisioned the union as both a labor organization and a civil rights movement for Chicano and Filipino workers.

cards.q: How did it pursue its goals?
cards.a: On September 8, 1965, Filipino workers of the AWOC, organized by Larry Itliong, struck nine farms near Delano. The NFWA voted to join on September 16.

entries.title: March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom
entries.subtitle: The 1963 march where King delivered “I Have a Dream”
entries.summary: On August 28, 1963, a crowd that the King Institute puts at more than 200,000 and the National Archives at more than 250,000 gathered in Washington, D.C., for the March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom. Conceived by the labor leader A. Philip Randolph and organized by Bayard Rustin in less than two months, it united the major civil rights organizations, labor unions, and churches. They demanded a strong civil rights law, voting rights, school desegregation, jobs, and fair employment. It closed at the Lincoln Memorial with Martin Luther King Jr.’s “I Have a Dream” speech. The march helped build pressure for the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and the Voting Rights Act of 1965, whose provisions reflected its demands.

cards.q: Why does March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom matter?
cards.a: The March on Washington joined the moral appeal of the civil rights movement to its economic demands. It showed the nation the movement’s size, discipline, and breadth, and it gave King’s dream of racial equality its most lasting expression.

cards.q: What led to March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom?
cards.a: The march’s official goals, as listed by the King Institute and the American Yawp, were a comprehensive civil rights bill ending segregation in public accommodations, protection of the right to vote, desegregation of all public schools in 1963, a federal works program to train and place unemployed workers, a federal fair employment law, and a higher minimum wage. Its full name, the March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom, reflected the economic demands at its heart, which came from Randolph’s labor background.
The day began with a rally at the Washington Monument featuring celebrities and musicians.

entries.title: Civil Rights Act of 1964
entries.subtitle: The law that outlawed segregation in public places and job discrimination
entries.summary: The Civil Rights Act of 1964, signed by President Lyndon B. Johnson on July 2, 1964, outlawed segregation in hotels, restaurants, theaters, and other public accommodations. It banned discrimination in employment, authorized federal action to desegregate schools and public facilities, and created the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission. The National Archives calls it “the most sweeping civil rights legislation since Reconstruction.” Proposed by John F. Kennedy after the protests of 1963, it was pushed through Congress after his assassination by Johnson and a bipartisan coalition, overcoming a Southern filibuster of 75 days. Together with the Voting Rights Act a year later, the American Yawp concludes, it “effectively ended Jim Crow.”

entries.title: The Great Society
entries.subtitle: Lyndon Johnson’s program to end poverty and racial injustice, 1964–1968
entries.summary: The Great Society was President Lyndon B. Johnson’s sweeping program of domestic reform. Announced in a May 1964 speech calling for “an end to poverty and racial injustice,” it produced the most ambitious burst of legislation since the New Deal: the War on Poverty, Medicare and Medicaid, federal aid to education, food stamps, the Civil Rights and Voting Rights Acts, and an immigration law that abolished the national-origins quotas of 1924. Much of it remains in place today.

cards.a: The Great Society expanded the federal government’s responsibility for health, education, and poverty more than any reform program since the New Deal.

cards.q: What led to the Great Society?
cards.a: Johnson, shaped by the New Deal and by his own family’s poverty in the Texas Hill Country, believed government could abolish poverty and racial injustice in an age of affluence.

The Economic Opportunity Act of 1964 launched the War on Poverty. Its most controversial program, Community Action, sought “maximum feasible participation” by the poor themselves in running antipoverty efforts.

entries.title: The Vietnam War
entries.subtitle: America’s longest war of the Cold War era, 1964–1973
entries.summary: The Vietnam War was a long struggle over the future of Vietnam in which the United States fought to keep a non-communist South Vietnam from being reunited with the communist North. It grew out of Vietnam’s war for independence from France and the American belief that if one country fell to communism, its neighbors would follow. American involvement deepened from advisers in the 1950s to more than 500,000 troops by 1968. Unable to win, the United States withdrew under the Paris Peace Accords of January 1973, and in April 1975 North Vietnamese forces took Saigon and reunified the country. The war killed 58,220 Americans, divided American society, and shook Americans’ trust in their government.

cards.q: Why does the Vietnam War matter?
cards.a: The Vietnam War was a defeat for American Cold War policy and a turning point in American history. It divided a generation, undermined faith in government, and made Americans wary of foreign wars for decades.

Vietnam had been ruled by France since the nineteenth century and was occupied by Japan during World War II. In 1945 the nationalist leader Ho Chi Minh declared Vietnam’s independence, quoting the American Declaration of Independence.

Dien Bien Phu (1954): the French defeat led to the partition of Vietnam and deepening American involvement. The Gulf of Tonkin Resolution (1964): gave Johnson a free hand to escalate the war. The Tet Offensive (1968): a military setback for the communists but a political turning point that turned many Americans against the war. Johnson’s withdrawal from the 1968 race: marked the end of escalation. The Paris Peace Accords (1973): ended direct American participation.

entries.title: Selma to Montgomery Marches

entries.summary: In early 1965, local activists, SNCC, and Martin Luther King Jr.’s SCLC campaigned for voting rights in Selma, Alabama, where only 2 percent of Black residents were registered. On March 7, remembered as “Bloody Sunday,” state troopers and local lawmen attacked peaceful marchers with clubs and tear gas at the Edmund Pettus Bridge. Televised images shocked the nation. Two weeks later, under federal protection, thousands marched the 54 miles to Montgomery. The campaign led directly to the Voting Rights Act of 1965.

cards.a: Selma turned the right to vote into a national cause and produced one of the most consequential laws in American history.

cards.q: What led to Selma to Montgomery Marches?
cards.a: On February 18, during a night march in nearby Marion, a state trooper shot Jimmie Lee Jackson, a 26-year-old church deacon, as he tried to protect his mother; he died eight days later. Activists resolved to march from Selma to the state capitol in Montgomery.

On Sunday, March 7, marchers crossed the Edmund Pettus Bridge and met a wall of state troopers and lawmen, who ordered them to disperse and then attacked, cheered on by white onlookers. John Lewis was severely beaten.

entries.title: Voting Rights Act of 1965
entries.subtitle: The law that enforced the Fifteenth Amendment
entries.summary: The Voting Rights Act of 1965, signed by President Lyndon B. Johnson on August 6, 1965, was “an act to enforce the fifteenth amendment,” passed ninety-five years after that amendment was ratified. It outlawed literacy tests and sent federal examiners to register voters in places with a history of discrimination. Its Section 5 required those places to get federal approval, called “preclearance,” before changing their voting rules. Congress acted after the violence of the Selma voting rights campaign, above all the attack on marchers on “Bloody Sunday,” March 7, 1965. Within months a quarter of a million new Black voters had registered. The Archives calls it the most significant change in federal–state relations over voting since Reconstruction.

cards.q: Why does Voting Rights Act of 1965 matter?
cards.a: The Voting Rights Act finally enforced the Fifteenth Amendment and transformed Southern politics. The American Yawp writes that together with the Civil Rights Act of 1964 it “effectively ended Jim Crow.” Johnson called the vote “the most powerful instrument ever devised by man for breaking down injustice.”

The Fifteenth Amendment (1870) forbade denying the vote on account of race, but from the 1890s Southern states had used literacy tests, poll taxes, and other devices to keep Black citizens from voting. Those who tried to register risked harassment, economic reprisals, and violence, and Black registration and political power stayed low. In the summer of 1964 three voting rights workers were murdered in Mississippi during Freedom Summer.
Section 2 applied nationwide. Closely following the Fifteenth Amendment, it forbade denying or abridging the right to vote on account of race or color.

entries.title: Miranda v. Arizona
entries.subtitle: The ruling that requires police to warn suspects of their rights
entries.summary: In Miranda v. Arizona (1966) the Supreme Court ruled 5 to 4 that the Fifth Amendment’s privilege against self-incrimination applies when police question a suspect in custody. Writing for the Court, Chief Justice Earl Warren held that before questioning, a person must be warned “that he has a right to remain silent, that any statement he does make may be used as evidence against him, and that he has a right to the presence of an attorney, either retained or appointed.” Statements taken without these safeguards could not be used in court. The “Miranda warnings” became a routine part of American policing, and in 2000 the Court declined to overrule the decision.

cards.q: Why does Miranda v. Arizona matter?
cards.a: Miranda v. Arizona turned the privilege against self-incrimination into a concrete routine that applies at the moment a person is most exposed to the power of the state.

cards.q: What question did the Court have to answer?
cards.a: Does the Fifth Amendment’s privilege against self-incrimination apply when police question a suspect in custody, and if so, what must police do to protect it?

The Court held that the prosecution “may not use statements, whether exculpatory or inculpatory, stemming from custodial interrogation of the defendant unless it demonstrates the use of procedural safeguards effective to secure the privilege against self-incrimination.” By custodial interrogation it meant “questioning initiated by law enforcement officers after a person has been taken into custody or otherwise deprived of his freedom of action in any significant way.”

entries.title: Loving v. Virginia
entries.subtitle: The Supreme Court strikes down bans on interracial marriage, 1967
entries.summary: Mildred Jeter, a woman of African American and Native descent, and Richard Loving, a white man, married in Washington, D.C., in 1958 and went home to Caroline County, Virginia. There they were arrested and convicted under the state’s ban on interracial marriage and ordered to leave Virginia for twenty-five years. In Loving v. Virginia (1967) a unanimous Supreme Court struck down the law, holding that it violated both the Equal Protection and Due Process Clauses of the Fourteenth Amendment. “Under our Constitution, the freedom to marry, or not marry, a person of another race resides with the individual and cannot be infringed by the State,” Chief Justice Earl Warren wrote. The decision ended such bans in Virginia and the fifteen other states that still had them.

entries.title: Apollo 11
entries.subtitle: The first human landing on the Moon, July 1969
entries.summary: On July 20, 1969, Apollo 11 astronauts Neil Armstrong and Edwin “Buzz” Aldrin landed the lunar module Eagle on the Moon’s Sea of Tranquility while Michael Collins orbited overhead in the command module Columbia. An estimated 650 million people watched as Armstrong stepped onto the surface, describing it as “one small step for a man, one giant leap for mankind.” The mission fulfilled President Kennedy’s 1961 goal of landing a man on the Moon and returning him safely to Earth, and it was a triumph for the United States in the space race with the Soviet Union.

entries.title: Woodstock
entries.subtitle: “3 Days of Peace and Music” that came to define a generation
entries.summary: In August 1969 nearly half a million young people gathered on Yasgur’s farm near Bethel, New York, for a music festival billed as “An Aquarian Exposition: 3 Days of Peace and Music.” Rain, mud, and shortages turned the weekend into an improvised city, and, for many, a demonstration of the counterculture’s ideals of peace and cooperation. Coming weeks after the Moon landing and amid conflict over the Vietnam War, civil rights, and sexual politics, Woodstock became shorthand for the youth culture of the 1960s.

videos.title: What Was the Original Woodstock Really Like

cards.a: “3 Days of Peace and Music” that came to define a generation

Woodstock is remembered as the high point of the 1960s counterculture, a symbol of a generation that challenged the values of its parents.

The festival took place weeks after Americans first walked on the Moon, against the backdrop of a nation divided over the Vietnam War, civil rights, and sexual politics. PBS describes a sense of an America in transition, a handoff between generations with very different values and ideals.

Over three days, a crowd of nearly half a million (rain-soaked, often hungry, many of them on drugs) turned a few acres of farmland into a swarming, impromptu city. PBS’s American Experience calls what happened “nothing less than a miracle of teamwork,” a demonstration of the “peace and love” the festival had promised.

entries.title: The Watergate Scandal
entries.subtitle: The abuses of power that forced President Nixon to resign, 1972–1974
entries.summary: On June 17, 1972, police arrested five men inside the Democratic National Committee offices in the Watergate complex as they tried to install bugging equipment. One worked for President Richard Nixon’s reelection committee. Nixon then joined a cover-up, which reporters, a Senate committee, special prosecutors, and the Supreme Court gradually exposed. His secret White House tapes proved he had obstructed justice. Facing impeachment, he resigned on August 9, 1974, the first and only president to do so, and a month later his successor pardoned him.

cards.q: Why does the Watergate Scandal matter?
cards.a: Watergate showed how far a president could go in abusing power and covering it up. It also showed that the press, Congress, and the courts could hold him to account, and that the law applied even to the president.

cards.q: What led to the Watergate Scandal?
cards.a: The break-in itself began as a routine security call. Frank Wills, a 24-year-old guard at the Watergate Office Building, found doors taped open shortly after midnight and called the police just before 2 a.m. on June 17, 1972. The police arrested five men inside the Democratic National Committee headquarters.

The cover-up (1972). Administration officials paid hush money to the burglars and White House aides. On August 1, 1972, the Washington Post reporters Bob Woodward and Carl Bernstein reported that a $25,000 check made out to the Nixon campaign had been deposited in a burglar’s bank account. Their informant, the FBI’s associate director Mark Felt, was known only as “Deep Throat”; his identity became public years later. The Post kept tying the burglars to the White House, but Nixon beat George McGovern in a landslide in November.

entries.title: Roe v. Wade
entries.subtitle: The Supreme Court recognizes a constitutional right to abortion, 1973
entries.summary: In Roe v. Wade (1973) the Supreme Court ruled 7 to 2 that a Texas law banning abortion except to save the mother’s life violated the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment. Writing for the Court, Justice Harry Blackmun held that the constitutional right of privacy “is broad enough to encompass a woman’s decision whether or not to terminate her pregnancy,” but that the right was “not unqualified” and had to be weighed against the state’s interests in health and in “potential life.” The Court set out a framework based on the trimesters of pregnancy. Roe became one of the most debated decisions in American history. The Court modified it in 1992 and overruled it in 2022, returning the question to the states.

cards.q: Why does Roe v. Wade matter?
cards.a: Roe v. Wade made the right to abortion a question of constitutional law for half a century and shaped American politics, elections, and Supreme Court nominations. Its overruling in 2022 returned the issue to the states and remains fiercely debated.

cards.q: What question did the Court have to answer?
cards.a: Does the Constitution protect a woman’s decision to end a pregnancy, and if so, how far may a state restrict or forbid abortion?

The Court held that a law like Texas’s, which allowed abortion only to save the mother’s life “without regard to pregnancy stage and without recognition of the other interests involved,” violated the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment. It then set out a framework.

entries.title: United States v. Nixon
entries.subtitle: The Supreme Court orders a president to surrender the Watergate tapes, 1974
entries.summary: In United States v. Nixon, decided July 24, 1974, the Supreme Court unanimously rejected President Richard Nixon’s claim that “executive privilege” allowed him to withhold White House tape recordings subpoenaed for the trial of his aides in the Watergate cover-up. The Court recognized that presidents have a real but limited privilege to keep their conversations confidential. It held that a “generalized” claim of confidentiality must yield to the needs of a criminal trial. Among the tapes Nixon was forced to release was the June 23, 1972, “smoking gun,” which proved he had obstructed the FBI’s investigation. Within sixteen days he resigned.

cards.q: Why does United States v. Nixon matter?
cards.a: United States v. Nixon showed that the president is not above the law. A unanimous Court ordered him to produce the evidence that ended his presidency.

cards.q: What question did the Court have to answer?
cards.a: Does the president have an absolute privilege, rooted in the separation of powers, to withhold confidential communications from a judicial subpoena in a criminal case? And is the courts’ power to decide that question limited by the fact that the special prosecutor worked inside the executive branch?
The Court ruled 8 to 0 against the president.

entries.title: The End of the Cold War
entries.subtitle: The fall of communism in Eastern Europe and the collapse of the Soviet Union, 1989–1991
entries.summary: Between 1989 and 1991, the communist regimes of Eastern Europe collapsed one after another, the Berlin Wall fell, and the Soviet Union itself dissolved. Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev’s reforms, perestroika (restructuring) and glasnost (openness), and his decision not to use force to prop up allied regimes made peaceful change possible. Presidents Ronald Reagan and George H. W. Bush combined pressure with negotiation. On December 25, 1991, Gorbachev resigned and the Soviet flag came down over the Kremlin, leaving the United States the world’s only superpower.

cards.q: Why does the End of the Cold War matter?
cards.a: The peaceful end of the Cold War closed a four-decade conflict that had shaped American life and lifted the threat of superpower nuclear war.

cards.q: What led to the End of the Cold War?
cards.a: Gorbachev, who came to power in 1985, believed the Soviet system needed reform and sought to end the ruinous arms race. He met Reagan at Geneva in 1985 and Reykjavik in 1986, and the two signed the Intermediate Nuclear Forces Treaty in 1987.

In Poland, round-table talks with the banned union Solidarity led to elections on June 4, 1989, which Solidarity won overwhelmingly; by August the country had Eastern Europe’s first non-communist prime minister. Hungary, Czechoslovakia, Romania, Bulgaria, and East Germany followed.

entries.title: Persian Gulf War
entries.subtitle: The U.S.-led coalition that expelled Iraq from Kuwait, 1990–1991
entries.summary: On August 2, 1990, Iraqi dictator Saddam Hussein invaded and annexed neighboring Kuwait. President George H. W. Bush organized a broad international coalition, backed by United Nations resolutions, and built up forces in Saudi Arabia (Operation Desert Shield). When Iraq refused to withdraw, the coalition launched an air war in January 1991 (Operation Desert Storm), followed by a ground offensive that drove Iraqi forces out of Kuwait in four days. The swift victory boosted Bush’s popularity and seemed to many to exorcise the “ghosts of Vietnam.”

cards.q: Why does Persian Gulf War matter?
cards.a: The Gulf War demonstrated American military dominance after the Cold War and began a long U.S. military involvement in the Persian Gulf.

Iraq emerged from its 1980–1988 war with Iran deeply in debt, owing some $37 billion to Gulf creditors. Saddam Hussein demanded that Kuwait and the United Arab Emirates forgive Iraq’s loans, accused Kuwait of overproducing oil and stealing from a shared oil field, and revived old territorial claims.
UN Resolution 678: gave the coalition international legal authority. Air supremacy in the first days of Desert Storm: crippled Iraq’s ability to fight.

entries.title: September 11 Attacks
entries.subtitle: The al-Qaeda terrorist attacks of 2001
entries.summary: On the morning of September 11, 2001, nineteen al-Qaeda terrorists hijacked four passenger planes. Two were flown into the towers of the World Trade Center in New York, which collapsed, and one into the Pentagon outside Washington. The fourth, United Flight 93, crashed in a Pennsylvania field after its passengers and crew fought back. Nearly 3,000 people were killed, more than at Pearl Harbor. The attacks led to the war in Afghanistan, a global “war on terror,” and the Iraq War, and to new security powers at home.

September 11 was the defining event of the early twenty-first century for the United States. It transformed its foreign policy, its sense of security, and the balance between liberty and security at home.

By late 1998 or early 1999 bin Laden had approved a plan brought to him by Khalid Sheikh Mohammed, the “planes operation.” Mohammed said his original idea had called for ten planes to attack both coasts. Training began in the fall of 1999.

The hijackers chose nonstop coast-to-coast flights that were lightly booked, full of fuel, and scheduled to leave at about the same time. In groups of four or five, armed only with small knives, box cutters, and Mace or pepper spray, they seized the planes.

entries.title: War in Afghanistan
entries.subtitle: America’s longest war, 2001–2021
entries.summary: After the September 11 attacks, the United States invaded Afghanistan to destroy al-Qaeda and topple the Taliban government that sheltered it. Kabul fell within weeks, but Osama bin Laden escaped, and the Taliban regrouped. For twenty years American and NATO forces fought an insurgency while trying to build a stable Afghan government. U.S. forces killed bin Laden in Pakistan in 2011. When the last American troops withdrew hastily in August 2021, the Taliban immediately retook the country. It was the longest war in American history.

cards.q: Why does War in Afghanistan matter?
cards.a: Afghanistan, America’s longest war, showed both the reach of U.S. military power and its limits in remaking another society.

During the 1980s the United States armed the Mujahideen resisting the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan; Osama bin Laden also fought with them. After the Soviets withdrew in 1989, civil war followed, and the Taliban took power in 1996 and sheltered al-Qaeda.

The fall of Kabul (November 2001): toppled the Taliban but let al-Qaeda’s leaders escape. The shift to Iraq (2003): drew U.S. resources away as the Taliban regrouped. Bin Laden’s death (2011): fulfilled a central goal and opened the way to drawdown.

entries.title: Iraq War
entries.subtitle: The U.S. invasion and occupation of Iraq, 2003–2011
entries.summary: In March 2003, the United States led an invasion of Iraq to overthrow Saddam Hussein, whom the Bush administration accused of possessing weapons of mass destruction and linked to terrorism. Baghdad fell within weeks, but no weapons of mass destruction were ever found, and a long, bloody insurgency followed. A 2007 troop “surge” reduced violence, and the last U.S. combat forces left in December 2011. The war remains one of the most controversial in American history.

The Iraq War became a cautionary tale about preventive war, faulty intelligence, and the difficulty of occupation.
After the 1991 Gulf War, the United States maintained sanctions, weapons inspections, and no-fly zones over Iraq. In 1998 President Clinton ordered strikes on suspected weapons sites.

The fall of Baghdad (April 2003): a quick conventional victory that gave way to occupation. The failure to find WMD: undermined the war’s justification. The surge (2007): reduced violence and enabled withdrawal.

entries.title: The Great Recession
entries.subtitle: The financial crisis and deep recession of 2007–2009
entries.summary: The Great Recession began in December 2007 and ended in June 2009, the longest recession since World War II. It grew out of a housing bubble fueled by risky “subprime” mortgages that were bundled into securities and sold throughout the financial system. When homeowners began to default, major financial firms such as Bear Stearns and Lehman Brothers collapsed. Home prices fell about 30 percent, stocks fell 57 percent, and unemployment peaked at 10 percent. The federal government and the Federal Reserve intervened on a massive scale to stabilize the financial system.

cards.q: Why does the Great Recession matter?
cards.a: The Great Recession was the longest recession since World War II, with the largest drop in output of the postwar era, and a defining event for a generation of Americans.

cards.q: What led to the Great Recession?
cards.a: The housing boom peaked in 2006. As prices fell and homeowners defaulted, losses spread through the heavily leveraged financial system, because mortgages had been bundled and resold so often that it was hard to tell who owned what.

Major firms such as Bear Stearns and Lehman Brothers disappeared almost overnight. President George W. Bush signed the Emergency Economic Stabilization Act, and the government poured billions into propping up banks.

entries.title: COVID-19 Pandemic
entries.subtitle: The coronavirus pandemic in the United States, 2020–2023
entries.summary: COVID-19, a disease caused by a new coronavirus first identified in Wuhan, China, in late 2019, reached the United States in January 2020. Within weeks schools, offices, and businesses closed. Unemployment reached 14.7 percent, the highest since the Great Depression, and hospitals, above all in New York, ran short of supplies. Vaccines developed at record speed were authorized in December 2020. But new variants kept the virus spreading, and masks and vaccines became politically divisive. By May 2022 more than one million Americans had died. The Miller Center counts more than 1.1 million deaths in all, the worst toll from one disease since the influenza pandemic of 1918.

With more than a million American deaths, COVID-19 was the defining public health crisis of the early twenty-first century and deepened the country’s political divisions.

On January 23, 2020, China placed Wuhan, a city of 11 million people, under lockdown, but the virus had already escaped through travel. At the end of January the World Health Organization declared a public health emergency of international concern. Early American testing was slow.

The first wave (spring 2020). The CDC confirmed the first American case on January 20, 2020, in Washington State. The CDC reported the first American death in Washington, and the Miller Center dates it to February. On March 11 the World Health Organization declared a pandemic, and on March 13 the Trump administration declared a national emergency. States began shutting down.

entries.title: Abigail Adams
entries.subtitle: Political partner, letter writer, and early voice for women’s rights
entries.summary: Abigail Adams was the wife of the second president, John Adams, the mother of the sixth, John Quincy Adams, and one of the sharpest political minds of the Revolutionary generation. Through a lifetime of letters she advised her husband, reported on the war around Boston, and ran the family farm and finances alone for years at a time. In March 1776 she urged him to “Remember the Ladies” in the new nation’s laws, warning that women would “not hold ourselves bound by any Laws in which we have no voice, or Representation.” She also wrote against slavery and argued for women’s education. As First Lady she was so influential that critics called her “Mrs. President.”

Abigail Adams’s letters are among the richest records of the Revolutionary era, and they show how a woman with no formal role shaped events through intelligence, management, and argument. Her “Remember the Ladies” letter is one of the earliest and best-known American appeals for women’s rights.

cards.q: What shaped Abigail Adams early in life?
cards.a: Abigail Smith was born in Weymouth, Massachusetts, in November 1744, the second child of Elizabeth Quincy Smith and the Reverend William Smith, pastor of the town’s North Parish Congregational Church. The Park Service and the National Women’s History Museum give different days for her birth, November 11 and November 22. New England schools usually admitted only boys, so she was taught at home and educated herself in her father’s library, regretting all her life that formal education had been closed to her. Her grandfather Colonel John Quincy, once speaker of the Massachusetts House, gave her a sense of public duty.

cards.q: What were Abigail Adams’s major achievements?
cards.a: Running the farm and the family. When John left for the First Continental Congress in 1774, Abigail stayed in Braintree to run the farm and teach their children, a role the National Women’s History Museum calls “deputy husband.” Married women then had few property rights, yet she began to call the family property her own, made profitable investments in war bonds, ran a small business importing European goods, and bought land her husband had not approved. The American Yawp describes her managing planting and harvest in the middle of severe labor shortages and inflation.

entries.title: Abraham Lincoln
entries.subtitle: Sixteenth president, who preserved the Union and ended slavery
entries.summary: Abraham Lincoln rose from a one-room log cabin on the Kentucky frontier to become the sixteenth president of the United States. Elected in 1860 as the first Republican president, he led the Union through the Civil War, issued the Emancipation Proclamation, and pushed the Thirteenth Amendment abolishing slavery through Congress. He was assassinated by John Wilkes Booth in April 1865, days after the war’s end. Historians and the public alike rank him as the nation’s greatest president.

Lincoln saved the Union and destroyed slavery, and he did both by appealing to the nation’s founding ideals, above all the Declaration’s promise that all men are created equal. His wartime presidency also transformed the office, setting precedents for presidential power in a national emergency that historians still debate.

cards.q: What shaped Abraham Lincoln early in life?
cards.a: Abraham Lincoln was born on February 12, 1809, in a one-room log cabin with a dirt floor in Hardin County, Kentucky. His father, Thomas, a farmer and carpenter who could barely sign his name, moved the family to the Indiana frontier when Abraham was seven.

cards.q: What were Abraham Lincoln’s major achievements?
cards.a: As a young legislator Lincoln was one of only six members, out of eighty-three, who voted against a 1837 resolution condemning abolitionists. Elected to Congress in 1846, he challenged President James Polk’s claim that Mexico had started the Mexican-American War on American soil, an unpopular stand at home, and served only a single term. After several years practicing law, he returned to politics in 1854, and in 1856 he joined the new Republican Party, which was dedicated to repealing the Kansas-Nebraska Act and stopping the spread of slavery into the West.

entries.title: African Americans in the Revolution
entries.subtitle: Free and enslaved Black Americans who fought, worked and fled on both sides of the war
entries.summary: The Revolution forced Black Americans to weigh which side offered a better chance of freedom. Black men fought at Lexington, Bunker Hill and Yorktown; others joined the British after Virginia’s royal governor, Lord Dunmore, promised freedom in 1775. When the war ended, the British carried thousands of formerly enslaved Loyalists away to freedom, while many Black veterans of the American army returned to slavery.

cards.q: Why does African Americans in the Revolution matter?
cards.a: The Revolution did not end slavery, but it shook it.

cards.q: What does “African Americans in the Revolution” mean?
cards.a: Black Americans, free and enslaved, took part in the Revolution from its first days to its last.

cards.q: Where did the idea come from?
cards.a: Black Americans were in the Revolution “from its very first minutes,” as the American Battlefield Trust puts it: Crispus Attucks was among those shot down at the Boston Massacre in 1770, and Black minutemen turned out at Lexington and Concord. About three dozen fought at Bunker Hill, among them Peter Salem and Salem Poor.

entries.title: Alcatraz Island
entries.subtitle: San Francisco Bay island: a prison, then the site of the 1969–1971 Indian occupation
entries.summary: Alcatraz Island in San Francisco Bay is best known as a former prison, but it is also a landmark of Native American activism. From November 1969 to June 1971, a group calling itself Indians of All Tribes occupied the island, demanding it for an Indian university and cultural center. Their nineteen-month occupation drew national attention to Native rights and helped change federal Indian policy. The island is now part of the Golden Gate National Recreation Area.

Though the occupiers did not win the island, the Park Service concludes that the occupation helped end the federal termination policy and gave birth to a lasting political movement for Indian self-determination.
Alcatraz is a rocky island in San Francisco Bay. It served for many years as a prison holding both military prisoners and civilians.

Before the prison. Ohlone people lived around San Francisco Bay for thousands of years; oral history suggests Alcatraz was used to isolate tribal members who had broken laws, to gather bird eggs and sea life, and as a hiding place for Indians escaping the Spanish missions.

entries.title: Alexander Hamilton
entries.subtitle: First secretary of the Treasury and architect of the federal financial system
entries.summary: Alexander Hamilton was born in the British West Indies, came to the mainland colonies as a teenager, and became one of the most influential of the nation’s founders. He served as George Washington’s aide during the Revolution, helped call the Constitutional Convention, and wrote most of the Federalist Papers in support of the Constitution. As the first secretary of the Treasury, from 1789 to 1795, he paid the Revolutionary War debts in full, had the federal government take over the states’ debts, and created the First Bank of the United States. His program and his preference for Britain divided the government and helped create the first political parties. He was killed in a duel with Vice President Aaron Burr in 1804.

entries.title: Amelia Earhart
entries.subtitle: The first woman to fly solo across the Atlantic, who vanished over the Pacific in 1937
entries.summary: Amelia Earhart was one of the most influential pioneers of American aviation. In 1928 she became the first woman to cross the Atlantic by air, as a passenger, and in 1932 she flew it alone, five years to the day after Charles Lindbergh. She set record after record, including the first solo flight from Hawaiʻi to California, and used her fame to argue that women could do any job that men could. On July 2, 1937, nearing the end of an attempt to fly around the world, she and her navigator, Fred Noonan, vanished near tiny Howland Island in the Pacific. No trace of them was ever found.

videos.title: Searching for Amelia Earhart (Full Episode) | SPECIAL | National Geographic
Amelia Earhart - First Woman To Fly Alone | Mini Bio | Biography
