Earhart turned aviation into a cause for women’s equality, proving in the most public way possible that women could match men in skill and daring. Her unexplained disappearance made her a lasting American legend.

cards.q: What shaped Amelia Earhart early in life?
cards.a: Amelia Mary Earhart was born in Atchison, Kansas, in 1897. As a girl she climbed trees, “belly slammed” her sled downhill, and hunted rats with a .22 rifle, and she kept a scrapbook about women succeeding in fields dominated by men.

cards.q: What were Amelia Earhart’s major achievements?
cards.a: In April 1928 the publisher George P. Putnam’s team asked her, “How would you like to be the first woman to fly the Atlantic?”

entries.title: Andrew Carnegie
entries.subtitle: Steel magnate and philanthropist of the Gilded Age
entries.summary: Andrew Carnegie arrived in Pennsylvania as a poor thirteen-year-old Scottish immigrant and built the largest and most profitable steel company in the world. In 1901 he sold it to J. P. Morgan, who used it to create U.S. Steel, and Carnegie spent the rest of his life giving his fortune away, funding thousands of public libraries and institutions. His mills were also the scene of the violent 1892 Homestead strike, and he remains a symbol of both the opportunity and the inequality of the Gilded Age.

videos.title: Andrew Carnegie: Robber Baron or America’s Greatest Philanthropist?
How Andrew Carnegie Became the Richest Man in the World (and then gave it all away)

Carnegie’s rise from immigrant mill boy to steel king made him the era’s emblem of the self-made man, while Homestead and his philanthropy raised enduring questions about wealth, power, and responsibility.

cards.q: What shaped Andrew Carnegie early in life?
cards.a: Carnegie was born in 1835 in a one-room house in Dunfermline, Scotland, the son of a handloom weaver. When machines took over weaving in the 1840s the family was impoverished, and in 1848 his strong-willed mother led them to Allegheny, Pennsylvania.

cards.q: What were Andrew Carnegie’s major achievements?
cards.a: Mentored by Scott, who helped him invest, often in insider deals, Carnegie was rich by the end of the Civil War. He bet on steel.

entries.title: Andrew Jackson
entries.subtitle: Seventh president, champion of the “common man,” and architect of Indian removal
entries.summary: Andrew Jackson was the dominant figure in American politics between Thomas Jefferson and Abraham Lincoln. He was the first president from the West and the first “self-made man” to reach the White House. Orphaned by the Revolution, he rose as a Tennessee lawyer, planter, and enslaver, and his victory at New Orleans in 1815 made him a national hero. As president from 1829 to 1837 he cast himself as the people’s champion against privilege, destroyed the Second Bank of the United States, faced down South Carolina’s nullification of federal law, and founded the Democratic Party. He also signed the Indian Removal Act, which drove the Native nations of the Southeast from their homelands and led to the Cherokee Trail of Tears.

Jackson turned the presidency into a direct link between the president and the voters and built the first modern mass party, while his opponents organized as the Whigs.

cards.q: What shaped Andrew Jackson early in life?
cards.a: Andrew Jackson was born on March 15, 1767, in the Waxhaw settlement, a community of Scotch-Irish immigrants on the border between North and South Carolina. His exact birthplace is disputed, but he considered himself a South Carolinian. His father died before he was born. The Revolution wiped out the rest of his family.

cards.q: What were Andrew Jackson’s major achievements?
cards.a: The road to the White House. In 1824 Jackson led a four-man field with 43 percent of the popular vote and 99 electoral votes, short of a majority.

entries.title: Babe Ruth
entries.subtitle: The slugger who transformed baseball and became the most celebrated athlete of the 1920s
entries.summary: Babe Ruth was a troubled Baltimore boy raised in a reform school who became the most celebrated athlete of his time. A star pitcher for the Boston Red Sox, he was sold to the New York Yankees in 1920 and turned the home run from a rarity into the heart of the game, hitting 54 that year, more than all but one other major league team, and 60 in 1927. Larger than life on and off the field, he embodied the boisterous 1920s, filled ballparks across the country, and retired with 714 home runs.

videos.title: Babe Ruth: American Sports Icon
Who was Babe Ruth?

cards.a: The slugger who transformed baseball and became the most celebrated athlete of the 1920s. Pitcher, Boston Red Sox (1914–1919); Outfielder, New York Yankees (1920–1934); Boston Braves (1935); One of the first five members of the Baseball Hall of Fame (1936)
Born February 6, 1895, Baltimore, Maryland; died August 16, 1948, New York City

Ruth changed how baseball was played, from a game of singles and stolen bases to one built on power, and, with the help of a ravenous press, made sports stardom a national obsession. He remains the standard against which American athletic greatness is measured.

cards.q: What shaped Babe Ruth early in life?
cards.a: George Herman Ruth was born on February 6, 1895, in Baltimore. His father ran a saloon and his mother was often ill, and by the age of six “Little George” was roaming the waterfront unsupervised, stealing, vandalizing, and drinking the dregs from beer glasses in his father’s bar.

cards.q: What were Babe Ruth’s major achievements?
cards.a: Ruth was first a superb left-handed pitcher. He won 23 games in 1916 with a league-leading 1.75 earned run average, pitched all fourteen innings of a World Series victory, and helped Boston win three championships.

entries.title: Barack Obama
entries.subtitle: Forty-fourth president and the first African American president
entries.summary: Barack Obama was inaugurated on January 20, 2009, as the forty-fourth president and the first African American to hold the office. The son of a white mother from Kansas and a Black Kenyan father, he grew up in Hawaii and Indonesia, worked as a community organizer in Chicago, and led the Harvard Law Review before entering politics. He took office in a deep recession, won an $800 billion stimulus, and signed the Affordable Care Act, which sharply reduced the number of uninsured Americans. Abroad he withdrew most American troops from Iraq, ordered the raid that killed Osama bin Laden, and pursued agreements on Iran’s nuclear program and climate change. Republican control of Congress after 2010 blocked much of his later agenda.

cards.a: Barack Hussein Obama II was born in Hawaii on August 4, 1961. His parents, who had met as students at the University of Hawaii, were Ann Dunham, a white American from Kansas, and Barack Obama Sr., a Black Kenyan studying in the United States. His father left the family when Obama was two and later returned to Kenya.

cards.q: What were Barack Obama’s major achievements?
cards.a: The 2008 election. Obama announced his candidacy in February 2007.

entries.title: Benjamin Franklin
entries.subtitle: Printer, scientist, diplomat, and the Revolution’s elder statesman
entries.summary: Benjamin Franklin rose from a Boston candlemaker’s son to become the best-known American of the eighteenth century, as a printer, writer, scientist, and statesman. In Philadelphia he published Poor Richard’s Almanack and founded a library, a fire company, a hospital, and the academy that became the University of Pennsylvania. His experiments with electricity won him international fame. He represented the colonies in London for nearly two decades, helped draft the Declaration of Independence, won the French alliance, and helped negotiate the peace with Britain. At eighty-one he was the oldest delegate to the Constitutional Convention. An enslaver earlier in life, he ended it as president of an abolition society.

Franklin signed the three documents that established the nation, the Declaration of Independence, the Treaty of Paris, and the Constitution, and the State Department’s historians call him the most distinguished scientific and literary American of the colonial era. His life became a model of the self-made American, and his civic projects, scientific work, and diplomacy helped shape both colonial society and the new nation.

cards.q: What shaped Benjamin Franklin early in life?
cards.a: Benjamin Franklin was born in Boston on January 17, 1706, to Josiah Franklin, a maker of candles and soap, and Abiah Folger. Lehigh University’s exhibit calls him the tenth child, and the Library of Congress the tenth son. He had only about two years of schooling.

cards.q: What were Benjamin Franklin’s major achievements?
cards.a: Scientist and inventor. Franklin’s electrical experiments, published as Experiments and Observations on Electricity, set out a theory of positive and negative charge, argued that lightning was electrical, and proposed a tall, grounded rod to protect buildings.

entries.title: Booker T. Washington
entries.subtitle: Educator and the most influential Black leader of his generation
entries.summary: Booker T. Washington was born into slavery in Virginia and became the most prominent Black educator and spokesman of his time. As the founding principal of Alabama’s Tuskegee Institute, he championed industrial and vocational education as the road to Black economic independence. His 1895 Atlanta Exposition address, which seemed to accept segregation in exchange for economic opportunity, made him famous and drew sharp criticism from W. E. B. Du Bois, who called it the “Atlanta Compromise.” In 1901 he became the first African American invited to dine at the White House.

cards.q: Why does Booker T. Washington matter?
cards.a: Washington built one of the most important Black institutions in the country and defined one side of a lasting debate over how Black Americans should pursue freedom in the age of Jim Crow.

cards.q: What shaped Booker T. Washington early in life?

entries.title: Cesar Chavez
entries.subtitle: Labor leader and co-founder of the United Farm Workers
entries.summary: Cesar Chavez was the Mexican American labor leader who, with Dolores Huerta, built the first lasting union of farmworkers in the United States. The son of migrant laborers who had lost their Arizona farm, he founded the National Farm Workers Association in 1962, joined the great Delano grape strike of 1965, and turned it into a national boycott of table grapes. Through strikes, marches, and long public fasts, always insisting on nonviolence, he made the United Farm Workers a union and a civil rights movement at once, and became the best-known figure of the Chicano movement.

cards.q: What shaped Cesar Chavez early in life?
cards.a: Cesar Estrada Chavez was born on March 31, 1927, near Yuma, Arizona, and named for his grandfather Cesario. He learned about injustice early: his father agreed to clear eighty acres in exchange for the deed to forty more beside their adobe home, but the bargain was broken, and after a lawyer’s scheme the family lost the land.

cards.q: What were Cesar Chavez’s major achievements?
cards.a: When the CSO refused to concentrate on farmworkers, Chavez quit and in 1962 founded the National Farm Workers Association in Delano, California, with Dolores Huerta; his brother Richard designed its black Aztec eagle on a red flag. For three years he traveled from town to town, meeting workers in their homes.

entries.title: Donald Trump
entries.subtitle: Forty-fifth and forty-seventh president, the second ever elected to non-consecutive terms
entries.summary: Donald Trump, a New York real estate developer and reality-television star, won the presidency in 2016 as a Republican in a surprise victory, without ever having held public office or military command. His first term brought a large tax cut, tighter immigration policies, new tariffs, and an “America First” foreign policy, along with intense partisan division and two impeachments, both ending in acquittal. He lost the 2020 election to Joe Biden, refused to concede, and his supporters attacked the Capitol on January 6, 2021. In 2024, after being convicted on state felony charges in New York, he won the presidency again, becoming only the second president elected to non-consecutive terms.

First president with no prior public office or military leadership; first impeached twice; first convicted of a felony
The second president elected to non-consecutive terms, and the first since the nineteenth century

Trump put populist nationalism, opposition to immigration and free trade and skepticism of foreign alliances, at the center of Republican politics, and he broke with long-standing norms, above all by refusing to concede the 2020 election.

cards.q: What shaped Donald Trump early in life?
cards.a: Donald John Trump was born on June 14, 1946, in the borough of Queens in New York City, the fourth of five children of Mary Anne MacLeod Trump and Fred Trump, a residential real estate developer.

cards.q: What were Donald Trump’s major achievements?
cards.a: Trump announced his candidacy on June 16, 2015, at Trump Tower in Manhattan, promising to “Make America Great Again,” to build a wall on the Mexican border, and to put “America First.”

entries.title: Dwight D. Eisenhower
entries.subtitle: Commander of the D-Day invasion and thirty-fourth president, who presided over the prosperous, anxious 1950s
entries.summary: Dwight D. Eisenhower rose in five years from an obscure lieutenant colonel to Supreme Commander of the Allied invasion of Nazi-occupied Europe on D-Day. Elected president in 1952 and 1956, “Ike” ended the Korean War, built the Interstate Highway System, and kept the country out of new wars while waging the Cold War with nuclear deterrence and CIA covert action. He sent troops to enforce school desegregation in Little Rock but never endorsed the Brown decision, and on leaving office he warned Americans against the “military-industrial complex.”

videos.title: The World Wars: Dwight Eisenhower | History
Dwight D. Eisenhower - 34th U.S. President & Commander of Allied Forces in WW2 | Mini Bio | BIO

cards.a: Commander of the D-Day invasion and thirty-fourth president, who presided over the prosperous, anxious 1950s. Supreme Allied Commander, D-Day invasion (1944); Army chief of staff (1945–1948); President of Columbia University; First Supreme Commander of NATO forces in Europe; Thirty-fourth president (1953–1961)

cards.q: When did Dwight D. Eisenhower live?
cards.a: Born October 14, 1890, Denison, Texas; died March 28, 1969

cards.q: Who is this? Commander of the D-Day invasion and thirty-fourth president, who presided over the prosperous, anxious 1950s
cards.a: Dwight D. Eisenhower
January 20, 1953 – January 20, 1961; Republican
Gave the order, “Okay, let’s go”, for the Normandy invasion of June 6, 1944
Launched in 1956: a 41,000-mile network, the largest public works program in U.S. history
1957: the first president since Reconstruction to send troops into the South to enforce federal law
Beware the “military-industrial complex” (January 1961)
Ranked 22nd by historians in 1962; 8th by 1994

cards.q: Why does Dwight D. Eisenhower matter?
cards.a: Eisenhower led the largest invasion in history and then, as president, accepted the New Deal, built the interstates, and kept the Cold War from turning hot. His caution on civil rights and his reliance on covert action left problems his successors had to face.

cards.q: What shaped Dwight D. Eisenhower early in life?
cards.a: Eisenhower was born on October 14, 1890, in a house by the railroad tracks in Denison, Texas, and grew up in the small farm town of Abilene, Kansas. His father worked as a mechanic in a creamery; his mother, Ida, a Mennonite, was a religious pacifist, though she did not try to stop her son from becoming a soldier.

cards.q: What were Dwight D. Eisenhower’s major achievements?
cards.a: Huge army maneuvers in Louisiana, with more than 400,000 troops, revealed his gift for strategic planning, and days after Pearl Harbor he was called to Washington to work on war plans. He so impressed the Army chief of staff, George C. Marshall, that promotions came quickly.

entries.title: Eleanor Roosevelt
entries.subtitle: First lady, reformer, and champion of human rights
entries.summary: Eleanor Roosevelt transformed the role of First Lady and became, in the words later used of her, the “First Lady of the World.” An orphaned girl from a wealthy family, she grew into a political force in her own right: during Franklin D. Roosevelt’s presidency she traveled the country as his “eyes, ears and legs,” pressed the New Deal to include women and Black Americans, and wrote a daily newspaper column. After his death she represented the United States at the United Nations, where she chaired the Human Rights Commission and helped write the Universal Declaration of Human Rights.

videos.title: Eleanor Roosevelt: Most Iconic First Lady - Fast Facts | History
Eleanor Roosevelt - The First Lady to the World

cards.a: First lady, reformer, and champion of human rights. First Lady (1933–1945); Delegate to the United Nations; Chair of the UN Human Rights Commission; Chair of the President’s Commission on the Status of Women
Born October 11, 1884, New York City; died November 7, 1962

cards.q: Who is this? First lady, reformer, and champion of human rights
cards.a: Eleanor Roosevelt
Franklin D. Roosevelt, a fifth cousin once removed, on March 17, 1905
Chaired the Human Rights Commission; Universal Declaration adopted December 10, 1948
Eleanor Roosevelt used an unelected position to become one of the most influential reformers of the twentieth century and a founding voice of the international human rights movement.

cards.q: What shaped Eleanor Roosevelt early in life?
cards.a: Anna Eleanor Roosevelt was born on October 11, 1884, in New York City, the niece of Theodore Roosevelt. Her privileged childhood was also a sad one: her father struggled with alcoholism, and by the time she was ten her mother, her father, and a brother had died.

cards.q: What were Eleanor Roosevelt’s major achievements?
cards.a: Her public life began in earnest during World War I, when she volunteered with the Red Cross and in Navy hospitals.

entries.title: Elizabeth Cady Stanton
entries.subtitle: Philosopher and strategist of the women’s rights movement
entries.summary: Elizabeth Cady Stanton was the chief philosopher of the American women’s rights movement. In 1848 she helped organize the Seneca Falls Convention and wrote its Declaration of Sentiments, which rewrote the Declaration of Independence to proclaim that “all men and women are created equal.” For half a century she supplied the ideas, and her partner Susan B. Anthony carried them across the country. A radical on marriage, divorce, and religion, she also opposed voting rights for Black men without women, a stance that split the suffrage movement.

videos.title: Who Was Elizabeth Cady Stanton?

cards.a: Philosopher and strategist of the women’s rights movement. Organizer of the Seneca Falls Convention; Author of the Declaration of Sentiments; President of the National Woman Suffrage Association; Author of *The Woman’s Bible*

cards.q: When did Elizabeth Cady Stanton live?
cards.a: Born November 12, 1815, Johnstown, New York; died October 1902, New York City

cards.q: Who is this? Philosopher and strategist of the women’s rights movement
cards.a: Elizabeth Cady Stanton
With Susan B. Anthony, from 1851, for more than fifty years
Co-founded the National Woman Suffrage Association (1869)
Declaration of Sentiments (1848); History of Woman Suffrage; The Woman’s Bible
1902, eighteen years before women of her social status could vote nationally

cards.q: Why does Elizabeth Cady Stanton matter?
cards.a: Stanton gave the women’s movement its ideas and much of its language. Her career also shows the movement’s internal conflicts over race, which shaped suffrage politics for decades.

cards.q: What shaped Elizabeth Cady Stanton early in life?
cards.a: Elizabeth Cady was born on November 12, 1815, in Johnstown, New York, the eighth of ten children of Margaret Livingston and Daniel Cady, a lawyer who became a state supreme court judge. Four of his five sons died in infancy, and the fifth when Elizabeth was eleven.

cards.q: What were Elizabeth Cady Stanton’s major achievements?
cards.a: In London, Stanton and the Quaker abolitionist Lucretia Mott were furious that women were barred from speaking, and they resolved to hold a convention on women’s rights. In 1848 they did so at Seneca Falls, New York.

entries.title: Elvis Presley
entries.subtitle: The “King of Rock & Roll,” who carried a blend of Black and white Southern music to a mass audience
entries.summary: Elvis Presley, a young truck driver from Tupelo, Mississippi, began recording at a Memphis studio in the early 1950s and, in 1954, set off a musical and cultural revolution. Mixing blues, rhythm and blues, country, and gospel, he brought music rooted in Black traditions to huge white audiences, and his hip-shaking performances shocked parents as much as they thrilled teenagers. After a string of number-one hits, national television appearances, and movies, he served in the Army, spent the 1960s making films, and returned to the stage in 1969. He died at his Memphis home, Graceland, in 1977, at forty-two.

videos.title: Elvis Presley: Life and Death of the King

cards.a: The “King of Rock & Roll,” who carried a blend of Black and white Southern music to a mass audience. Singer; Film actor; U.S. Army soldier (1958–1960)
Born January 8, 1935, Tupelo, Mississippi; died August 16, 1977, Graceland, Memphis, Tennessee

cards.q: Who is this? The “King of Rock & Roll,” who carried a blend of Black and white Southern music to a mass audience
cards.a: Elvis Presley

Presley was the figure through whom rock & roll exploded into mainstream culture. By bringing Black-influenced music to white audiences in the segregated 1950s, he helped remake American popular music and youth culture.

cards.q: What shaped Elvis Presley early in life?
cards.a: Elvis Aron Presley was born on January 8, 1935, in a two-room house in Tupelo, Mississippi, to Vernon and Gladys Presley. His twin brother, Jessie Garon, was stillborn, so Elvis grew up an only child.

cards.q: What were Elvis Presley’s major achievements?
cards.a: In 1953 and 1954 Presley cut demo records at Sun Records, whose owner, Sam Phillips, had been looking for a white singer who could perform in the style of traditionally Black music.

entries.title: Federalism
entries.subtitle: How power is divided between the national government and the states
entries.summary: Federalism is the division of governing power between a national government and the states. The Constitution lists the powers of the federal government, makes federal law “the supreme Law of the Land,” and, through the Tenth Amendment, reserves the rest “to the States respectively, or to the people.” James Madison called the result “neither a national nor a federal Constitution, but a composition of both.” Where to draw the line between the two levels has been fought over ever since, in disputes over banking, tariffs, slavery, civil rights, and much else.

videos.title: The Constitution, the Articles, and Federalism: Crash Course US History #8
Federalism: Crash Course Government and Politics #4

quotes.text: The proposed Constitution, therefore, is, in strictness, neither a national nor a federal Constitution, but a composition of both.
quotes.speaker: James Madison

quotes.text: The powers delegated by the proposed Constitution to the federal government are few and defined. Those which are to remain in the State governments are numerous and indefinite.
quotes.speaker: James Madison

quotes.text: That the power to tax involves the power to destroy.
quotes.speaker: Chief Justice John Marshall

cards.a: Federalism
Enumerated powers (Article I), the supremacy clause (Article VI), and the Tenth Amendment
Under the Articles of Confederation each state kept its “sovereignty, freedom and independence”
Federal powers “few and defined”; state powers “numerous and indefinite”
McCulloch v. Maryland (1819); the Nullification Crisis; the Civil War; federal enforcement of civil rights
Federalism shapes almost every American political fight, because the question of which government should decide is often as contested as the decision itself.

In a federal system, two levels of government each have real authority over the same people. The Constitution lists the powers of Congress, among them to tax, regulate commerce, coin money, and declare war, and to make all laws “necessary and proper” for carrying them out.

cards.q: Where did the idea come from?
cards.a: The framers designed federalism as a middle path. Under the Articles of Confederation the states were bound only in “a firm league of friendship,” and each kept its “sovereignty, freedom and independence.”

entries.title: Franklin D. Roosevelt
entries.subtitle: Thirty-second president, architect of the New Deal and wartime leader
entries.summary: Franklin D. Roosevelt led the United States through the two great crises of the twentieth century, the Great Depression and World War II, and was the only president elected four times. Born to wealth and paralyzed by polio at thirty-nine, he returned to politics and won the presidency in 1932 by promising “a new deal for the American people.” His New Deal transformed the federal government’s role in American life. As commander in chief after Pearl Harbor, he built the alliance with Britain, the Soviet Union, and China that defeated Germany and Japan. He died in April 1945, weeks before victory in Europe.

cards.q: When did Franklin D. Roosevelt live?
cards.a: Born January 30, 1882, Hyde Park, New York; died April 12, 1945, Warm Springs, Georgia

cards.q: Why does Franklin D. Roosevelt matter?
cards.a: Roosevelt changed what Americans expected from their government and their president. Under him the federal government took responsibility for the economic security of ordinary citizens, the Democratic Party became the nation’s majority party, and the United States emerged from World War II as a global power.

cards.q: What shaped Franklin D. Roosevelt early in life?
cards.a: Franklin Delano Roosevelt was born on January 30, 1882, at Hyde Park, New York, the only child of James Roosevelt, a wealthy landowner and businessman, and Sara Delano Roosevelt, who devoted herself to her son throughout her long life. He grew up on the family estate on the Hudson River, taught by tutors until he was fourteen, when he entered the Groton School.

cards.q: What were Franklin D. Roosevelt’s major achievements?
cards.a: Election and the New Deal. At the 1932 Democratic convention in Chicago, Roosevelt broke with tradition by flying there to accept the nomination in person.

entries.title: Frederick Douglass
entries.subtitle: Escaped slave, orator, editor, and the foremost Black leader of the nineteenth century
entries.summary: Frederick Douglass escaped from slavery in Maryland in 1838 and became the most important leader of the movement for African American civil rights in the nineteenth century. His Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, an American Slave (1845) became a bestseller, and his speeches, above all “What to the Slave Is the Fourth of July?” (1852), made him the nation’s most famous abolitionist orator. He edited his own newspaper, supported women’s rights from the Seneca Falls Convention onward, recruited Black soldiers during the Civil War, and pressed Abraham Lincoln face to face for equal treatment. After the war he held federal office under five presidents.

videos.title: Frederick Douglass: Crash Course Black American History #17
Frederick Douglass’ Incredible Legacy | Told by Laurence Fishburne | History at Home

quotes.text: What, to the American slave, is your 4th of July? I answer: a day that reveals to him, more than all other days in the year, the gross injustice and cruelty to which he is the constant victim.
quotes.speaker: Frederick Douglass
quotes.context: “What to the Slave Is the Fourth of July?”, Rochester, July 5, 1852

quotes.speaker: Frederick Douglass
quotes.context: recalling his first visit to Lincoln at the White House, 1863

quotes.speaker: Frederick Douglass

Abolitionist lecturer and author; Editor of *The North Star*; Recruiter of Black Union soldiers; President of the Freedman’s Bank (1874); U.S. Marshal for D.C. (1877–1881); Recorder of Deeds for D.C. (1881–1886); Minister Resident and Consul General to Haiti (1889–1891)
Born February 1818, Talbot County, Eastern Shore of Maryland; died February 20, 1895, Cedar Hill, Washington, D.C.

Narrative (1845), My Bondage and My Freedom (1855), Life and Times (1881)
The North Star, first issue December 3, 1847, Rochester, New York
1846, for £150 raised by British supporters
U.S. Marshal and Recorder of Deeds for D.C.; minister to Haiti (1889–1891)

Douglass turned his own life into the most powerful argument against slavery that Americans ever heard, and then spent thirty years after emancipation insisting that freedom meant nothing without citizenship, the vote, and equal rights. He judged the nation by its own founding words, and he believed in building alliances across racial and political lines to make them true.

cards.q: What shaped Frederick Douglass early in life?
cards.a: Frederick Augustus Washington Bailey was born into slavery on the Eastern Shore of Maryland in February 1818. He barely knew his mother, who was forced to work on a distant farm and died when he was about seven, and he never knew his father.

cards.q: What were Frederick Douglass’s major achievements?
cards.a: Abolitionist. In August 1841, at an antislavery convention on Nantucket, Douglass spoke to a large, mostly white audience, and the Massachusetts Anti-Slavery Society hired him as a lecturer. He toured the North and Midwest.

entries.title: George Washington
entries.subtitle: Commander of the Continental Army and first president
entries.summary: George Washington commanded the Continental Army through eight years of war, presided over the convention that wrote the Constitution, and served as the first president of the United States. Twice he gave up power when he could have kept it, by resigning his command in 1783 and by retiring after two terms as president, and those choices, more than any battle, made him the “indispensable man” of the founding. A Virginia planter who held hundreds of people in slavery, he arranged in his will to free those he owned, but only after his wife’s death.

quotes.speaker: George Washington

Washington’s greatest contribution was his restraint. Americans trusted him with immense power because he had given it up once before, and his conduct as president created the cabinet, the two-term tradition, and the dignity of the office. His slaveholding is the most troubling part of his legacy.

cards.q: What shaped George Washington early in life?
cards.a: Washington was born on February 22, 1732, at Popes Creek farm in Westmoreland County, Virginia.

cards.q: What were George Washington’s major achievements?
cards.a: Commander in chief. Washington attended the Second Continental Congress in uniform.

entries.title: Harpers Ferry
entries.subtitle: Armory town where John Brown struck at slavery
entries.summary: Harpers Ferry, a small town where the Potomac and Shenandoah Rivers cut through the Blue Ridge, packs an unusual amount of American history into a few streets. A federal armory built there in the 1790s became a center of early industry, where John H. Hall made rifles with interchangeable parts. In October 1859 the abolitionist John Brown seized the armory in a failed attempt to start a war against slavery, a raid that pushed the country closer to civil war. In 1862 Confederate troops captured the Union garrison there, the largest surrender of Federal troops in the war. After the war Storer College educated formerly enslaved people, and in 1906 W. E. B. Du Bois and the Niagara Movement met on its campus.

videos.title: The Raid on Harper’s Ferry  - John Brown - US History - Part 4 - Extra History
The Raid on Harpers Ferry

Harpers Ferry concentrates several stories of the nineteenth century in one small town: the rise of machine-made manufacturing, the violent struggle over slavery that John Brown’s raid sharpened, the Civil War, and the long fight for Black education and civil rights that carried on at Storer College and the Niagara Movement.
The town stands on steep ground at the point where the Potomac and Shenandoah Rivers meet and break through the Blue Ridge.
The armory. In 1794 Congress approved a bill “for the erecting and repairing of Arsenals and Magazines.”

entries.title: Harriet Tubman
entries.subtitle: Freedom seeker, Underground Railroad conductor, Union scout
entries.summary: Harriet Tubman was born into slavery on Maryland’s Eastern Shore around 1822, escaped in 1849, and then went back again and again to lead family members and friends to freedom, becoming the most famous conductor of the Underground Railroad. During the Civil War she served the Union Army as a nurse, scout, and spy, and in June 1863 she helped plan and lead the Combahee River Raid in South Carolina, which freed more than 700 enslaved people. In her later years in Auburn, New York, she supported women’s suffrage and opened a home for elderly and poor African Americans.

cards.a: Harriet Tubman was born Araminta Ross around 1822 in Dorchester County, on the Eastern Shore of Maryland, one of nine children of Harriet “Rit” Green Ross and Benjamin Ross. Under slavery the children of an enslaved mother were enslaved too, whatever their father’s status; Ben Ross was free, but Rit and her children were held by a man named Edward Brodess. Brodess broke the family apart.

cards.q: What were Harriet Tubman’s major achievements?
cards.a: In March 1849 Edward Brodess died.

entries.title: Harry S. Truman
entries.subtitle: Thirty-third president: ended World War II and launched the Cold War containment policy
entries.summary: Harry S. Truman, the thirty-third president of the United States (1945–1953), was a Missouri farmer, artillery captain, and failed shopkeeper who became president when Franklin Roosevelt died in April 1945, after just eighty-two days as vice president. Within months he approved the atomic bombing of Japan; over the next seven years he shaped America’s response to the Soviet Union with the Truman Doctrine, the Marshall Plan and NATO, desegregated the armed forces, and led the country into the Korean War. He left office deeply unpopular, but historians now rank him among the best presidents.

videos.title: Harry S. Truman: The Accidental President
The World Wars: Harry S. Truman | History

cards.a: Thirty-third president: ended World War II and launched the Cold War containment policy. Presiding judge, Jackson County, Missouri; U.S. Senator from Missouri (elected 1934); Vice President (1945); Thirty-third president (1945–1953)

cards.q: When did Harry S. Truman live?
cards.a: Born May 8, 1884, Lamar, Missouri; died December 26, 1972

cards.q: Who is this? Thirty-third president: ended World War II and launched the Cold War containment policy
cards.a: Harry S. Truman
April 12, 1945 – January 1953; Democrat
Truman Doctrine (1947), Marshall Plan, Berlin Airlift, NATO (1949), Korean War
Executive Order 9981 (1948) desegregated the armed forces

cards.q: Why does Harry S. Truman matter?
cards.a: Truman made the decisions that ended World War II and set the course of American foreign policy for the next four decades.

cards.q: What shaped Harry S. Truman early in life?
cards.a: Truman was born on May 8, 1884, in Lamar, Missouri, and grew up in Independence, a small town with Southern ways on the old trails to the West. Born with poor eyesight and kept by his mother from rough games, he became a passionate reader of history and a fine pianist who briefly considered a concert career.

cards.q: What were Harry S. Truman’s major achievements?
cards.a: In 1922 Tom Pendergast, Kansas City’s Democratic boss, backed Truman for county judge, an administrative post. As presiding judge from 1926 he rebuilt Jackson County’s roads and managed its finances in the early Depression, earning a reputation for honesty inside a corrupt machine.

entries.title: Henry Ford
entries.subtitle: Automaker who put America on wheels with the Model T, the moving assembly line, and the Five Dollar Day
entries.summary: Henry Ford did not invent the automobile or the assembly line, but more than anyone else he turned the car from a rich man’s novelty into a machine for the multitude. His Model T of 1908 was cheap, rugged, and easy to fix; his moving assembly line of 1913 cut its assembly time dramatically; and his Five Dollar Day of 1914 doubled workers’ pay so that they could buy the cars they built. Ford became a folk hero, and also one of the most notorious antisemites in American history, whose newspaper spread conspiracy theories that the Nazis admired.

Ford’s methods of mass production and mass consumption (standardized products, assembly lines, and high wages that let workers buy what they made) became a model for twentieth-century industry. His career also shows how fame and wealth could amplify hatred: his antisemitic publications circulated worldwide for decades.

cards.q: What shaped Henry Ford early in life?
cards.a: Henry Ford was born on July 30, 1863, on a farm in what is now Dearborn, Michigan. As a boy he showed a gift for machinery, a talent for leadership, and a preference for learning by trial and error.

cards.q: What were Henry Ford’s major achievements?
cards.a: Ford’s first two car companies failed. In 1901 his racing car beat the era’s top driver, and on June 16, 1903, a new group of investors founded the Ford Motor Company; its first Model A sold on July 23, and by October the company had turned a profit.

entries.title: Ida B. Wells
entries.subtitle: Journalist who exposed lynching and fought for civil rights and suffrage
entries.summary: Ida B. Wells was born into slavery in Mississippi in 1862 and became the leading crusader against lynching in American history. After a Memphis mob lynched three Black grocers, one of them her close friend, in 1892, she investigated lynchings across the South. In Southern Horrors and A Red Record she exposed the charge of rape used to justify them as a myth. A white mob destroyed her newspaper, and she carried her campaign to the North and to Britain. In Chicago she helped found Black women’s clubs, helped organize the NAACP, and fought for women’s suffrage. In 2020 she was awarded a posthumous Pulitzer Prize.

cards.q: Why does Ida B. Wells matter?
cards.a: Wells used investigative journalism, statistics, and the reports of white newspapers themselves to expose lynching and the excuses made for it. She linked the fight against racial violence to the fight for women’s votes, and her career shows how Black women shaped both the civil rights and suffrage movements.

cards.q: What shaped Ida B. Wells early in life?
cards.a: Ida Bell Wells was born enslaved in Holly Springs, Mississippi, on July 16, 1862, the oldest daughter of James and Elizabeth (Lizzie) Wells. She and her parents were freed at the end of the Civil War. During Reconstruction her parents were active in the Republican Party, and her father helped found Rust College, a historically Black college, where she studied. In the fall of 1878 yellow fever killed both of her parents and one of her siblings.

cards.q: What were Ida B. Wells’s major achievements?
cards.a: The Memphis lynching. In 1892 a white mob lynched Thomas Moss, Calvin McDowell, and a third man (the National Park Service names him Will Stewart, the National Women’s History Museum Henry Steward). They owned the People’s Grocery, which had drawn customers from a white-owned store.

entries.title: Independence Hall
entries.subtitle: Where the Declaration and the Constitution were debated and signed
entries.summary: Built as the Pennsylvania State House, Independence Hall is where the Second Continental Congress adopted the Declaration of Independence in 1776 and where the Constitutional Convention wrote the Constitution in 1787. The National Park Service calls it “the birthplace of America.” After the founding it became a shrine to the Revolution, visited by Lafayette in 1824 and by Abraham Lincoln in 1861, and today it is part of Independence National Historical Park and a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

Independence Hall is a red-brick building in the Georgian style, which the Park Service says looks more like a country house than an urban public building. Its plan includes a 105-foot main block joined by covered arcades to two wing buildings, and its tower and steeple were added around 1750. The rotted wooden steeple was removed in 1781, and in 1828 the architect William Strickland built a new one with a clock. Inside, the Assembly Room has been restored with tables for each colony, though no one knows exactly how the delegates were seated.

The State House. Speaker Andrew Hamilton oversaw construction, and the master builder Edmund Woolley drew the designs. Work began in 1732. The Pennsylvania Assembly was already meeting there in 1735, and the main building was finished in 1748. It housed all three branches of Pennsylvania’s colonial government.

entries.title: Jackie Robinson
entries.subtitle: The ballplayer who broke baseball’s color barrier in 1947, and a civil rights advocate
entries.summary: On April 15, 1947, Jackie Robinson took the field for the Brooklyn Dodgers and became the first African American player in the twentieth century in the American or National League. Chosen by Dodgers executive Branch Rickey, he endured hostile crowds, opposed teammates, and threats while starring on the field: Rookie of the Year in 1947, Most Valuable Player in 1949, and six pennants in ten seasons. After retiring he became an outspoken advocate for civil rights.

Robinson integrated the national pastime in 1947, showing millions of Americans what equal opportunity could look like, and then used his fame to press for civil rights.

cards.q: What shaped Jackie Robinson early in life?
cards.a: Jack Roosevelt Robinson was born on January 31, 1919, in Cairo, Georgia, the youngest of five children of sharecroppers Jerry and Mallie Robinson. His father left the family when Jackie was an infant, and in 1920 his mother moved the children by train to Pasadena, California, where she worked as a domestic.

cards.q: What were Jackie Robinson’s major achievements?
cards.a: Brooklyn Dodgers president Branch Rickey chose Robinson to break baseball’s unwritten color line: for his talent, but also because he was college-educated, had competed with and against white athletes, and could stand the spotlight.

entries.title: James Madison
entries.subtitle: Architect of the Constitution and fourth president
entries.summary: James Madison, a Virginia planter and enslaver, did more than anyone to design the Constitution of the United States. His exertions earned him the title “Father of the Constitution,” though he insisted the document was the work of “many heads & many hands.” He drafted the Virginia Plan that framed the Convention’s debates, wrote twenty-nine of the Federalist Papers, and steered the Bill of Rights through the first Congress. With Thomas Jefferson he founded the Republican Party, which opposed Hamilton’s Federalists. As Jefferson’s secretary of state and then as president from 1809 to 1817, he led the country through the troubled years before and during the War of 1812.

Madison’s ideas about large republics, factions, and checks and balances, set out in the Federalist Papers, remain central to American constitutional thought.

cards.q: What shaped James Madison early in life?
cards.a: James Madison was born on March 16, 1751, at Belle Grove, his mother’s family plantation at Port Conway in King George County, Virginia.

cards.q: What were James Madison’s major achievements?
cards.a: The Constitution. Madison studied the failures of earlier confederacies and concluded that the United States needed a strong national republic. His Virginia Plan, adopted in May 1787 as the Convention’s agenda, proposed three branches of government and a two-house legislature based on population. He won on representation by population in the House and on separate executive and judicial branches, but he lost on equal representation in the Senate and on a congressional veto over state laws, and for a time he doubted the new government could succeed. Throughout the Convention he kept detailed notes of the debates.

entries.title: Jazz
entries.subtitle: America’s homegrown music, born in New Orleans
entries.summary: Jazz is an American musical style built on improvisation and syncopated rhythm. It grew out of New Orleans around 1900, where African, Caribbean, Creole, and European traditions, brass bands, ragtime, and the blues met. Popularized by the city’s African American community and spread by records and radio, it became a national sensation in the 1920s, the decade often called the Jazz Age, and then a music heard around the world.

cards.a: America’s homegrown music, born in New Orleans

cards.q: Name it: America’s homegrown music, born in New Orleans
cards.a: Jazz

Jazz is one of the clearest examples of how African American culture shaped the whole nation’s, it gave the 1920s their name and became one of America’s best-known contributions to world music.
Jazz, in the words of The American Yawp, is “a uniquely American musical style” popularized by the African American community in New Orleans.

cards.q: Where did the idea come from?
cards.a: New Orleans had a culture unlike the rest of the young United States: Catholic and French-speaking, fond of festivals and dancing, and shaped by Africans and people of African descent, who made up more than half the city’s population by the end of the 1700s.

entries.title: Jim Crow
entries.subtitle: The system of legal segregation and disenfranchisement, 1880s–1960s
entries.summary: “Jim Crow” was the system of laws and customs that segregated Black Americans and stripped them of the vote after Reconstruction, named after a Black character in minstrel shows. From the 1880s into the 1960s, Southern states, and many others, required separate schools, railroad cars, waiting rooms, and cemeteries, and they barred Black men from voting with poll taxes and literacy tests. The Supreme Court approved “separate but equal” facilities in Plessy v. Ferguson in 1896, and the whole system was enforced by violence, including thousands of lynchings. The civil rights movement, Brown v. Board of Education, and the civil rights laws of 1964 and 1965 finally dismantled it.

videos.title: Jim Crow and America's Racism Explained

cards.a: The system of legal segregation and disenfranchisement, 1880s–1960s

cards.q: Name it: The system of legal segregation and disenfranchisement, 1880s–1960s
cards.a: Jim Crow
From a Black character in minstrel shows
From the 1880s into the 1960s
Plessy v. Ferguson (May 18, 1896), “equal but separate accommodations”
Poll taxes, literacy tests, and “grandfather clauses,” adopted mostly from about 1890 to 1908
White mobs killed roughly 5,000 African Americans between the 1880s and the 1950s
Brown v. Board (1954), the Civil Rights Act (1964), and the Voting Rights Act (1965)
Jim Crow made a mockery of the Fourteenth and Fifteenth Amendments for most of a century.

Jim Crow was a system of white supremacy built on three foundations: segregation, disenfranchisement, and violence. Segregation laws separated Black and white Americans in public life, from schools and trains to restaurants, theaters, restrooms, hospitals, and graveyards, and banned marriage between the races, punishing violators under the law. Disenfranchisement laws used poll taxes, literacy tests, and other devices to keep Black men from voting despite the Fifteenth Amendment. And lynching and mob violence punished anyone who challenged the order. The name came from “Jim Crow,” a Black character in minstrel shows. Although Jim Crow is most associated with the South, the National Park Service notes that a majority of states, from Delaware to California and from North Dakota to Texas, had such laws at some point.

cards.q: Where did the idea come from?
cards.a: The end of Reconstruction. When federal troops withdrew from the South in 1877, white Democrats who called themselves “Redeemers” regained power across the region, and the number of Black officeholders declined significantly. At first segregation was often a matter of custom.

entries.title: Joe Biden
entries.subtitle: Forty-sixth president, after thirty-six years in the Senate and eight as vice president
entries.summary: Joe Biden, a working-class Catholic from Scranton who overcame a severe childhood stutter, was elected to the Senate at twenty-nine, weeks before a car crash killed his wife and baby daughter. He served thirty-six years in the Senate and eight as Barack Obama’s vice president, then defeated Donald Trump in 2020 to become, at seventy-eight, the oldest president inaugurated up to that time. He led the country through the end of the Covid-19 pandemic and signed major laws on economic relief, infrastructure, semiconductors, and clean energy, but faced high inflation, a chaotic withdrawal from Afghanistan, and doubts about his age, and he withdrew from the 2024 race.

videos.title: Biden's long and painful path to Democratic presidential nomination

Biden’s long career spanned the Senate of the 1970s to the polarized politics of the 2020s. His presidency combined major new federal investments with an effort to rebuild alliances after the Trump years; its record on the pandemic, inflation, immigration, and foreign wars remains a subject of debate.

cards.q: What shaped Joe Biden early in life?
cards.a: Joseph Robinette Biden Jr. was born on November 20, 1942, in Scranton, Pennsylvania, the oldest child of a working-class Irish Catholic family. When his father’s business fortunes collapsed after World War II, Joe Sr. took whatever work he could find; in 1953 he found a job selling cars and moved the family to Delaware.

cards.q: What were Joe Biden’s major achievements?
cards.a: In the Senate Biden became a leading figure on the Judiciary and Foreign Relations Committees and chaired the confirmation hearings of five Supreme Court justices, including the bitterly contested nominations of Robert Bork and Clarence Thomas.

entries.title: John Adams
entries.subtitle: Revolutionary leader, diplomat, and second president, who kept the young nation out of war with France
entries.summary: John Adams was a blunt, brilliant Massachusetts lawyer who became one of the leading voices for American independence, a diplomat who helped negotiate the peace with Britain, the nation’s first vice president, and its second president. In the Continental Congress he nominated George Washington to command the army, led the faction pushing for independence, and served on the committee that prepared the Declaration. As president he faced an undeclared naval war with Revolutionary France; he built up the navy and signed the Alien and Sedition Acts, but he refused to let the conflict become a full war and made peace instead. Split from his own Federalist Party, he lost the election of 1800 to Thomas Jefferson. He died on July 4, 1826, the same day as Jefferson.

John Adams helped lead the colonies to independence, secured the peace that recognized it, and as president kept the new nation out of a war it might not have survived, at the cost of his own reelection. His peaceful handover of power to a political rival in 1801 set an important precedent.

cards.q: What shaped John Adams early in life?
cards.a: Adams was born on October 30, 1735, into a comfortable but not wealthy farming family in Braintree, Massachusetts, about fifteen miles south of Boston.

cards.q: What were John Adams’s major achievements?
cards.a: The Boston Massacre trial. In 1770 Adams agreed to defend the British soldiers charged after the Boston Massacre, a decision that angered many patriots. Through his defense, none of the accused was sent to jail.

entries.title: John Brown
entries.subtitle: Abolitionist who led the 1859 raid on Harpers Ferry
entries.summary: John Brown was a white abolitionist who believed slavery was a sin that only violence could end. After killing pro-slavery settlers in “Bleeding Kansas,” he led twenty-one men in an attack on the federal armory at Harpers Ferry, Virginia, in October 1859, hoping to spark an uprising of enslaved people. The raid collapsed within thirty-six hours; Brown was captured, tried for treason, and hanged. Hailed as a martyr in the North and denounced as a terrorist in the South, he deepened the division that led to the Civil War.

videos.title: The Life and Times of John Brown

cards.a: Abolitionist who led the 1859 raid on Harpers Ferry. Abolitionist; Tanner, farmer, and wool merchant; Antislavery fighter in Kansas; Leader of the raid on Harpers Ferry

cards.q: Who is this? Abolitionist who led the 1859 raid on Harpers Ferry
cards.a: John Brown
October 16–18, 1859, with 21 followers
U.S. Marines commanded by Colonel Robert E. Lee

John Brown’s raid convinced many Southerners that the North would not leave slavery alone, and many Northerners that slavery could not be ended peacefully, pushing the nation closer to civil war.

cards.q: What shaped John Brown early in life?
cards.a: Brown was born on May 9, 1800, in Torrington, Connecticut, and grew up in Hudson, Ohio. As a boy he saw an enslaved boy he had befriended savagely beaten, a sight that, with his conviction that slavery was a sin against God, shaped the rest of his life.

cards.q: What were John Brown’s major achievements?
cards.a: When the Kansas-Nebraska Act turned Kansas into a battleground over slavery, Brown followed members of his family there to “strike a blow for freedom.”

entries.title: John F. Kennedy
entries.subtitle: Thirty-fifth president: the youngest ever elected, assassinated in Dallas in 1963
entries.summary: John F. Kennedy was the youngest person ever elected president and the first Roman Catholic to hold the office. A rich Bostonian who became a war hero in the Pacific, he beat Richard Nixon in 1960 in one of the closest elections in American history, helped by a series of televised debates. In less than three years he faced the Bay of Pigs fiasco, the building of the Berlin Wall, and the Cuban Missile Crisis, launched the race to the moon, and sent a civil rights bill to Congress. His assassination in Dallas on November 22, 1963, became one of the great national traumas.

videos.title: Assassination of John F. Kennedy (1963)

cards.q: Why does John F. Kennedy matter?
cards.a: Kennedy's presidency brought the Cold War to its most dangerous moment and then to a first step back from it, the 1963 test ban treaty. His youth, eloquence, and command of television changed American politics, and his murder left a lasting sense of what might have been.

cards.q: What shaped John F. Kennedy early in life?
cards.a: John Fitzgerald Kennedy was born on May 29, 1917, in Brookline, Massachusetts, into a rich, politically connected family of Irish Catholics; his maternal grandfather had been mayor of Boston, and his father, Joseph P. Kennedy, had made a fortune in the stock market and entertainment and pulled his money out just before the crash of 1929.

cards.q: What were John F. Kennedy’s major achievements?
cards.a: In 1960 Kennedy won the Democratic nomination by beating Hubert Humphrey in the primaries, above all in heavily Protestant West Virginia, where he had to prove a wealthy Catholic could win.

entries.title: John Marshall
entries.subtitle: The chief justice who made the Supreme Court a co-equal branch of government
entries.summary: John Marshall was the fourth Chief Justice of the United States, presiding over the Supreme Court from 1801 until his death in 1835. A Revolutionary War officer and Virginia lawyer, he took over a weak tribunal whose first justices had complained of its “limited stature,” and his leadership, the Court’s own history says, was “central to the development of its prominent role in American government.” In Marbury v. Madison he established the Court’s power to strike down unconstitutional laws. In McCulloch v. Maryland and Gibbons v. Ogden he gave the federal government broad power. More than any other judge, he defined what the Constitution would mean in practice.

cards.q: What shaped John Marshall early in life?
cards.a: Marshall was born on September 24, 1755, in Virginia and grew up on his father’s estate, Oak Hill.

cards.q: What were John Marshall’s major achievements?
cards.a: The XYZ Affair. In 1797 President John Adams sent Marshall, Elbridge Gerry and Charles Cotesworth Pinckney to France to stop French seizures of American ships.

entries.title: Little Rock Central High School
entries.subtitle: Site of the 1957 desegregation crisis, now a National Historic Site
entries.summary: Little Rock Central High School became the center of a national crisis in September 1957, when nine Black students, the Little Rock Nine, tried to enter under a court-approved desegregation plan. Governor Orval Faubus sent the Arkansas National Guard to keep them out, and President Dwight D. Eisenhower answered by sending the Army’s 101st Airborne Division to protect them. The standoff led to Cooper v. Aaron (1958), in which the Supreme Court unanimously ruled that states could not nullify its desegregation decisions. Central High is still an operating public high school and is also a National Historic Site run by the National Park Service.

entries.title: Louis Armstrong
entries.subtitle: New Orleans trumpeter and singer who made jazz a soloist’s art and a world music
entries.summary: Louis Armstrong grew up poor in New Orleans, learned the cornet in a reform school, and followed his mentor Joe “King” Oliver to Chicago in 1922. His Hot Five and Hot Seven recordings of the 1920s put the improvising soloist at the center of jazz and popularized scat singing. Over a career of relentless touring, radio, and film, from “Heebie Jeebies” to “Hello, Dolly!” and “What a Wonderful World,” “Satchmo” became one of the most famous musicians in the world.

cards.q: What were Louis Armstrong’s major achievements?
cards.a: In 1922 Oliver sent for Armstrong to join his Creole Jazz Band in Chicago, where their intricate two-cornet breaks became the talk of the town; they began recording in 1923. Armstrong married the band’s pianist, Lil Hardin, in 1924, and she urged him to strike out on his own.

entries.title: Loyalists
entries.subtitle: The Americans who stayed loyal to the British Crown during the Revolution
entries.summary: The Revolution was also a civil war. Loyalists fought Patriots in their own neighborhoods, often “pitting family members against one another,” as the Yawp puts it. Some Loyalists were prominent, like Governor Thomas Hutchinson of Massachusetts or William Franklin, the royal governor of New Jersey and son of Benjamin Franklin. When Britain lost, Loyalists lost their homes and property, and tens of thousands left for Britain, Canada and other corners of the empire.

Loyalists remind us that independence was not a unanimous choice. Their defeat reshaped the British Empire as well as America: Loyalist exiles settled in large numbers in British Canada, and Black Loyalists helped settle Nova Scotia and Sierra Leone.
Loyalists, also called Tories, were colonists who remained loyal to King George III and opposed independence.

cards.q: Where did the idea come from?
cards.a: Loyalism had many roots.

entries.title: Lyndon B. Johnson
entries.subtitle: Thirty-sixth president: the Great Society, civil rights, and Vietnam
entries.summary: Lyndon Baines Johnson, the thirty-sixth president of the United States (1963–1969), was a Texas Hill Country schoolteacher who became one of the most skilled legislators in American history. Thrust into the presidency by John F. Kennedy’s assassination in November 1963, he pushed through the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and the Voting Rights Act of 1965, won a historic landslide, and launched the Great Society: Medicare, Medicaid, federal aid to education, and the War on Poverty. But his escalation of the Vietnam War tore the country apart, and in 1968 he declined to seek another term.

cards.a: Johnson enacted the most sweeping domestic reforms since the New Deal, while his Vietnam policy tore the country apart.

cards.q: What shaped Lyndon B. Johnson early in life?
cards.a: Johnson was born on August 27, 1908, in a farmhouse on the Pedernales River, the first of five children; his father, a state legislator, rode up and down the river announcing that his son would be governor of Texas someday. Their house in Johnson City had neither electricity nor indoor plumbing.

cards.q: What were Lyndon B. Johnson’s major achievements?
cards.a: Appointed Texas director of the New Deal’s National Youth Administration in 1935, Johnson helped young people stay in school and find work. In 1937, at twenty-eight, he won a seat in Congress as a Roosevelt ally and brought electricity to the Hill Country of his youth, the achievement he called his proudest.

entries.title: Malcolm X
entries.subtitle: Black nationalist leader and critic of nonviolence
entries.summary: Malcolm X was the most visible voice of Black nationalism in the 1960s. Born Malcolm Little, he rose from a shattered childhood and a prison cell to become the national spokesman of the Nation of Islam, denouncing white racism and rejecting Martin Luther King Jr.’s nonviolence; he urged Black Americans to seek freedom “by any means necessary.” In 1964 he broke with the Nation, made the pilgrimage to Mecca, and began building bridges to the civil rights movement. He was assassinated in February 1965; his ideas shaped the Black Power movement.

videos.title: Malcolm X: The Defender of Human Rights
Malcolm X and the Rise of Black Power: Crash Course Black American History #38

cards.a: Black nationalist leader and critic of nonviolence. Minister and national spokesman, Nation of Islam; Founder, Organization of Afro-American Unity (1964)

cards.a: Malcolm X

Malcolm X gave voice to Black anger and pride and offered a radical alternative to King’s philosophy, and his influence grew after his death.

cards.q: What shaped Malcolm X early in life?
cards.a: Malcolm Little was born on May 19, 1925, in Omaha, Nebraska. His parents were active in Marcus Garvey’s movement, his father led a chapter of the Universal Negro Improvement Association, and his father’s activism drew threats from a white supremacist group, the Black Legion.

cards.q: What were Malcolm X’s major achievements?
cards.a: Brilliant and charismatic, Malcolm X became a minister and national spokesman of the Nation of Islam, founding mosques in cities such as Detroit and Harlem and using newspaper columns, radio, and television to spread its message.

entries.title: Manifest Destiny
entries.subtitle: The belief that the United States was destined to spread across the continent
entries.summary: “Manifest destiny” was a phrase coined in 1845 by the editor John L. O’Sullivan, who wrote of America’s “manifest destiny to overspread the continent allotted by Providence for the free development of our yearly multiplying millions.” It named a belief much older than the phrase: that the United States had a God-given mission to spread its democracy, and that the lands to the west were meant for American settlement. The idea drove the annexation of Texas, the acquisition of Oregon, and the Mexican-American War. It also rested on assumptions of white racial superiority, and it was disastrous for the Native peoples and Mexicans who stood in its way. Critics from Emerson to Lincoln mocked it, and the expansion it justified deepened the conflict over slavery.

videos.title: Westward Expansion: Crash Course US History #24
Manifest Destiny Explained in 5 Minutes: US History Review

quotes.text: The fulfillment of our manifest destiny to overspread the continent allotted by Providence for the free development of our yearly multiplying millions.
quotes.speaker: John L. O’Sullivan

quotes.speaker: Abraham Lincoln

quotes.speaker: Horace Greeley

cards.a: The belief that the United States was destined to spread across the continent

cards.q: Name it: The belief that the United States was destined to spread across the continent
cards.a: Manifest Destiny

The Young America movement, President James K. Polk, and the Democratic Party

Manifest Destiny gave a confident, providential name to the conquest of the continent. The American Yawp concludes that westward expansion “exacerbated the slavery question, pushed Americans toward civil war, and, ultimately, threatened the very mission of American democracy it was designed to aid.”

The American Yawp describes Manifest Destiny as a widely held but vaguely defined belief made of three claims. The first was that the strength of American values and institutions justified a moral claim to leadership in the hemisphere.

cards.q: Where did the idea come from?
cards.a: The belief dated back to the founding, even if the name did not. The State Department’s historians note that by the mid-1800s, the Monroe Doctrine together with ideas of Manifest Destiny “provided precedent and support for U.S. expansion on the American continent.” Its champions in the 1840s included the Young America movement, strongest among Democrats, which emphasized American exceptionalism, territorial expansion, and democratic participation and played down divisions over slavery. In 1841 the publisher Horace Greeley urged Americans to “Go west, before you are fitted for no life but that of the factory.”

entries.title: Manzanar
entries.subtitle: A War Relocation Center in California’s Owens Valley, now a National Historic Site
entries.summary: Manzanar was one of ten War Relocation Centers where Japanese Americans were incarcerated during World War II. Built in 1942 on land the Army leased from the city of Los Angeles in California’s Owens Valley, at the foot of the Sierra Nevada, it held families forcibly removed from the West Coast under Executive Order 9066. Today it is a National Historic Site that preserves the camp’s story, and the earlier displacement of the valley’s Paiute people and farm settlers.

videos.title: THE NATIONAL PARKS | Manzanar: "Never Again" | PBS

cards.a: A War Relocation Center in California’s Owens Valley, now a National Historic Site
Owens Valley, Inyo County, California (between Lone Pine and Independence on U.S. 395) · West

cards.q: Name it: A War Relocation Center in California’s Owens Valley, now a National Historic Site
cards.a: Manzanar

Manzanar’s layered history of removal (Paiute, settler, and Japanese American) makes it a powerful place to reflect on who has been forced from the land.

Manzanar lies on the floor of the Owens Valley, with Mount Williamson rising directly to the west. Most of the camp’s buildings are gone; the site includes a cemetery, historic orchards, and a visitor center.

Earlier displacements. People used the Owens Valley for almost 10,000 years, and about 1,500 years ago the Owens Valley Paiute established settlements there, practicing a form of irrigated agriculture. After miners and ranchers moved in during the 1860s, the Army forcibly relocated nearly 1,000 Paiute to Fort Tejon in 1863.

entries.title: Mark Twain
entries.subtitle: Humorist and novelist who turned American speech into literature
entries.summary: Samuel Clemens grew up in Hannibal, Missouri, on the Mississippi River, worked as a printer, riverboat pilot, and frontier journalist, and as “Mark Twain” became the best-loved American writer of his age. Books such as The Adventures of Tom Sawyer and Adventures of Huckleberry Finn drew on his Missouri boyhood, while The Gilded Age and later works attacked corruption, greed, racism, and imperialism. In his time he was considered the funniest man on earth.

cards.q: What were Mark Twain’s major achievements?
cards.a: His comic story about a jumping frog, reprinted in papers across the country in 1865, was his first big break. Sent to report from the Sandwich Islands (Hawaii) in 1866, he came back and launched a career as a stage lecturer.

entries.title: Marquis de Lafayette
entries.subtitle: The young French nobleman who became Washington’s general and “The Hero of the Two Worlds”
entries.summary: The Marquis de Lafayette was a wealthy French nobleman who defied a royal ban and sailed to America in 1777 on a ship he had bought himself to fight for independence. Congress made him a major general, and he became one of George Washington’s closest companions, wintering with the army at Valley Forge and helping to trap the British at Yorktown in 1781. Back in France he helped write the Declaration of the Rights of Man during the French Revolution. On his triumphant tour of the United States in 1824 crowds greeted him in every city, and he is remembered as “The Hero of the Two Worlds.”

cards.q: Why does Marquis de Lafayette matter?
cards.a: Lafayette tied the American Revolution to France, the ally that made victory possible, and carried its ideals back to Europe. For Americans he became a symbol of the friendship between the two nations.

entries.title: Martin Luther King Jr.
entries.subtitle: Minister and leader of the nonviolent civil rights movement
entries.summary: Martin Luther King Jr., a Baptist minister from Atlanta, became the most prominent leader of the civil rights movement. Chosen to lead the Montgomery bus boycott soon after he arrived in the city as a young pastor, he joined the ideals of Christianity to Gandhi’s methods of nonviolent resistance. He led campaigns in Birmingham and Selma, delivered “I Have a Dream” at the March on Washington, and helped win the Civil Rights Act and the Voting Rights Act. At thirty-five he became the youngest man to receive the Nobel Peace Prize. He was assassinated in Memphis in 1968, while supporting a strike of sanitation workers.

entries.title: Muhammad Ali
entries.subtitle: Three-time heavyweight champion who gave up his title rather than fight in Vietnam
entries.summary: Muhammad Ali, born Cassius Clay in segregated Louisville, won Olympic gold at eighteen and the world heavyweight title at twenty-two. That year he announced that he had joined the Nation of Islam and taken a new name. In 1967 he refused induction into the Army during the Vietnam War, citing his faith; he was stripped of his title, convicted, and barred from boxing until the Supreme Court overturned his conviction in 1971. He regained the championship twice, and after Parkinson’s disease ended his public career he became a worldwide symbol of conviction and humanitarian work.

entries.title: Phillis Wheatley
entries.subtitle: Enslaved poet of revolutionary Boston, the first African American to publish a book of poetry
entries.summary: Phillis Wheatley was kidnapped in West Africa as a child, sold in Boston in 1761, and within a few years became one of the best-known poets in the English-speaking world. Her Poems on Various Subjects, Religious and Moral, published in London in 1773, made her the first African American and the second woman in what became the United States to publish a book of poetry. She supported the Revolution, wrote a poem in honor of George Washington in 1775, and in her verse tied the colonists’ cry for liberty to her own enslavement.

entries.title: Republicanism
entries.subtitle: The founders’ ideal of self-government by virtuous citizens
entries.summary: In the founding era, republicanism meant government without a king, deriving its powers from the people and run by their elected representatives. It also meant a set of fears and hopes about liberty. Republicans believed that power corrupts and that a free people must be virtuous, putting the public good above their own interests, or they would lose their freedom. These ideas, widely held in the colonies though only by a fringe in Britain, shaped how Americans saw British policy, why they rebelled, and how they designed their new governments. Philosophers today describe the heart of the tradition as liberty understood as freedom from arbitrary power.

videos.title: Who Won the American Revolution?: Crash Course US History #7
How Revolutionary IDEAS Caused the American Revolution [APUSH Review]

quotes.text: We may define a republic to be, or at least may bestow that name on, a government which derives all its powers directly or indirectly from the great body of the people.
quotes.speaker: James Madison

quotes.speaker: James Madison

cards.a: The founders’ ideal of self-government by virtuous citizens

The later Republican Party, or Jefferson’s Democratic-Republicans, though both took the name

Republicanism gave Americans the language they used to justify independence and to design their governments, and its fear of concentrated power helped shape the separation of powers and the federal system. It also assigned roles: women, under the ideal of Republican Motherhood, were valued chiefly for raising virtuous citizens. Its idea that liberty means freedom from arbitrary power remains influential in political philosophy today.

The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy describes two meanings. Historically, republicanism names a loose tradition of writers, from Machiavelli and the English republicans Milton, Harrington, and Sidney to Montesquieu, the English commonwealthmen, and “many Americans of the founding era.”

cards.q: Where did the idea come from?
cards.a: Colonial political culture drew on the ideas of Britain’s opposition “country” party.

entries.title: Richard Nixon
entries.subtitle: Thirty-seventh president: opened relations with China, then became the only president to resign
entries.summary: Richard Nixon rose from a small California town to the vice presidency in six years, lost the presidency to John F. Kennedy in 1960, and won it in 1968. A lifelong anticommunist, he stunned the world by visiting Communist China in 1972, signed landmark nuclear arms limitation treaties with the Soviet Union, and ended the American ground war in Vietnam; at home he created the Environmental Protection Agency. Reelected in a 49-state landslide, he was brought down by the Watergate scandal and in 1974 became the first and only president to resign.

The Rise and Fall of Richard Nixon | Full Documentary | American Experience PBS

cards.a: Thirty-seventh president: opened relations with China, then became the only president to resign. U.S. Representative from California (1947–1950); U.S. Senator from California (1950–1953); Vice president under Eisenhower (1953–1961); Thirty-seventh president (1969–1974)
Born January 9, 1913, Yorba Linda, California; died April 22, 1994

Nixon's diplomacy with China and the Soviet Union reshaped the Cold War and set the stage for its end, and his presidency marked the shift from liberal Democratic to conservative Republican dominance. Watergate made him a lasting symbol of the abuse of presidential power and deepened Americans' distrust of their leaders.

cards.q: What shaped Richard Nixon early in life?
cards.a: Nixon was born on January 9, 1913, in Yorba Linda, California, and grew up in another small town, East Whittier. His father, Frank, was argumentative, his mother, Hannah, sweet-tempered.

cards.q: What were Richard Nixon’s major achievements?
cards.a: In 1952 Dwight Eisenhower chose Nixon as his running mate. When a newspaper charged that a secret fund kept him in style, he defended himself on national television, promising his little daughter Tricia that he would never return one campaign gift, a cocker spaniel puppy named Checkers.

entries.title: Ronald Reagan
entries.subtitle: Fortieth president and leader of the conservative revival
entries.summary: Ronald Reagan, a former radio announcer, film actor, and governor of California, was elected president in 1980 at a time of economic trouble and setbacks abroad. He cut income taxes, broke an air traffic controllers’ strike, and built up the military as deficits and the national debt soared. After denouncing the Soviet Union, he worked with Mikhail Gorbachev on the 1987 INF Treaty, the first Cold War agreement to reduce nuclear arsenals. Despite the Iran-Contra affair, he left office in 1989 highly popular, having reshaped American conservatism.

Reagan made conservatism, with its calls for lower taxes, less regulation, a strong military, and firm anticommunism, the dominant force in the Republican Party and a powerful one in American politics. His partnership with Gorbachev helped bring the Cold War toward a peaceful end, while his economic record, with long growth, low inflation, and record deficits, is still debated.

cards.q: What shaped Ronald Reagan early in life?
cards.a: Ronald Wilson Reagan was born on February 6, 1911, in an apartment above a general store in Tampico, Illinois.

cards.q: What were Ronald Reagan’s major achievements?
cards.a: A Time for Choosing. On October 27, 1964, Reagan gave a nationally televised speech for the Republican presidential candidate Barry Goldwater. He warned that government was eroding individual freedom and that the country was too weak against the Soviet Union, and told viewers, “You and I have a rendezvous with destiny.”

entries.title: Rosa Parks
entries.subtitle: Activist whose arrest sparked the Montgomery bus boycott
entries.summary: Rosa Parks was the seamstress and veteran NAACP activist whose arrest on December 1, 1955, for refusing to give up her seat to a white passenger on a Montgomery, Alabama, bus sparked the Montgomery bus boycott. The thirteen-month protest ended with bus segregation struck down and made Martin Luther King Jr. a national leader. Long remembered as a tired woman who simply wanted to sit down, Parks was in fact a seasoned organizer who had fought Jim Crow for more than a decade. “The only tired I was,” she wrote, “was tired of giving in.”

videos.title: Rosa Parks - Civil Rights Activist | Mini Bio | BIO
The hidden life of Rosa Parks -  Riché D. Richardson

quotes.text: I was not tired physically, or no more tired than I usually was at the end of a working day. I was not old, although some people have an image of me as being old then. I was forty-two. No, the only tired I was, was tired of giving in.
quotes.speaker: Rosa Parks

quotes.speaker: Rosa Parks
