Parks’s refusal became the most famous single act of the civil rights movement, but its power came from years of organizing behind it. Her arrest gave Montgomery’s Black community the rallying point it had been looking for, and the boycott that followed showed that nonviolent mass protest could defeat segregation.

cards.q: What shaped Rosa Parks early in life?
cards.a: Rosa Louise McCauley was born on February 4, 1913, in Tuskegee, Alabama, and spent her first years on a small farm with her mother, grandparents, and brother. As a child she watched the Ku Klux Klan ride at night and listened in fear to news of lynchings near her home. She grew up in Montgomery, attended an industrial school for girls and the laboratory school of Alabama State College, and later enrolled at Alabama State Teachers College, but had to withdraw when her grandmother fell ill.

cards.q: What were Rosa Parks’s major achievements?
cards.a: On the evening of December 1, 1955, Parks, then forty-two, boarded a city bus on her way home from the Montgomery Fair department store, where she worked as a seamstress. Montgomery reserved the front ten seats of each bus for white passengers, and Parks sat in the first row behind them.

entries.title: Sacagawea
entries.subtitle: The Lemhi Shoshone woman who traveled with Lewis and Clark to the Pacific and back
entries.summary: Sacagawea was a Lemhi Shoshone woman who, at sixteen or seventeen and carrying her newborn son, traveled with the Lewis and Clark Expedition to the Pacific and back. She was the only woman in the Corps of Discovery. She is often remembered as its guide, but the journals show something different and arguably more important. Her presence told the tribes they met that the party was not a war party, and when the explorers reached her homeland in the Rockies, she helped them find the Shoshone and the horses they needed to cross the mountains. Little else about her is certain, from the spelling of her name to the date of her death.

videos.title: Sacagawea - Explorer | Biography

quotes.speaker: Meriwether Lewis

Sacagawea is one of the most commemorated women in American history and a reminder that the expedition depended on Native people.

cards.q: What shaped Sacagawea early in life?
cards.a: Sacagawea was born around 1788 among the Lemhi Shoshone in the mountains of present-day Idaho. When she was eleven or twelve, a Hidatsa raiding party captured her and carried her east to the Knife River villages in present-day North Dakota, where she lived at the Awatixa village. There Toussaint Charbonneau, a French-Canadian fur trader living among the Hidatsa, claimed her as one of his wives.

On the river. Sacagawea, Charbonneau and the baby left Fort Mandan with the Corps on April 7, 1805. She dug roots and found other food, and showed the men how to make leather clothing and moccasins. On May 14, 1805, when a gust of wind nearly overturned the boat Charbonneau was steering, she calmly rescued instruments, books, medicines and other supplies from the water. A token of peace. Her presence dispelled the idea that the party was a war party.

entries.title: Sitting Bull
entries.subtitle: Hunkpapa Lakota leader who refused the reservation
entries.summary: Sitting Bull (Tatanka-Iyotanka) was a Hunkpapa Lakota war chief and holy man who led the Lakota who refused to accept life on a reservation. He rejected the 1868 Treaty of Fort Laramie and kept his people hunting buffalo on the open plains. In June 1876 his vision of soldiers “falling into camp” came before the Lakota and Cheyenne victory over George Armstrong Custer at the Little Bighorn. Pursued by the army, he led his followers into Canada and surrendered in 1881. He toured briefly with Buffalo Bill’s Wild West and lived at Standing Rock. In December 1890, amid fears of the Ghost Dance, he was killed by Lakota reservation police sent to arrest him.

Sitting Bull became the best-known symbol of Native resistance to American conquest of the Great Plains. His refusal to sign away Lakota land or way of life, and the victory at the Little Bighorn associated with his name, made him famous among white Americans as well as his own people.

cards.q: What shaped Sitting Bull early in life?
cards.a: Sitting Bull was born into a prominent Hunkpapa Lakota family sometime between 1831 and 1837, near where the Grand River meets the Missouri in present-day South Dakota.

cards.q: What were Sitting Bull’s major achievements?
cards.a: The non-treaty Lakota. In 1866 the Lakota leader Red Cloud waged a successful war against forts along the Bozeman Trail, and in 1868 he and other leaders signed the Treaty of Fort Laramie.

entries.title: Slavery in America
entries.subtitle: The institution that shaped the nation’s economy, politics, and conflicts for nearly 250 years
entries.summary: Slavery, the ownership of human beings as property, inherited by their children and enforced by law and violence, was legal in every one of the thirteen colonies and lasted in the United States until 1865. Enslaved Africans and their descendants grew the tobacco, rice, and above all the cotton that made the South rich and drove the nation’s exports. By 1860 the census counted 3,953,760 enslaved people, about one in eight Americans. The struggle over slavery shaped the Constitution, split the nation in the 1850s, and ended only with the Civil War and the Thirteenth Amendment.

cards.a: Slavery was not a regional exception to American history but one of its central forces.
Chattel slavery treated enslaved people as movable property that could be bought, sold, mortgaged, and inherited. In the English colonies and the United States, it became tied to race.

cards.q: Where did the idea come from?
cards.a: Origins. Slavery in the Americas grew out of a much older Atlantic trade.

entries.title: Sojourner Truth
entries.subtitle: Abolitionist and women’s rights speaker who escaped slavery in New York
entries.summary: Sojourner Truth was born into slavery in New York as Isabella Baumfree, freed herself in 1826, and became one of the most powerful speakers of the nineteenth century against slavery and for women’s rights. She was the first Black woman to win a lawsuit against a white man, for the return of her son, sold illegally into Alabama. Never formally educated, she dictated a celebrated autobiography and moved audiences with speeches such as the one at Akron in 1851 later known as “Ain’t I a Woman?” In 2009 she became the first Black woman honored with a bust in the U.S. Capitol.

videos.title: The electrifying speeches of Sojourner Truth - Daina Ramey Berry

cards.a: Abolitionist and women’s rights speaker who escaped slavery in New York. Abolitionist and women’s rights lecturer; Preacher; Recruiter for Black Union troops; Freedmen’s relief worker

cards.q: Who is this? Abolitionist and women’s rights speaker who escaped slavery in New York
cards.a: Sojourner Truth

Sojourner Truth made the case, from her own experience, that the struggles against slavery and for women’s rights were one struggle, and that neither could succeed while ignoring Black women.

cards.q: What shaped Sojourner Truth early in life?
cards.a: Isabella Baumfree was born about 1797 in Ulster County, New York, one of perhaps ten to twelve children of enslaved parents, James and Elizabeth; all her siblings were sold away. Her first language was the Dutch of her enslavers.

cards.q: What were Sojourner Truth’s major achievements?
cards.a: When Dumont illegally sold her five-year-old son Peter to an enslaver in Alabama, she took the case to court and, after a long fight, won his return in 1828: becoming, the National Women’s History Museum notes, the first Black woman to sue a white man and win. A religious awakening followed.

entries.title: Susan B. Anthony
entries.subtitle: Organizer and public face of the woman suffrage movement
entries.summary: Susan B. Anthony was the best-known organizer of the nineteenth-century woman suffrage movement. For more than fifty years, often in partnership with Elizabeth Cady Stanton, she traveled the country giving speeches, circulating petitions, and building organizations. Raised a Quaker, she began as a temperance and antislavery reformer. After the Civil War she opposed the Fifteenth Amendment because it enfranchised Black men but not women, and she co-founded the National Woman Suffrage Association. In 1872 she was arrested and convicted for voting. She died in 1906. The Nineteenth Amendment, ratified in 1920, was widely called the “Susan B. Anthony Amendment.”

videos.title: What Crime Did Susan B. Anthony Commit?

quotes.speaker: Susan B. Anthony

Teacher; Temperance and antislavery reformer; American Anti-Slavery Society agent; Co-founder of the National Woman Suffrage Association (1869); Publisher of *The Revolution*; President of the National American Woman Suffrage Association (1892–1900)

cards.q: When did Susan B. Anthony live?
cards.a: Born February 15, 1820, Adams, Massachusetts; died March 13, 1906, Rochester, New York

cards.q: Why does Susan B. Anthony matter?
cards.a: Anthony turned woman suffrage into a national, organized movement and kept it focused on a federal constitutional amendment. Her record also includes the racist arguments she adopted after the Civil War, which divided the movement and alienated former allies such as Frederick Douglass.

cards.q: What shaped Susan B. Anthony early in life?
cards.a: Susan Brownell Anthony was born on February 15, 1820, in Adams, Massachusetts, the second of seven children of Daniel and Lucy Anthony. Her father, a Quaker, built a cotton mill, where Susan worked for a time with one of her sisters.

cards.q: What were Susan B. Anthony’s major achievements?
cards.a: Partnership with Stanton. In 1851, on a street corner in Seneca Falls, Amelia Bloomer introduced Anthony to Elizabeth Cady Stanton, the organizer of the 1848 Seneca Falls convention. Their partnership lasted the rest of their lives.

entries.title: Tecumseh
entries.subtitle: Shawnee leader who tried to unite Native nations against American expansion
entries.summary: Tecumseh was a Shawnee leader who, with his brother Tenskwatawa, “the Prophet,” tried to build an alliance of Native nations from the Great Lakes to the Gulf of Mexico to stop American expansion. He traveled from Canada to Georgia calling for unity, resistance and “the restoration of sacred power,” and he refused to concede any more land. After American troops destroyed his headquarters at Prophetstown in 1811, his confederacy fought alongside Britain in the War of 1812. His death at the Battle of the Thames on October 5, 1813, broke the confederacy apart.

videos.title: Tecumseh and the Native American Resistance
The OTHER United States of America | The Life & Times of Tecumseh

cards.a: Shawnee leader who tried to unite Native nations against American expansion. Shawnee war leader and diplomat; Organizer of a pan-Native confederacy; British ally in the War of 1812

cards.a: Tecumseh
1769, in a Kispoko Shawnee village in the Scioto River valley, Ohio country

Tecumseh led the last great attempt to unite the Native nations east of the Mississippi against American expansion. With his death, the American Battlefield Trust writes, “many tribes who followed his leadership peeled away,” and organized resistance in the Old Northwest ended.

cards.q: What shaped Tecumseh early in life?
cards.a: Tecumseh was born in 1769 while his parents, Pukeshinwau of the Kispoko Shawnee Panther Clan and Methoataaskee of the Piqua Shawnee Turtle Clan, were staying in a village in the Scioto River valley of present-day Ohio.

The Prophet’s revival. Tenskwatawa preached that the Master of Life had charged the brothers with returning Native peoples to “the one true path” and ridding their communities of the corrupting influence of American trade and culture. The brothers founded towns at Greenville and then Prophetstown, in present-day Indiana, in defiance of the Greenville treaty. A confederacy. Tecumseh turned the revival into a political and military alliance.

entries.title: The Blues
entries.subtitle: The African American music of the Deep South that became the root of jazz, rock and roll, and soul
entries.summary: The blues is a music created by African Americans in the Deep South around the 1880s and 1890s, at about the same time as jazz and ragtime. Built on a twelve-bar pattern of chords and the bent “blue notes” that give it its sound, it grew from work songs, field hollers, and spirituals, and it spoke of hard labor, poverty, love, and life under Jim Crow. The Mississippi Delta, often called its birthplace, produced many of its greatest performers. Carried north by the Great Migration and electrified in Chicago, the blues became a foundation for much of American popular music.

cards.a: The African American music of the Deep South that became the root of jazz, rock and roll, and soul

cards.q: Name it: The African American music of the Deep South that became the root of jazz, rock and roll, and soul
cards.a: The Blues
Probably in the 1880s or 1890s, in the Deep South
Usually twelve bars, using three basic chords and flattened “blue notes”
W. C. Handy heard a guitarist play with a knife for a slide at Tutwiler, Mississippi, around 1903
No African American recorded the blues until 1920; women vaudeville singers dominated 1920–1925
Charley Patton, Son House, Robert Johnson, Muddy Waters, Howlin’ Wolf, B. B. King

The blues documented the experience of Black Southerners more fully than perhaps any other form of expression, and its forms, sounds, and spirit fed directly into jazz, rhythm and blues, rock and roll, and soul, making it one of the most influential musical traditions in the world.

Musically, the blues is typified by a twelve-bar chord progression, each verse stretches over twelve measures using set patterns of three basic chords, although other lengths are common. Its signature is the “blue note,” a flattened third, fifth, or seventh that gives the music its aching sound.

cards.q: Where did the idea come from?
cards.a: The blues grew out of the music that enslaved Africans and their descendants made in the South: work songs and field hollers sung in the fields, and the spirituals of Black churches. It appeared in recognizable form in the 1880s or 1890s, and by the early 1900s it was spreading across the South from Virginia to Texas.

entries.title: The Columbian Exchange
entries.subtitle: The transfer of plants, animals, people, and diseases between the hemispheres after 1492
entries.summary: The “Columbian Exchange,” a term coined by the historian Alfred W. Crosby, describes the enormous transfer of crops, livestock, people, and microbes between the Eastern and Western Hemispheres that followed 1492. Maize and potatoes transformed diets in Europe, Africa, and Asia; horses, cattle, and wheat transformed the Americas. Most devastating of all, Old World diseases such as smallpox and measles killed a large share of the Native peoples of the Americas.

videos.title: The Columbian Exchange: Crash Course World History #23
The Columbian Exchange

cards.a: The transfer of plants, animals, people, and diseases between the hemispheres after 1492

cards.q: Name it: The transfer of plants, animals, people, and diseases between the hemispheres after 1492
cards.a: The Columbian Exchange
Maize, white and sweet potatoes, manioc, peanuts, tomatoes, squash, pineapples, avocados
Wheat, rice, barley, sugar, horses, cattle, pigs, sheep, goats
Smallpox, measles, malaria, yellow fever, typhoid, and others
Alfred W. Crosby, in his 1972 book The Columbian Exchange

cards.q: Why does the Columbian Exchange matter?
cards.a: The Columbian Exchange reshaped ecosystems, diets, and populations on every inhabited continent. For the Americas it meant both the arrival of new livestock and crops and the greatest population collapse in human history, a central reason why European colonization succeeded.

The Columbian Exchange is the movement of living things (plants, animals, and pathogens) and of people between the Old World and the New after Columbus’s voyages reconnected hemispheres that had developed separately for thousands of years.

cards.q: Where did the idea come from?
cards.a: Before 1492, the Americas and the Eastern Hemisphere had very different inventories of life. The Americas had few domesticated animals (dogs, llamas, guinea pigs, and a few fowl) and no wild horses or cattle to tame.

entries.title: The Digital Revolution
entries.subtitle: Computers, the internet, and smartphones transform American life
entries.summary: The digital revolution is the transformation of the economy and daily life by computers and networked communication. Its roots lie in government-funded research: the Defense Department’s ARPANET began with four computers in 1969, and the National Science Foundation’s NSFNET, launched in 1986, became the backbone of the early internet. In the 1990s personal computers and the web turned the internet into a mass phenomenon and fueled the dot-com boom; after 2007, smartphones and social media put the internet in Americans’ pockets.

This Is The History Of The Internet | Mach | NBC News

Launched 1986; grew from about 2,000 connected computers to more than 2 million by 1993

The iPhone (2007) popularized smartphones; about two-thirds of Americans owned one by about 2015

cards.q: Why does the Digital Revolution matter?
cards.a: The digital revolution remade how Americans work, shop, learn, communicate, and get their news, and created new questions about privacy, misinformation, and economic inequality.

The term describes the shift, beginning in the late twentieth century, from industrial and analog technologies to digital computing and communications, and the economic, social, and political changes that followed.

cards.q: Where did the idea come from?
cards.a: In the early 1960s J. C. R. Licklider imagined an “Intergalactic Computer Network.” Defense Department researchers built ARPANET and developed the TCP/IP protocols that let computers exchange email and files.

entries.title: The Gilded Age
entries.subtitle: An era of industrial wealth, inequality, and corruption, c. 1870–1900
entries.summary: “The Gilded Age” names the decades after Reconstruction, when the United States became the world’s leading industrial economy. The term comes from an 1873 satirical novel by Mark Twain and Charles Dudley Warner, and it describes a glittering surface of wealth and innovation covering deep inequality and corruption. Railroads, steel, oil, and finance created vast fortunes, while millions of workers and immigrants crowded into cities and fought for decent wages and conditions.

videos.title: Gilded Age Politics: Crash Course US History #26
Chapter 1 | The Gilded Age | American Experience | PBS

cards.a: An era of industrial wealth, inequality, and corruption, c. 1870–1900

cards.q: Name it: An era of industrial wealth, inequality, and corruption, c. 1870–1900
cards.a: The Gilded Age
From The Gilded Age: A Tale of Today (1873) by Mark Twain and Charles Dudley Warner

Labor unions, Populism, and later Progressivism

cards.q: Why does the Gilded Age matter?
cards.a: The Gilded Age created modern industrial America, and the inequalities and conflicts that reformers in the Populist and Progressive movements set out to address.

A gilded object is covered with a thin layer of gold over a cheaper material. By calling their era “gilded” rather than golden, Twain and Warner mocked a society whose dazzling wealth and technological marvels masked massive social inequities and deep-seated corruption.

cards.q: Where did the idea come from?
cards.a: After the Civil War, industrial capitalism transformed the country. The transcontinental railroad and a vast rail network created national markets.

entries.title: The National Mall
entries.subtitle: “America’s Front Yard” in Washington, D.C.
entries.summary: The National Mall is the long open space at the heart of Washington, D.C., running from the U.S. Capitol to the Potomac River. Its open spaces go back to Pierre L’Enfant’s plan for the capital, commissioned by George Washington, and it was reshaped in the early twentieth century to frame the Washington Monument and the Lincoln Memorial. Lined with monuments and memorials, it has also been the nation’s stage for inaugurations, celebrations, and protests, most famously the 1963 March on Washington, where Martin Luther King Jr. gave his “I Have a Dream” speech.

quotes.speaker: Royal Cortissoz
quotes.context: inscription above the statue in the Lincoln Memorial, dedicated 1922

quotes.text: Everyone who believed in man’s capacity to better himself had a moment of inspiration and confidence in the future of the human race.
quotes.speaker: Martin Luther King Jr.

cards.q: Why does the National Mall matter?
cards.a: The National Mall is the premier civic and symbolic space of the United States. Its monuments show how Americans have chosen to remember their past, and its lawns have been where citizens come to celebrate, mourn, and demand that the country live up to its founding promises.

The Mall is a long swath of lawn and elm trees with the Capitol at one end, the Washington Monument near the middle, and the Lincoln Memorial and its Reflecting Pool at the western end. The National Park Service unit that cares for it manages more than 1,000 acres, including the Washington Monument; the Jefferson, Lincoln, Franklin Delano Roosevelt, World War I, World War II, Korean War Veterans, Vietnam Veterans, and Martin Luther King Jr. memorials; Constitution Gardens; and Pennsylvania Avenue from the Capitol to the White House. About 2,000 American elms line the Mall, and 3,000 Japanese cherry trees grow around the nearby Tidal Basin.
L’Enfant’s plan. The Park Service traces the Mall’s origins to the 1791 plan for the Federal City drawn by Pierre L’Enfant at George Washington’s request.

entries.title: The Underground Railroad
entries.subtitle: Escape from slavery, and the networks that helped freedom seekers reach liberty
entries.summary: The Underground Railroad was not a railroad and not underground. The National Park Service defines it as “the efforts of enslaved African Americans to gain their freedom by escaping bondage,” and the help others gave them. Those helpers included free and enslaved Black people, white abolitionists, American Indians and others. Freedom seekers fled to the North, Canada, Mexico, Spanish Florida, Indian territory, the West, the Caribbean and Europe, sometimes guided by “conductors” such as Harriet Tubman. After the Fugitive Slave Act of 1850 made helping them more dangerous, the networks grew more organized, and the Underground Railroad became, in the Park Service’s words, a “widespread form of civil disobedience.”

cards.a: The Underground Railroad

cards.q: Why does the Underground Railroad matter?
cards.a: The Park Service calls the Underground Railroad “one of the earliest grass roots movements in the United States in which people united across racial, gender, religious, and class lines in hopes of promoting social change.” At its center were the freedom seekers themselves.
The goal was freedom. Enslaved people sought to escape bondage and reach places beyond the reach of recapture.

cards.q: How did it pursue its goals?
cards.a: Escape began at home. The Underground Railroad “started at the place of enslavement.”

entries.title: Theodore Roosevelt
entries.subtitle: Twenty-sixth president and champion of the “Square Deal”
entries.summary: Theodore Roosevelt became president in 1901, at forty-two, after the assassination of William McKinley. He was the youngest person ever to hold the office. Historians often call him the first modern president, because he made the White House, rather than Congress or the parties, the center of American politics. His “Square Deal” used federal power to regulate big business, protect consumers, and conserve the nation’s forests and wild lands. Abroad he built up the Navy, secured the Panama Canal, and declared the United States the “policeman” of the Western Hemisphere. In 1912 he ran again as the candidate of his own Progressive Party.

cards.a: Theodore Roosevelt

Roosevelt changed what Americans expected of a president.

cards.q: What shaped Theodore Roosevelt early in life?
cards.a: Theodore Roosevelt was born in New York City on October 27, 1858, the second of four children of Theodore Roosevelt Sr., a wealthy businessman and philanthropist, and Martha “Mittie” Roosevelt, who had grown up on a Georgia plantation. A sickly child with asthma, “Teedie” resolved as a teenager to “make his body” through gymnastics and weight-lifting, and he remained a lifelong champion of exercise and what he called the “strenuous life.” He was taught at home, traveled with his family in Europe and the Middle East, and entered Harvard College in 1876, where he studied natural history and took up boxing and wrestling. In October 1880 he married Alice Hathaway Lee.

cards.q: What were Theodore Roosevelt’s major achievements?
cards.a: The Square Deal. Roosevelt believed government had the right to regulate big business for the public good, though he did not want to abolish it. In 1902 his Justice Department sued the Northern Securities Company, a giant railroad combination organized by J. P. Morgan and other financiers, under the Sherman Antitrust Act.

entries.title: Thomas Edison
entries.subtitle: Inventor of the phonograph and a practical electric light, and creator of the modern research laboratory
entries.summary: Thomas Edison, a boy with only a few months of schooling who sold newspapers on a Michigan railroad, became one of the most celebrated inventors in American history. At his Menlo Park, New Jersey, laboratory, the first industrial research lab, he invented the phonograph in 1877 and developed a practical electric light and the whole system needed to power it; in 1882 his Pearl Street station began lighting lower Manhattan. Later, at West Orange, he helped create the recording and motion picture industries. To his countrymen he became a living symbol of American ingenuity.

videos.title: Thomas Edison: His Kaleidoscope Mind

cards.a: Inventor of the phonograph and a practical electric light, and creator of the modern research laboratory. Telegrapher; Inventor; Industrialist; Head of the Naval Consulting Board (World War I)
Born February 11, 1847, Milan, Ohio; died October 18, 1931, West Orange, New Jersey

cards.q: Who is this? Inventor of the phonograph and a practical electric light, and creator of the modern research laboratory
cards.a: Thomas Edison
1877: the first machine that could record and play back sound
A carbonized-thread filament burned for 13½ hours; Menlo Park was lit up in December 1879

Edison did not just invent devices; he built complete systems (power plants, wiring, records, film studios) that turned inventions into industries, and his research laboratory became the model for modern corporate science. Electric light, recorded sound, and movies reshaped everyday American life.

cards.q: What shaped Thomas Edison early in life?
cards.a: Thomas Alva Edison was born on February 11, 1847, in Milan, Ohio, the seventh and last child of Samuel and Nancy Edison; when he was seven the family moved to Port Huron, Michigan. He attended school for only a few months.

cards.q: What were Thomas Edison’s major achievements?
cards.a: In 1876 Edison moved to the village of Menlo Park, New Jersey, and built a laboratory equipped to work on any invention, the first research and development lab anywhere, sometimes called his greatest invention.

entries.title: Thomas Jefferson
entries.subtitle: Author of the Declaration of Independence and third president
entries.summary: Thomas Jefferson wrote the Declaration of Independence, served as the first secretary of state and the third president, doubled the size of the nation with the Louisiana Purchase, and founded the University of Virginia. He was the leading voice of a republic of independent farmers, limited government, and religious freedom. He was also a lifelong slaveholder who owned more than 600 people over his lifetime, freed only a handful, and most likely fathered six children with Sally Hemings, an enslaved woman in his household. As Encyclopedia Virginia puts it, each generation has claimed him “on both sides of almost every important question.”

Republican (Democratic-Republican), which he founded with James Madison in the 1790s

Jefferson wrote the creed of the American nation, that “all men are created equal,” and later Americans have used it against the very inequalities he lived with. As president he cut the federal government, doubled the nation’s territory, and built the first opposition party to win power peacefully.

cards.q: What shaped Thomas Jefferson early in life?
cards.a: Jefferson was born on April 13, 1743 (April 2 by the Old Style calendar), at Shadwell, on the Rivanna River in what became Albemarle County, Virginia. His father, Peter Jefferson, was a surveyor and planter who helped make the famous Fry-Jefferson map of Virginia; his mother, Jane Randolph, came from one of the colony’s most powerful families. When his father died in 1757, the fourteen-year-old inherited more than 5,000 acres and about twenty enslaved people. At the College of William and Mary he studied mathematics and science with the Scottish professor William Small and law with George Wythe.

cards.q: What were Thomas Jefferson’s major achievements?
cards.a: Revolutionary. A member of the House of Burgesses from 1769, Jefferson won fame in 1774 with A Summary View of the Rights of British America, which argued that Parliament had no authority over the colonies at all. In the Second Continental Congress he was named to the committee to draft a declaration of independence.

entries.title: Thurgood Marshall
entries.subtitle: Civil rights lawyer and first Black justice of the Supreme Court
entries.summary: Thurgood Marshall was the lawyer who led the legal campaign against segregation and, in 1967, became the first African American justice of the Supreme Court. As chief counsel of the NAACP and director of its Legal Defense and Educational Fund, he won nearly thirty Supreme Court cases, above all Brown v. Board of Education (1954), which struck down school segregation. He then served as a federal appeals judge and as solicitor general before joining the Court, where until 1991 he was a forceful liberal voice for individual and civil rights.

videos.title: Thurgood Marshall and Brown v. Board of Education

cards.a: Civil rights lawyer and first Black justice of the Supreme Court. Chief counsel, NAACP (from 1938); Director, NAACP Legal Defense and Educational Fund (from 1940); Judge, U.S. Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit (1961); Solicitor General (1965–1967); Associate Justice of the Supreme Court (1967–1991)
Born July 2, 1908, Baltimore, Maryland; died January 24, 1993, Bethesda, Maryland

cards.q: Who is this? Civil rights lawyer and first Black justice of the Supreme Court
cards.a: Thurgood Marshall
Lincoln University (B.A. 1930); Howard University Law School (J.D. 1933)

1967–1991; first African American justice
Thurgood Marshall led the legal assault that dismantled segregation and became a pioneering figure on the nation’s highest court.

cards.q: What shaped Thurgood Marshall early in life?
cards.a: Marshall was born on July 2, 1908, in Baltimore, the son of a kindergarten teacher and a railroad dining-car waiter. On his days off, his father took the boys to watch trials and then made them argue legal questions at home, challenging every point.

cards.q: What were Thurgood Marshall’s major achievements?
cards.a: One of Marshall’s first victories forced the University of Maryland’s law school, the school that had rejected him, to admit a Black student. He joined the NAACP’s national staff, succeeded Houston as its chief counsel in 1938, and from 1940 directed the new NAACP Legal Defense and Educational Fund.

entries.title: Ulysses S. Grant
entries.subtitle: Union general who won the Civil War and eighteenth president
entries.summary: Ulysses S. Grant was the Union general who won the Civil War and the eighteenth president of the United States (1869–1877). A quiet tanner’s son who failed at farming and business before the war, he rose in four years to command all Union armies, took Vicksburg, wore down Robert E. Lee’s army, and accepted its surrender at Appomattox. As president he fought for the Fifteenth Amendment and sent troops against the Ku Klux Klan, but scandals among his appointees long dominated his reputation, which historians are now reassessing.

cards.q: Why does Ulysses S. Grant matter?
cards.a: Grant won the war that ended slavery and, as president, tried, more than most Northern leaders of his time, to secure the rights of the people it had freed.

cards.q: What shaped Ulysses S. Grant early in life?
cards.a: Hiram Ulysses Grant was born on April 27, 1822, in Point Pleasant, Ohio, the eldest of six children of a tanner. He hated the stinking tannery and swore he would never work in one as an adult.

cards.q: What were Ulysses S. Grant’s major achievements?
cards.a: When the Civil War began, the Union needed trained officers. Grant turned an unruly Illinois regiment into a disciplined unit and was soon a brigadier general.

entries.title: W. E. B. Du Bois
entries.subtitle: Scholar, editor, and co-founder of the NAACP
entries.summary: W. E. B. Du Bois was the foremost Black intellectual of the early twentieth century and one of its most uncompromising voices for civil rights. The first African American to earn a PhD at Harvard, he pioneered the sociological study of Black life and wrote The Souls of Black Folk (1903), which challenged Booker T. Washington’s accommodation to segregation. He founded the Niagara Movement in 1905, helped found the NAACP in 1909, and for nearly a quarter century edited its magazine, The Crisis. He was also a leader of the Pan-African movement. He died in Ghana on the eve of the 1963 March on Washington.

videos.title: Booker T. Washington and W.E.B DuBois: Crash Course Black American History #22

cards.q: Why does W. E. B. Du Bois matter?
cards.a: Du Bois insisted that Black Americans demand full civil and political equality without compromise, and he used scholarship, journalism, and organizing to press that demand.

cards.q: What shaped W. E. B. Du Bois early in life?
cards.a: William Edward Burghardt Du Bois was born in Great Barrington, Massachusetts, in 1868, three years after the end of the Civil War. The American Yawp and the Library of Congress give 1868.

cards.q: What were W. E. B. Du Bois’s major achievements?
cards.a: The Souls of Black Folk. In 1903 Du Bois published The Souls of Black Folk, a collection of essays that combined history, sociology, and literature. It opened with a prophecy: “The problem of the Twentieth Century is the problem of the color-line.” It described the “double-consciousness” of Black Americans, “this sense of always looking at one’s self through the eyes of others,” and the feeling of being “an American, a Negro; two souls, two thoughts, two unreconciled strivings.” In the chapter “Of Mr. Booker T. Washington and Others,” Du Bois criticized Washington’s accommodationism, which, he said later, had “implicitly abandoned all political and social rights.” Du Bois argued instead that a “Talented Tenth” of educated Black leaders should guide the race and press for civil rights immediately and without compromise.

entries.title: Walt Disney
entries.subtitle: Creator of Mickey Mouse, the animated feature film, and Disneyland
entries.summary: Walt Disney grew up on a Missouri farm and in Kansas City, went bankrupt with his first cartoon studio, and moved to Hollywood with almost nothing. With his brother Roy and the animator Ub Iwerks he created Mickey Mouse, who became a star in Steamboat Willie (1928), a cartoon with synchronized music that became the most successful sound cartoon of its day. His studio made Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs (1937), the first full-length animated feature, and later used television to build a new kind of entertainment empire, crowned by Disneyland in 1955. He won more Academy Awards than anyone in history.

videos.title: Walt Disney: Entrepreneur & Producer | Mini Bio | BIO

cards.a: Creator of Mickey Mouse, the animated feature film, and Disneyland. Animator and cartoon producer; Co-founder of the Walt Disney Studio; Film and television producer; Creator of Disneyland (1955)
Born December 5, 1901, Chicago, Illinois; died December 15, 1966
Debuted in Steamboat Willie (1928); Disney himself was Mickey’s voice
Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs (1937)
Opened in 1955 with financial backing from ABC; Main Street, U.S.A. was modeled on Marceline, Missouri
Holds the record for most Academy Awards won
Presidential Medal of Freedom from Lyndon Johnson

Disney turned animated cartoons into feature-length art and an industry, and pioneered the merging of film, television, merchandise, and theme parks that defines modern entertainment. His sentimental vision of small-town America shaped how generations of Americans imagined childhood and their own past.

cards.q: What shaped Walt Disney early in life?
cards.a: Walter Elias Disney was born on December 5, 1901, in Chicago, the son of Elias and Flora Disney; his brother Roy would later run the business side of his company. In 1906 the family moved to a farm near Marceline, Missouri, where Walt began to draw animals.

cards.q: What were Walt Disney’s major achievements?
cards.a: With $500 borrowed from an uncle, Walt and Roy started the Disney Brothers Studio and sold a series of Alice Comedies. In 1927 they had a hit with Oswald the Lucky Rabbit, until their New York distributor hired away most of the animators and claimed that Universal owned the character.

entries.title: Woodrow Wilson
entries.subtitle: Twenty-eighth president: progressive reformer, wartime leader, and segregationist
entries.summary: Woodrow Wilson, the twenty-eighth president of the United States (1913–1921), was a political scientist who rose within three years from president of Princeton University to the White House. His “New Freedom” reforms created the Federal Reserve and expanded federal regulation of business; he led the nation into World War I and proposed, in his Fourteen Points, a League of Nations to keep the peace. The Senate rejected his treaty, and a stroke left him incapacitated. His vision shaped American internationalism, but he also extended segregation in the federal government and suppressed wartime dissent.

videos.title: Woodrow Wilson's Fourteen Points | History
Woodrow Wilson: The Worst Great President?

cards.a: Twenty-eighth president: progressive reformer, wartime leader, and segregationist. President of Princeton University; Governor of New Jersey; Twenty-eighth president (1913–1921); Architect of the League of Nations
Born December 28, 1856, Staunton, Virginia

cards.q: Who is this? Twenty-eighth president: progressive reformer, wartime leader, and segregationist
cards.a: Woodrow Wilson
1913–1921; Democrat
The New Freedom: tariff reduction, the Federal Reserve Act (1913), regulation of corporations
Neutrality, then war against Germany (1917); the Fourteen Points (1918)
Incapacitated by a stroke in October 1919 for the last seventeen months of his term
Wilson expanded the federal government’s role in the economy and defined a vision of American internationalism, while his own policies showed the racial limits of Progressive-era democracy.

cards.q: What shaped Woodrow Wilson early in life?
cards.a: Thomas Woodrow Wilson was born on December 28, 1856, in Staunton, Virginia, the son of a Presbyterian minister, and grew up in Augusta, Georgia, and Columbia, South Carolina. His earliest memories were of the Civil War: Union soldiers marching into Augusta and his mother nursing wounded Confederates.

cards.q: What were Woodrow Wilson’s major achievements?
cards.a: Wilson taught at Bryn Mawr, Wesleyan, and Princeton, publishing books including a five-volume history of the United States. In 1902 he became Princeton’s first president who was not a clergyman and began remaking it into a modern university, introducing small-group “preceptorials.”
